title: Context parameters in production Kotlin: what the docs don’t emphasise
excerpt: They became Stable in Kotlin 2.4.0. Here’s where they replace a ThreadLocal, where they lose to constructor injection, and what breaks if… Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinJavaSoftware DevelopmentSpring BootBackend DevelopmentContext parameters in production Kotlin: what the docs don’t emphasiseRaphael PantaleãoFollow7 min read·Aug 3, 2026ListenShareThey became Stable in Kotlin 2.4.0. Here’s where they replace a ThreadLocal, where they lose to constructor injection, and what breaks if you reach for them everywhere.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeRunnable code for everything below: kotlin-context-parameters-demoThe problemOpen a service you didn’t write and follow a tenant ID.It arrives on an HTTP header. A filter reads it, a controller receives it, and from there it travels down: controller → service → another service → repository. Four signatures, one consumer. Along the way it picks up company: a trace ID, a locale, an Actor for audit logging. By the time you're three services deep, half your parameter lists are plumbing.So teams do one of two things.They put it in a ThreadLocal, or an MDC, or a coroutine ThreadContextElement. The signatures get clean and the problem moves: now the value is invisible at every call site, and whether it's actually there depends on runtime control flow. Someone launches work on a different dispatcher, the context doesn't propagate, and you find out from a log line with the wrong tenant in it.Or they pass a RequestContext object as the first parameter everywhere. Explicit, honest, and it means every function that merely forwards the context — most of them — has an extra parameter it never reads.Kotlin 2.4.0, released 3 June 2026, made context parameters Stable. They’re the third option: the value is declared, type-checked and lexically scoped like a parameter, but you don’t write it at the call site.What a context parameter actually isA function declares that it needs a value of some type from its surroundings:data class RequestContext( val tenant: String, val traceId: String,)context(ctx: RequestContext)fun loadOrders(): List<Order> = repository.findByTenant(ctx.tenant)loadOrders() takes no parameters. It reads ctx.tenant anyway, because ctx is a context parameter — the compiler supplies it from whatever RequestContext is in scope at the call site.You bring one into scope the way you’d expect:fun handle(request: HttpRequest) { val ctx = request.toRequestContext() with(ctx) { loadOrders() // no argument passed }}If no RequestContext is in scope, loadOrders() doesn't compile. That sentence is the whole value proposition, and it's worth sitting with: the failure mode moved from runtime to compile time.Context parameters work on properties too, and they compose — a function with a context parameter can call another function with the same context parameter without reopening anything, because the context is already in scope inside the callee.context(ctx: RequestContext)fun placeOrder(order: Order): OrderId { // audit() also declares context(ctx: RequestContext), // so it resolves from the context already in scope audit("order.placed") return repository.save(ctx.tenant, order)}That transitivity is what removes the plumbing. Middle-of-the-chain functions declare the context and forward it for free.Where this beats a ThreadLocalThe honest framing is that a ThreadLocal and a context parameter solve the same problem with opposite failure modes.A ThreadLocal fails open at runtime. The compiler is fine with reading it anywhere. Whether a value is there depends on whether some code, somewhere up the stack, set it — and, in a coroutine world, on whether it propagated across every dispatcher switch and every launch. When it doesn't, you get a null, a default, or worse, the previous request's value on a pooled thread.A context parameter fails closed at compile time. Scope is lexical, not dynamic. If you write a function that reads the context and call it from somewhere the context isn’t in scope, the build breaks. There is no propagation to get wrong, because there’s nothing being propagated at runtime — under the hood, the compiler is passing an ordinary argument.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThis is the reason context parameters survive structured concurrency and ThreadLocals need help to. Launching a coroutine inside a with(ctx) { } block keeps the context in lexical scope, so the call inside the coroutine resolves the same way it would anywhere else. No ThreadContextElement, no propagation config, no test that passes on a single-threaded dispatcher and fails in production.The cost is symmetric and you should say it out loud: a ThreadLocal can be introduced into an existing codebase without touching a single signature. Context parameters change signatures. That's not a small difference on a large service.Where constructor injection still winsThis is the part I’d want a reviewer to push me on.Context parameters are good at values that are per-call and ambient: request context, tenant, actor, trace ID, a clock you want to control in tests, a transaction handle scoped to a unit of work.Constructor injection is still better for values that are per-instance and stable: your repositories, HTTP clients, config, the things Spring or Koin already wire once at startup. Nothing about a OrderRepository varies per call, and turning it into a context parameter buys you nothing while making every signature longer and every call site dependent on scope.Get Raphael Pantaleão’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe rule I’ve landed on: if it changes per request, consider a context parameter. If it’s wired at startup, keep it in the constructor.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThere’s a second, blunter test. If a value is needed by exactly one function, don’t make it a context parameter — make it a parameter. Context parameters earn their keep when a value crosses three or more frames.Two details that decide production fitOverload resolution is realTwo functions that differ only by their context parameter are distinct

title: Thinking Like the Compose Runtime — Part 3: How Compose Never Loses Its Place
excerpt: In Part 2, we ended with an important question. Continue reading on Dev Genius »
content: Jetpack ComposeKotlinCompose MultiplatformAndroid App DevelopmentAndroid DevelopmentThinking Like the Compose Runtime — Part 3: How Compose Never Loses Its PlaceNeeraja GandlaFollow5 min read·Aug 3, 20262ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeIn Part 2, we ended with an important question.Every recomposition starts by executing your composable functions again. Yet somehow, the runtime doesn’t treat every execution as a completely new UI.It recognizes that a composable being executed now is the same one that was executed during the previous composition.But how?At first glance, that sounds impossible.A Kotlin function doesn’t remember its previous execution. Every time it’s called, it simply starts from the beginning.@Composablefun Screen() { Header() Message() Footer()}During recomposition, Screen() executes again.So do Header(), Message(), and Footer().Nothing in Kotlin says,“This Header() is the same Header() that executed a few milliseconds ago."As far as the language is concerned, they’re just function calls.So where does this sense of continuity come from?The Runtime Needs More Than ExecutionLet’s imagine Compose didn’t remember anything.The first composition builds the UI.Then a state change happens.The runtime starts recomposition and executes Screen() again.How would it know whether the Message() being executed now corresponds to the Message() from the previous composition?It wouldn’t.Every execution would look completely new.That creates a much bigger problem than simply redrawing the screen.The runtime would have no reliable way to associate any information with a composable across recompositions.And that information is everywhere.Values that should survive recomposition.Information about which state objects were read.Metadata needed to efficiently update the UI.The hierarchy created during the previous composition.Without identity, all of these become meaningless.Before the runtime can remember anything, it first needs to answer a much simpler question.Who am I looking at?Identity Before MemoryImagine you have three people with exactly the same name.If someone tells you,“Rahul called.”you immediately ask,“Which Rahul?”A name alone isn’t enough.You need something that uniquely identifies the person.The Compose Runtime faces a surprisingly similar problem.During recomposition, it sees composable function calls.But how does it know which composable from the previous composition each call corresponds to?The answer begins with something surprisingly simple.Where the composable is called.Call Site IdentityConsider this code.@Composablefun Screen() { Header() Message() Footer()}Even though Header(), Message(), and Footer() are all just composable function calls, each one appears at a different location in the source code.That location is called the call site.The runtime uses the call site as the primary identity of a composable.So when recomposition happens, it doesn’t simply see,“Here’s a call to Header()."Instead, it recognizes,“This is the call to Header() from this exact location in the source code."That becomes the composable’s identity.But What About Loops?Things become more interesting when the same composable is called multiple times.LazyColumn { items(movies) { movie -> MovieCard(movie) }}Every iteration executes the exact same line.The call site is identical.So how does the runtime distinguish one MovieCard() from another?It combines the call site with the order in which the calls occur.The first execution represents the first item.The second execution represents the second item.The third execution represents the third item.Together, the call site and execution order are usually enough to uniquely identify each composable.Until the Order ChangesNow suppose a new movie is inserted at the beginning of the list.Every existing item shifts down by one position.The runtime suddenly observes something like this:Previously:Movie AMovie BMovie CNow:Movie XMovie AMovie BMovie CIf identity were based only on execution order, today’s first MovieCard() would incorrectly be matched with yesterday's first MovieCard().Get Neeraja Gandla’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe runtime would think that Movie A suddenly became Movie X.That’s clearly wrong.This is exactly why Compose provides the key() API.It allows developers to supply a stable identity that remains the same even when execution order changes.We’ll leave key() for a deeper discussion another time.For now, the important idea is this:The runtime must always be able to recognize which composable it is dealing with.Identity comes first.Everything else depends on it.Now Comes the Bigger QuestionSuppose the runtime has successfully identified every composable.Great.Now where does it keep all the information associated with them?Imagine reading a book without bookmarks.Every time you closed it, you’d have to start from page one again.Instead, you place a bookmark exactly where you left off.The next time you open the book, you continue from the same place.The Compose Runtime needs something very similar.It needs a place where it can store information about every composable it encounters during composition.That place is called the Slot Table.Meet the Slot TableDespite its intimidating name, the Slot Table isn’t a table of UI elements.It isn’t a tree of composables either.Think of it as the runtime’s notebook.As the Composer walks through your composable functions, it records information in the Slot Table.Each composable gets an entry associated with its identity.Later, during recomposition, the Composer walks through the same composable hierarchy again.Whenever it recognizes a composable’s identity, it returns to the corresponding location in the Slot Table and continues from there.In other words,the Slot Table doesn’t identify composables.Identity tells the Composer where to look.The Slot Table stores what the Composer knows about

content: NewsletterKotlinAndroidEpisode #38Donald IsoeFollowSent as aNewsletter·4 min read·Aug 3, 20263ListenShareKnow your memeWelcome and BienvenueHello friend. How was your July? Did you invest in sweaters as discussed last month? Did you expand your horizons? Perhaps visited an office you hadn’t been to before? If you came to the last meetup, you already have one of those covered (unless you work there). Okay, enough with the cryptic welcome address.This July, the Kotliners convened at the offices of Terra Softworks Ltd. We had a few new faces and a lot of familiar ones. We talked product, engineering, users, and everything in between. But instead of me trying to summarise it all, why not just show you?Welcome Address: Martin NyagaPress enter or click to view image in full sizeMartin explaining why every startup begins with “Hear me out…”To acknowledge that we had not crashed into an office space unannounced, the CTO of Terra Softworks Ltd, Martin Nyaga, left a recorded message welcoming us to the house he co-built. He gave an inspiring call to action to build, ship, and iterate with intent.Chronos under the Hood — Felix BiegoPress enter or click to view image in full sizeFelix, moments after saying his watch sometimes tiktoksEver wondered how your favourite smartwatch companion app works under the hood? How does your watch talk to your phone and exchange everything from wallpapers to health data? Then I hope you did not miss Felix’s session as he dove into how the Chronos app pushes BLE technology to its limits.Panel Discussion: Beyond the Code — Building Products That Users Love: Valentine Rutto, Annunziata Kinya && Collins MuriukiPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThe joke is Don actually works at Terra and this question made them question their hiring decisions 👀Quick question: how many products do you currently have in production? Have you iterated on user feedback? Ever wondered how industry leaders do it at scale? This panel had plenty of differing opinions, but everyone agreed on one thing: build for users first. We talked about deciding which features deserve attention, which bugs deserve urgency, and why becoming a product engineer often matters more than becoming just a good engineer. Also, that some clients are worth firing 👀👀.Thank You TerraPress enter or click to view image in full sizeSiri, play Amapiano jazz mix.Not only did Terra host us, provide snacks, and generally make us feel at home, their CEO also jumped onto the panel to share his perspective on building products that matter.If you haven’t come across Terra Softworks before, they’re doing some genuinely interesting work with NFC and GPS to solve real-world problems, particularly in education across Sub-Saharan Africa. Give them a follow on Instagram (insert link) or LinkedIn (insert link) and see what they’ve been building.JetBrains says HelloPress enter or click to view image in full sizeOur good friends at JetBrains, the creators of Kotlin, once again sent their support (and gifts 👀) to the community. No, unfortunately they didn’t send free IntelliJ Ultimate licenses for everyone.From active community members to regular speakers, it’s always good to see contributors being recognised by the wider Kotlin ecosystem.DroidCon x FlutterCon Kenya 2026Press enter or click to view image in full sizeWe are well into the third quarter of the year. Meaning, tickets are going fast. Do you have yours yet? Why not? No seriously, I’m curious. If you still intend on attending the biggest mobile event in Subsaharan Africa, you still have time to procure your ticket. Just click here to see more.Before you goThinking about speaking at one of our upcoming meetups?Get Donald Isoe’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inGot a topic, a project, or an idea you can’t stop talking about? This is your chance to share it with the community. Submit a talk, or if crowds aren’t your thing, submit an article instead.We’re always looking for new voices, fresh perspectives, and people ready to teach (or at least attempt to).See you in AugustWe’re looking forward to seeing you in August. title: 13/28: The 16ms Frame Budget Is a Lie (Now)
excerpt: Refresh rates, VRR, and why you actually drop frames Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidPerformanceAospAndroid InternalsKotlin13/28: The 16ms Frame Budget Is a Lie (Now)Pramod PatelFollow7 min read·Aug 3, 2026350ListenShareRefresh rates, VRR, and why you actually drop framesPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThe “frame budget” is just 1000 / refreshRate. At 60Hz it's 16.6ms. At 120Hz it's 8.3ms, less than half. The number every blog quotes is the slowest one.If you're still optimizing to a 16ms frame budget, you're optimizing for a phone from 2014.That number, 16ms, sometimes written 16.6ms, is the single most repeated figure in Android performance advice, and it has a hard dependency nobody says out loud: it is only true at 60Hz. It is literally 1000 / 60. The reciprocal of a refresh rate that stopped being universal years ago. Your users are on 90Hz, 120Hz, 144Hz panels, and the budget on those devices is 11ms, 8.3ms, 6.9ms, and on the newest hardware it isn't even a fixed number anymore. So when you profile to "under 16ms" and your flagship-owning users still report jank, you're not unlucky. You shipped to a budget that's nearly twice too generous for their screen.Where did 16ms even come from?It's not a law of physics. It's arithmetic against one specific assumption.A display refreshes at a fixed cadence, its refresh rate, in hertz. The screen physically scans out a new image that many times per second, and your app gets exactly one shot to have a finished frame ready before each scan-out. Miss it, the screen shows the previous frame again, and the user sees a stutter. So the time you have per frame is the time between scan-outs:budget per frame (ms) = 1000 / refreshRateAt 60Hz that's 1000 / 60 = 16.67ms. At 90Hz it's 11.1ms. At 120Hz it's 8.33ms. At 144Hz it's 6.94ms. The "16ms" everyone quotes is just this formula with the slowest refresh rate plugged in, the one every Android phone happened to ship with a decade ago. The advice fossilized; the hardware didn't.This matters more than it sounds, because the relationship is unforgiving in the wrong direction. A frame that takes 12ms of work is comfortably under budget at 60Hz and drops at 90Hz and 120Hz. You did everything the old advice told you to. You measured. You came in under 16ms. And you still janked on the exact devices your most engaged users paid the most money for.Who actually decides when your frame is due?The display's vsync signal, and Choreographer is the framework's middleman that snaps your frame work to it. That's the clock your whole UI runs on, and it's the entire subject of Episode 10, so I'll keep it to one sentence here: you don't render when you decide to; you render when vsync says go, and the gap between two vsyncs is your budget.The important consequence for this episode is that the budget is not a constant your code carries around. It's a property of the display, read at runtime. And the framework already knows it, which is why the famous "Skipped frames!" warning is computed against the real interval, not against 16ms.What does "Skipped N frames!" actually measure?Everyone has seen this in Logcat:I/Choreographer: Skipped 47 frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread.Most developers read it as a vague scold. It's not vague at all. It's a precise division, and reading the source tells you two things the message hides. Here's doFrame in Choreographer.java:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeChoreographer.doFrame on cs.android.com. jitterNanos is how late this frame is versus its intended vsync; frameIntervalNanos is the real per-frame interval derived from the display's refresh rate. The warning only fires when skippedFrames >= SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT.// frameworks/base/core/java/android/view/Choreographer.javafinal long skippedFrames = jitterNanos / frameIntervalNanos;if (skippedFrames >= SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT) { Log.i(TAG, "Skipped " + skippedFrames + " frames! " + "The application may be doing too much work on its main " + "thread.");}First: skippedFrames is jitterNanos / frameIntervalNanos. frameIntervalNanos is the actual interval for the current display: at 120Hz it's about 8.3 million nanos, not 16. The system divides by the real budget. It always knew the number you've been ignoring.Second, and this is the trap: SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT defaults to 30.private static final int SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT = SystemProperties.getInt( "debug.choreographer.skipwarning", 30);Thirty skipped frames. At 60Hz that's half a second of frozen UI before Logcat says one word. At 120Hz it's a quarter second. The absence of "Skipped frames!" does not mean your app is smooth. It means you haven't stalled for 30 consecutive frames. Single dropped frames, the ones that read as visible hitching during a scroll, never trip this log at all. If you've been using its silence as a green light, you've been grading yourself on a test that only fails catastrophic freezes.So what moves the budget at runtime?Variable refresh rate. On modern panels the refresh rate isn't even fixed for the life of your app. The system raises and lowers it to match content and save power, which means the budget target slides out from under you while you run.Get Pramod Patel’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inAndroid 15 formalized this as Adaptive Refresh Rate (ARR): with the right HAL support, the display continuously adapts its refresh rate to the content's frame rate using discrete VSync steps, rather than being pinned to one mode. You feed the system your intent with the frame rate API, Surface.setFrameRate(...), available since Android 11 (API 30), and it picks a refresh rate to match. A video scene might run the panel at 60Hz; a flung list might push it to 120Hz; an idle screen might drop to 1Hz to save battery.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeVRR/ARR in one picture: as the panel shifts refresh rate to match content and save power, the per-frame budget shifts wi

title: Preventing Race Conditions with Mutex in Kotlin Coroutines
excerpt: Modern mobile applications perform many operations concurrently. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Race ConditionKotlinKotlin CoroutinesAndroidAndroid DevelopmentPreventing Race Conditions with Mutex in Kotlin CoroutinesMohamed NabilFollow5 min read·Aug 3, 2026ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeModern mobile applications perform many operations concurrently.A chat application, for example, may receive messages through a socket connection, synchronize older messages from an API, update a local database, download media files, and refresh the UI almost at the same time.Concurrency improves responsiveness and performance, but it can also introduce bugs that are difficult to reproduce.One of these bugs is a race condition.In this article, we will explore a real-world race condition involving voice-note caching, understand why it happened, and see how Kotlin’s Mutex can solve it without removing the benefits of concurrency.The Real-World ScenarioWhile working on an offline-first chat feature, every incoming message was stored immediately in the local database.This made the local database the single source of truth for the UI.For a text message, the process was simple:Receive messageSave it in the local databaseDisplay it in the conversationVoice notes required additional work:Receive messageSave it in the local databaseDownload the audio fileSave the file in the local cacheUpdate the message with the local file pathAt first, this flow appeared straightforward.The problem was not that multiple different voice notes were downloaded concurrently. Different messages can usually be processed independently without any issue.The actual problem occurred when the same voice-note message could be scheduled for processing from more than one flow at the same time.How Can the Same Message Be Processed Twice?A chat application may receive the same message through different sources.For example, a message may arrive from the real-time socket:Socket event ↓Process message 123At almost the same moment, an API synchronization request may return the same message:API synchronization ↓Process message 123Both flows may now attempt to cache the same voice note.Each coroutine reads the current message state and sees that the voice note has not been downloaded yet.They may then both start the same operation:Coroutine A Coroutine BRead message 123 Read message 123Status: NOT_DOWNLOADED Status: NOT_DOWNLOADEDSet status to DOWNLOADING Set status to DOWNLOADINGDownload the audio file Download the audio fileSave the local file Save the local fileUpdate the database Update the databaseThis creates duplicate work, but duplicate work alone is not necessarily a race condition.The real race appears when the final result depends on which coroutine finishes last.An Example of the Incorrect ResultImagine that the first coroutine completes successfully:Coroutine A:Download completedFile savedStatus updated to DOWNLOADEDThe second coroutine may then fail or get cancelled:Coroutine B:Download failedStatus updated to FAILEDThe final database state becomes: FAILEDHowever, the file was already downloaded successfully by the first coroutine.The opposite can also happen. A cancelled coroutine may reset the state to NOT_DOWNLOADED after another coroutine has already completed the operation.The code may work correctly many times before failing under the right timing conditions.That is what makes race conditions difficult to debug.What Is a Race Condition?A race condition happens when the result of an operation depends on the timing or execution order of concurrent tasks.Consider this simplified example:var counter = 0suspend fun increment() { counter++}The expression counter++ looks like one operation, but internally it involves multiple steps:Read the current valueIncrease the valueWrite the new valueIf two coroutines execute these steps concurrently, they may both read the same value before either writes the result.Some updates can therefore be lost.The same issue can happen with:Cached filesDatabase updatesShared collectionsMessage statesIn-memory application stateThe Naive Global Mutex SolutionKotlin Coroutines provides Mutex for protecting critical sections.A simple solution may look like this:private val cacheMutex = Mutex()suspend fun cacheVoiceNote(message: Message) { cacheMutex.withLock { downloadVoiceFile(message) saveVoiceFile(message) updateLocalMessage(message) }}This prevents concurrent access because only one coroutine can enter the withLock block at a time.However, it also serializes every voice-note download.Even completely independent messages must wait for one another:Download message 100 ↓Download message 200 ↓Download message 300This removes useful concurrency and may significantly slow down media caching.Get Mohamed Nabil’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe goal is not to prevent all voice notes from running concurrently.The goal is to prevent the same voice note from being processed twice at the same time.Tracking Active Message IDsA better approach is to maintain a set containing the IDs currently being processed:private val activeDownloadIds = mutableSetOf<String>()However, MutableSet is shared mutable state.The check and insertion must happen atomically.Without synchronization, code like this is unsafe:if (messageId !in activeDownloadIds) { activeDownloadIds.add(messageId) downloadVoiceNote(messageId)}Two coroutines could both check the set before either of them adds the ID.Both would see that the ID is missing, and both would start the download.We can protect the set using a Mutex:private val activeDownloadsMutex = Mutex()private val activeDownloadIds = mutableSetOf<String>()Then create an atomic claim operation:private suspend fun claimDownload(messageId: String): Boolean = activeDownloadsMutex.withLock { activeDownloadIds.add(messageId) }MutableSet.add() returns:true when the ID was added.false when the ID already existed.This allows us to atomically check and register the operation in one step.Pr

title: Google Play Asked Me to Remove Storage Permissions from My Flutter App — Here’s the Fix
excerpt: Avoid Play Console warnings by migrating to Android Photo Picker and removing unnecessary storage permissions. Continue reading on CodeX »
content: FlutterAndroidGoogle Play Asked Me to Remove Storage Permissions from My Flutter App — Here’s the FixAvoid Play Console warnings by migrating to Android Photo Picker and removing unnecessary storage permissions.Flutter GuruFollow3 min read·Aug 3, 202681ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeStop Requesting Storage Permission in Flutter: Migrate to Android Photo Picker Before Play Store Rejects Your AppIf you’re a Flutter developer, you may have recently received a warning from the Google Play Console asking you to:Upgrade image_picker_androidUpgrade image_picker_platform_interfaceRemove READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, and READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permissionsIf you’re wondering why this is happening and how to fix it, this guide covers everything you need.Why Google Play Is Asking You to ChangeGoogle has tightened its Photo and Video Permissions policy.Apps that only allow users to select photos or videos occasionally should not request broad access to the device’s media library.Instead, they should use the Android Photo Picker, which provides secure access to user-selected files without requiring storage permissions.This improves:User privacySecurityPlay Store complianceUser trustWho Needs to Update?If your Flutter app uses:image_pickerProfile image uploadDocument uploadReceipt uploadAvatar selectionGallery image attachmentVideo selectionthen this migration is for you.If your app is not a gallery app, file manager, backup app, or media editor that genuinely needs full library access, you should migrate.The Good NewsIf you’re already using Flutter’s image_picker, your Dart code probably doesn't need to change.Most of the work involves:Updating packagesRemoving unnecessary permissionsStep 1: Update Your PackagesUpgrade to the latest image_picker.dependencies: image_picker: ^1.2.0If Google specifically asks for newer Android implementations, you can temporarily use:dependency_overrides: image_picker_android: ^0.8.13 image_picker_platform_interface: ^2.10.0Afterwards run:flutter pub upgradeorflutter pub getStep 2: Remove Media PermissionsDelete these permissions from your AndroidManifest.xml.<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES"/><uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VIDEO"/><uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE"/><uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE"/>If another dependency is adding them during manifest merging, explicitly remove them.<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android" xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES" tools:node="remove"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VIDEO" tools:node="remove"/> <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE" tools:node="remove"/></manifest>Step 3: Remove Runtime Permission RequestsMany apps still do this:await Permission.photos.request();await Permission.storage.request();await Permission.videos.request();These are no longer needed for normal image selection with image_picker.Get Flutter Guru’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inSimply remove them.Step 4: Keep Using ImagePicker NormallyYour existing code can remain exactly the same.final picker = ImagePicker();final image = await picker.pickImage( source: ImageSource.gallery,);final video = await picker.pickVideo( source: ImageSource.gallery,);On supported Android versions, Flutter automatically uses the Android Photo Picker behind the scenes.No storage permission dialog appears.Step 5: Verify Your Release BuildAfter building your app:flutter build appbundleCheck the generated bundle.If you still seeREAD_MEDIA_IMAGESREAD_MEDIA_VIDEOREAD_EXTERNAL_STORAGEthen another dependency is adding them.You can inspect the merged manifest with:./gradlew app:processReleaseMainManifestCommon MistakesUsing permission_handler unnecessarilyIf you’re only selecting images from the gallery, don’t request storage permissions.Old image_picker versionsOlder versions don’t fully support Android Photo Picker.Always update to the latest stable release.A dependency reintroduces permissionsSome camera, file picker, or media packages may still declare storage permissions.Inspect your merged manifest before publishing.What If My App Really Needs Full Gallery Access?Some apps legitimately require broad media access, such as:Gallery appsPhoto editorsBackup applicationsFile managersMedia management toolsIn those cases, you may still request the necessary permissions, but you’ll need to justify them in the Google Play Console and comply with Google’s Photo and Video Permissions policy.Benefits of MigratingNo storage permission dialogBetter user privacyEasier Play Store approvalCleaner AndroidManifestLess permission-related codeFuture-proof for upcoming Android versionsFinal ThoughtsGoogle is clearly moving Android toward user-selected media access instead of full storage access. The Android Photo Picker is now the recommended approach for most Flutter apps.For most developers, the migration is surprisingly simple:Update image_pickerRemove storage permissionsStop requesting runtime storage permissionsPublish with confidenceA few minutes of work today can save you from Play Console warnings — or even app update rejections — in the future.ReferencesGoogle Play — Photo and Video Permissions Policy: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/15800983Android Developers — Photo Picker: https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/shared/photopickerFlutter image_picker package: https://pub.dev/packages/image_picker

title: MVVM vs MVI in Android: XML Views and Jetpack Compose, Side by Side
excerpt: By Awais — Android developer, devawais.com Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidMobile App DevelopmentMvvmJetpack ComposeMVVM vs MVI in Android: XML Views and Jetpack Compose, Side by SideMuhammad AwaisFollow5 min read·Aug 3, 202614ListenShareBy Awais — Android developer, devawais.comPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThis image was generated using chatgptI already wrote about when to pick MVVM vs MVI — that’s a separate piece if you want the decision framework without wading through code. This one’s the opposite: no philosophy, just what these two patterns actually look like when you build the same screen four ways — MVVM with XML, MVI with XML, MVVM with Compose, MVI with Compose.Get Muhammad Awais’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inI used the same test case for all four: a “search and filter a list of products” screen, backed by the same repository, same Clean Architecture use case underneath. Only the presentation layer changes. If you want to run them yourself — the snippets here are trimmed for readability.The setupdata class Product(val id: String, val name: String, val price: Double)interface ProductRepository { suspend fun search(query: String): List<Product>}That’s it, that’s the whole domain contract. Everything below is just presentation.MVVM — XML / View systemThe ViewModel exposes several independent StateFlows:class ProductViewModel( private val repository: ProductRepository) : ViewModel() {private val _products = MutableStateFlow<List<Product>>(emptyList()) val products: StateFlow<List<Product>> = _products private val _isLoading = MutableStateFlow(false) val isLoading: StateFlow<Boolean> = _isLoading private val _error = MutableStateFlow<String?>(null) val error: StateFlow<String?> = _error private val _searchQuery = MutableStateFlow("") val searchQuery: StateFlow<String> = _searchQuery fun onSearchQueryChanged(query: String) { _searchQuery.value = query fetchProducts(query) } private fun fetchProducts(query: String) { viewModelScope.launch { _isLoading.value = true try { _products.value = repository.search(query) _error.value = null } catch (e: Exception) { _error.value = e.message } finally { _isLoading.value = false } } }}And the Fragment ends up combining those streams manually, because a derived condition like “show empty state” depends on all three at once:viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { combine(viewModel.products, viewModel.isLoading, viewModel.error) { products, loading, error -> Triple(products, loading, error) }.collect { (products, loading, error) -> emptyStateView.isVisible = products.isEmpty() && !loading && error == null loadingView.isVisible = loading errorView.isVisible = error != null recyclerAdapter.submitList(products) }}searchBar.doOnTextChanged { text, _, _, _ -> viewModel.onSearchQueryChanged(text.toString())}Works fine. But that combine {} block is doing real work the ViewModel could've done for it — and it's the kind of code that gets copy-pasted into every screen that needs a derived UI state.MVI — XML / View systemSame repository, one State object instead of four flows:data class ProductScreenState( val products: List<Product> = emptyList(), val isLoading: Boolean = false, val error: String? = null, val searchQuery: String = "") { val isEmptyStateVisible: Boolean get() = products.isEmpty() && !isLoading && error == null}sealed interface ProductIntent { data class SearchQueryChanged(val query: String) : ProductIntent object Retry : ProductIntent}class ProductViewModel( private val repository: ProductRepository) : ViewModel() { private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ProductScreenState()) val state: StateFlow<ProductScreenState> = _state fun onIntent(intent: ProductIntent) { when (intent) { is ProductIntent.SearchQueryChanged -> search(intent.query) is ProductIntent.Retry -> search(_state.value.searchQuery) } } private fun search(query: String) { _state.update { it.copy(searchQuery = query, isLoading = true, error = null) } viewModelScope.launch { try { val results = repository.search(query) _state.update { it.copy(products = results, isLoading = false) } } catch (e: Exception) { _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = false, error = e.message) } } } }}The Fragment collapses to one collector, and isEmptyStateVisible is a derived property on the State itself — it can never disagree with the rest of the snapshot, because it's computed from the same object, not from streams racing each other:viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.state.collect { state -> emptyStateView.isVisible = state.isEmptyStateVisible loadingView.isVisible = state.isLoading errorView.isVisible = state.error != null recyclerAdapter.submitList(state.products) }}searchBar.doOnTextChanged { text, _, _, _ -> viewModel.onIntent(ProductIntent.SearchQueryChanged(text.toString()))}MVVM — Jetpack ComposeSame multi-field ViewModel from above, consumed with collectAsStateWithLifecycle():@Composablefun ProductScreen(viewModel: ProductViewModel = viewModel()) { val products by viewModel.products.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() val isLoading by viewModel.isLoading.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() val error by viewModel.error.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() val searchQuery by viewModel.searchQuery.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()val isEmptyStateVisible = products.isEmpty() && !isLoading && error == null Column { SearchBar(query = searchQuery, onQueryChanged = viewModel::onSearchQueryChanged) when { isLoading -> LoadingIndicator() error != null -> ErrorView(message = error) isEmptyStateVisible -> EmptyStateView() else -> ProductList(products) } }}This reads fine, but I ran it through the layout inspector’s recomposition counter and noticed each StateFlow triggers its own recomposition independently — including searchQuery updates that happen before products has even arrived. Not a big deal at four fields; it compounds fast at eight or nine.MVI — Jetpack ComposeSame reducer-based ViewModel, one collection point:@Composablefun ProductScreen(viewModel: ProductVi

title: MVVM vs MVI in Android: A Practical Guide to Choosing the Right Architecture
excerpt: By Awais — Senior Mobile App Developer, devawais.com Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android ArchitectureMvvmClean ArchitectureAndroidMobile App DevelopmentMVVM vs MVI in Android: A Practical Guide to Choosing the Right ArchitectureMuhammad AwaisFollow6 min read·Aug 3, 202622ListenShareBy Awais — Senior Mobile App Developer, devawais.comPress enter or click to view image in full sizeThis image was created using CHAT GPTI’m Awais, and I want to start with a confession — I used to think MVI was just MVVM with extra steps. I said that out loud in a code review once and got roasted for it, rightfully so. So I went and actually built the same feature — a fairly boring “search and filter a list of products” screen — in both patterns, back to back, over a weekend, just to settle the argument in my own head.This article is the “which one should I actually use” side of that experiment — no code walkthroughs here, I’ve got a separate implementation-focused piece for that (linked at the bottom, with full XML and Jetpack Compose examples side by side). This one’s for the decision itself: what each pattern is actually good at, where each one quietly falls apart, and how I now decide per-screen instead of picking a side once and defending it forever.If your team is arguing about this in Slack right now — mine did — hopefully this settles it faster than my weekend did.What these two patterns are actually solvingBoth MVVM and MVI exist to separate your UI from your logic. Neither one is “the architecture” for your app — they’re presentation-layer patterns, usually sitting on top of a Clean Architecture setup with use cases and repositories underneath. The real difference between them isn’t philosophical; it’s mechanical: how they handle state.MVVM — Model, View, ViewModel. The ViewModel exposes state, often as several independent LiveData or StateFlow fields (loading, data, error, and so on). The View observes each of them and calls functions on the ViewModel in response to user actions.MVI — Model, View, Intent. The View sends Intents — user actions represented as data — into the ViewModel, which acts as a reducer and produces one single, immutable State object. The View has exactly one thing to render.That “one state object vs several independent fields” distinction is the whole ballgame. Every pro and con below traces back to it.Where MVVM genuinely shinesI want to say this clearly, because a lot of MVI-evangelist content makes MVVM sound broken, and it isn’t:Lower learning curve. Almost every Android dev already half-knows this pattern from tutorials, docs, and general industry exposure.Less boilerplate for simple screens. A settings toggle or a static info screen doesn’t need a sealed Intent hierarchy — that’s just ceremony for something trivial.Deep tooling alignment. Data Binding, LiveData, and ViewModel scoping were largely designed with MVVM assumptions in mind, so things tend to “just work.”Faster to prototype. If you’re quickly validating a UI idea, MVVM gets you there with less setup.Where MVVM starts to hurtThe problem shows up the moment a screen needs a derived condition — say, an “empty state” that depends on loading, data, and error all being in a specific combination at once. You end up combining several independent streams manually in the View to answer “what should actually be on screen right now.”Get Muhammad Awais’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inAnd that’s the real issue: nothing structurally stops your state fields from drifting out of sync with each other. You can genuinely end up with isLoading = true and non-empty data at the same moment, for a fraction of a frame, and now your UI is defensively guessing what's "really" happening instead of just rendering a fact.State fragmentation across multiple independent fields.Debugging is harder — there’s no single “here’s exactly what the screen looked like at 3:42:10pm” snapshot to inspect.Testing gets awkward past five or six interacting fields; you end up combining them manually in tests too.Encourages state-combination logic to leak into the View layer, which is exactly where you don’t want business-adjacent logic living.Where MVI genuinely shinesSingle source of truth. One state, one render function. This alone eliminates a whole category of “how did the UI get into this combination” bugs.Predictable and testable. Every state transition is a near-pure function of (currentState, intent), so you can unit test the reducer without touching a single Android framework class.Trivial state logging and time-travel debugging, since every emission is a complete snapshot you can just log and replay.Scales well on genuinely stateful screens — checkout flows, multi-step forms, anything with a lot of conditional UI.Fits naturally with Clean Architecture and unidirectional data flow, if your domain layer already returns sealed Result types from use cases — MVI just continues that same philosophy up into the presentation layer instead of breaking it.Where MVI starts to hurtMore boilerplate up front — a sealed Intent hierarchy, a State data class, often a separate Effect channel for one-off events.Genuinely overkill for simple screens. I wouldn’t reach for full MVI on a static “About” page.Real learning curve for teams new to unidirectional data flow — “why can’t I just update this one field” is a question I’ve answered more than once.Without discipline, you can still end up with a 300-line when block in the reducer — it's one big function instead of scattered fields, but it's still a mess if nobody's watching it.So how do I actually decide, per screenI stopped treating this as an ideological, project-wide choice a while ago. It’s a per-screen decision now, and here’s roughly the checklist I run through:Reach for MVVM when:The screen has one to three independent pieces of state that genuinely don’t interact much — a settings screen is the classic example.You’re prototyping, and speed matters more than long-term maintainability right now.Junio

title: Reality : Anxiety Is Real And I Think We All Have It
excerpt: Do you know that strange dread that washes over you when you close TikTok and just sit there? That’s not boredom. That’s reality anxiety. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Mental HealthAISocial MediaAndroidPapercraft PublisherReality : Anxiety Is Real And I Think We All Have ItPapercraft PublishersFollow3 min read·Aug 3, 2026ListenShareDo you know that strange dread that washes over you when you close TikTok and just sit there? That’s not boredom. That’s reality anxiety.Almost every Gen Z I know experiences it.We grew up with a phone in our hand, an algorithm giving us a dopamine hit every eight seconds. We got accustomed to life being fast, loud, edited, and filtered. Now, real life feels slow, quiet, and unedited. Our brains struggle to handle this shift. The moment we’re not stimulated, we panic. We call it "being bored," but it’s really anxiety. Anxiety that nothing’s happening. Anxiety that we might be missing out. Anxiety that if we’re not scrolling, producing, or posting, we’re falling behind.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe issue is we never learned how to just exist. We learned to react. To a trend, to a meme, to other people’s lives. But sitting with your own thoughts, without music, a screen, or a plan? That feels wrong. It feels like wasting time. I caught myself feeling guilty for taking a 20-minute walk without a podcast. It seemed like I should’ve been "using that time" for something. That’s crazy.Reality anxiety shows up in small ways. Checking your phone mid-conversation. Needing background noise to fall asleep. Feeling restless on weekends. Thinking you must turn everything into content or it didn’t count. We’re so afraid of missing out that we miss living our own lives.I don’t think the solution is deleting everything and moving to the mountains. But I do believe we need to retrain our brains to be okay with being bored. Boredom is where ideas are born. Calm is where healing happens. Silence is where you truly hear yourself.Get Papercraft Publishers’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inSo, I’m trying this: 10 minutes a day with no phone. No music. No goal. Just me and my thoughts. The first week was torture. Now it’s the only time I feel like myself again.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeIf you’ve ever felt anxious for no reason after putting your phone down, that’s it. That’s reality anxiety. And you’re not broken. You’re just overstimulated.Let’s start getting comfortable with real life again. One boring, quiet, unproductive minute at a time.

title: How I Built a Flipkart-Style Order Tracking Timeline in Flutter
excerpt: When we shop online, one of the first things we check after placing an order is where our package has reached. Continue reading on Medium »
content: FlutterAndroidIOSOrder TrackingDartHow I Built a Flipkart-Style Order Tracking Timeline in FlutterAnkit MehraFollow4 min read·Aug 3, 20261502ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhen we shop online, one of the first things we check after placing an order is where our package has reached. Whether it’s a phone, a pair of shoes, or groceries, tracking the delivery has become a normal part of the shopping experience.Apps like Flipkart make this experience simple by displaying every stage of an order in a clean vertical timeline. Instead of showing only the current status, they let us see the complete journey — from order placement to delivery — along with timestamps for each update.Recently, I wanted to add a similar tracking experience to one of our Flutter applications. Rather than building the entire timeline from scratch, I explored an approach that provides a smooth animated order tracker while still allowing customization of the tracking information.In this article, i will explain that how i implemented a Flipkart-style order tracking timeline in Flutter and how easily it can be integrated into any e-commerce, food delivery, pharmacy, or logistics application.Why we should add an Order Tracking Timeline?An order tracking screen is much more than a progress indicator.It helps users:(i). Understand the current delivery stage.(ii). See every completed milestone.(iii). Reduce uncertainty after placing an order.(iv). Improve trust in the application.(v). Get a familiar shopping experience similar to popular e-commerce apps.Even if your application isn’t an online shopping platform, this type of timeline works well for:(i). Food delivery(ii). Medicine delivery(iii). Courier services(iv). Laundry applications(v). Parcel tracking(vi). Service booking appsAdding the DependencyWe have to add the order_tracker package in our pubspec.yaml file.dependencies: order_tracker: ^0.0.2Then we have to run this command for install this package.flutter pub getPreparing the Tracking DataEach stage contains a title and an optional date.List<TextDto> orderList = [ TextDto( "Your order has been placed", "Fri, 25th Mar '22 - 10:47pm", ), TextDto( "Seller has processed your order", "Sun, 27th Mar '22 - 10:19am", ), TextDto( "Courier partner picked up your order", "Tue, 29th Mar '22 - 5:00pm", ),];The same structure can be used for every delivery stage.List<TextDto> shippedList = [ TextDto( "Your order has been shipped", "Tue, 29th Mar '22 - 5:04pm", ), TextDto( "Package reached the nearest hub", null, ),];List<TextDto> outForDeliveryList = [ TextDto( "Your order is out for delivery", "Thu, 31st Mar '22 - 2:27pm", ),];List<TextDto> deliveredList = [ TextDto( "Your order has been delivered", "Thu, 31st Mar '22 - 3:58pm", ),];Keeping every milestone in a separate list makes the tracking information much easier to organize and update.Building the TimelineOnce the data is ready, displaying the tracker only requires a single widget.OrderTracker( status: Status.delivered, activeColor: Colors.green, inActiveColor: Colors.grey[300], orderTitleAndDateList: orderList, shippedTitleAndDateList: shippedList, outOfDeliveryTitleAndDateList: outForDeliveryList, deliveredTitleAndDateList: deliveredList,)The widget automatically displays the completed steps and highlights the current delivery status.Understanding the StatusThe status property controls which step is currently active.Get Ankit Mehra’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inFor example:Status.ordershows that the order has just been placed.Status.shippedupdates the UI until the shipping stage.Status.outOfDeliverymarks the package as out for delivery.Status.deliveredcompletes the entire tracking timeline.Changing a single value is enough to update the complete progress indicator.Customizing the AppearanceThe timeline can easily match your application’s branding.activeColor: Colors.green,inActiveColor: Colors.grey.shade300,The active color highlights completed milestones, while inactive sections remain subtle until they are completed.This small customization helps maintain visual consistency with the rest of the application.Where this UI can be usedAlthough this design is commonly seen in shopping applications, it works well in many other scenarios.(i). Online shopping(ii). Grocery delivery(iii). Food delivery(iv). Medicine delivery(v). Courier tracking(vi). Laundry services(vii). Home service booking(viii). Document delivery(ix). Repair service trackingAny workflow that moves through multiple stages can benefit from this timeline layout.Things to keep in mindBefore integrating this into a production application, consider a few improvements.(i). Fetch tracking data from an API instead of hardcoding it.(ii). Update the timeline in real time whenever the order status changes.(iii). Localize timestamps for different regions.(iv). Display estimated delivery dates.(v). Show courier information and tracking IDs.(vi). Handle cancelled or returned orders.(vii). Add notifications whenever the order moves to the next stage.These additions create a much more complete delivery experience.Final ThoughtsOrder tracking has become an expected feature in modern applications. Users don’t just want to know that an order exists — they want to follow its entire journey.By implementing a Flipkart-style tracking timeline, we can present every delivery milestone in a clean, familiar, and easy-to-understand format. The implementation is straightforward, requires very little code, and significantly improves the overall user experience.If your Flutter application includes deliveries, bookings, shipments, or service requests, adding a timeline like this is a simple way to make the experience feel more polished and professional.

title: Update Your Target API Level by August 31, 2026: What It Means, Why It Matters, and How to Prepare
excerpt: Google Play’s latest Target API Level requirement is approaching. Here’s everything Android developers need to know before the August 31… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidAndroid DevelopmentGoogle PlayMobile DevelopmentAndroid StudioUpdate Your Target API Level by August 31, 2026: What It Means, Why It Matters, and How to PrepareAmitGuptaAppschanceFollow5 min read·Aug 3, 20269ListenShareGoogle Play’s latest Target API Level requirement is approaching. Here’s everything Android developers need to know before the August 31, 2026 deadline.Every year, Google updates its Target API Level requirements for apps published on the Google Play Store. If you’re an Android developer, you’ve probably received an email or Play Console notification that says:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeUpdate your target API level by August 31, 2026.For many developers, especially solo developers and startups, this notification can be stressful.Questions immediately come to mind:Will my app be removed from Google Play?Do I need to rewrite my application?Will existing users lose access?What happens if I miss the deadline?How long will it take to update?The good news is that there’s no need to panic. However, this isn’t something you should postpone until the last week of August.Let’s break everything down.What Is Target API Level?Every Android application includes two important SDK versions:Minimum SDK (minSdk) — The oldest Android version your app supports.Target SDK (targetSdk) — The Android version your app is optimized and tested for.Example:android { compileSdk 36 defaultConfig { minSdk 24 targetSdk 36 }}The Target SDK tells Android:“This app understands the latest Android behaviors, permissions, privacy rules, and security requirements.”Why Does Google Increase the Target API Every Year?Android evolves rapidly.Each Android version introduces improvements such as:Better privacy controlsImproved securityBackground execution limitsBattery optimizationsNew permissionsBetter performanceEnhanced user experienceGoogle wants developers to adopt these improvements so users have a safer and more consistent experience across the Play Store.Why This Update MattersMany developers think:“My app works perfectly. Why should I update?”The answer is simple.Google Play is constantly raising quality standards.Apps targeting very old Android versions may not support:Latest privacy protectionsModern permission modelsCurrent Play policiesSecurity improvementsKeeping your Target SDK updated helps ensure compatibility with new Android devices.What Happens If You Ignore the Deadline?If your app doesn’t meet Google’s required Target API Level after August 31, 2026, the consequences depend on your app’s status and Play policies.Possible outcomes include:You may not be able to publish updates.Your app may become less discoverable for users on newer Android versions.New submissions using older Target SDK versions may be rejected.Google announces these requirements well in advance to give developers enough time to prepare.Do Existing Apps Need Immediate Changes?Not necessarily.If your app is stable and actively maintained, updating the Target SDK is often straightforward.However, newer Android versions introduce behavioral changes that may require code updates and additional testing.Common Issues Developers Face After Updating1. Notification PermissionAndroid now requires explicit user permission before sending notifications on newer versions.If your app relies on notifications, you should implement the new permission flow.2. Storage AccessLegacy storage APIs have changed significantly.Apps should use:Media PickerScoped StorageStorage Access Frameworkwhere appropriate.3. Background ServicesAndroid continues to restrict background execution.Long-running background services should be reviewed and updated.4. Foreground ServicesForeground services now require more specific declarations depending on the task being performed.5. Exact AlarmsApps using alarms should review whether they require special permissions on newer Android versions.6. Camera and Media PermissionsPermission requests are becoming more granular.Instead of requesting broad access, developers should request only what’s necessary.How to Update Your ProjectStep 1Update Android Studio.Use the latest stable version.Step 2Update Gradle.Get AmitGuptaAppschance’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inUpgrade:Android Gradle PluginGradle WrapperStep 3Update Compile SDK.compileSdk 36Step 4Update Target SDK.targetSdk 36Step 5Update Dependencies.Review:AndroidX librariesFirebase SDKsGoogle Play ServicesBilling LibraryWorkManagerCameraXML KitThird-party librariesOlder dependencies may not support the latest Target SDK.Step 6Run Full Testing.Verify:LoginSignupNotificationsDeep LinksCameraGalleryPaymentsPush NotificationsBackground SyncFile UploadDownloadsTesting is the most important step.Don’t Just Increase the NumberOne common mistake developers make is changing:targetSdk = 36and immediately publishing.This approach can introduce unexpected crashes or behavioral issues.Instead:Read Android behavior changes.Fix deprecated APIs.Resolve warnings.Test on multiple Android versions.Best PracticesKeep Dependencies UpdatedDon’t wait several years before upgrading.Smaller updates are much easier to manage.Use Firebase CrashlyticsMonitor crashes after rollout.Fix issues before expanding the release.Roll Out GraduallyInstead of releasing to everyone:Internal TestingClosed TestingOpen TestingProductionThis helps catch problems early.Read Release NotesEvery Android release includes behavior changes.Understanding them saves hours of debugging.Tips for Solo DevelopersIf you’re maintaining apps alone:✅ Upgrade incrementally.✅ Test on Android 13, 14, 15, and the latest supported version.✅ Backup your project before updating.✅ Review all third-party SDK compatibility.✅ Don’t update on the deadline day.What About New Developers?If you’re publishing your first Android application, remember that updating the Target API Level is only one part of the process.Many new personal de

title: How to Use Crunchyroll for Free in 2025 — Every Option Explained
excerpt: Crunchyroll's premium plan not fitting your budget? Here's a complete, honest breakdown of every free option available — from the official… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AnimeCrunchyrollAndroidStreamingTechnologyHow to Use Crunchyroll for Free in 2025 — Every Option ExplainedCRUNCHYROLL MOD APKFollow5 min read·Aug 3, 2026ListenShareCrunchyroll's premium plan not fitting your budget? Here's a complete, honest breakdown of every free option available — from the official trial to the MOD APK — and what each one actually gives you.---Crunchyroll is the largest dedicated anime streaming platform on the internet. Over 25,000 titles, same-day simulcast from Japan, HD quality, manga access — all in one app. The problem is what the free tier withholds.Ads between scenes. A seven-day delay on new episodes that exists purely as a business decision, not a technical constraint. Standard definition video on a phone that costs $600. Every restriction is deliberate, and the intention is to make paying feel like relief.For a lot of people, $7.99 a month is fine. For students, or anyone in a country where that price converts into something that requires real thought — particularly users checking the Crunchyroll subscription price in India — the math doesn't always work out.So what are the actual options?---OPTION 1 — THE OFFICIAL FREE TIERCrunchyroll's free account still works. You get a limited catalog, ads throughout every episode, and a seven-day simulcast delay. It's legal, completely safe, and costs nothing. If you watch casually and don't mind ads, this is enough.Just download the app from the Play Store or App Store, create an account with your email, and start watching. No payment details required.---OPTION 2 — THE 14-DAY FREE TRIALCrunchyroll offers an official 14-day free trial on any paid plan. During those two weeks you get:- The full catalog — all 25,000+ titles- Same-day simulcast with no delay- HD and Ultra HD quality- Zero ads- Offline downloads (on Mega Fan and above)If you're considering subscribing, use the trial to actually test the platform first. Canceling is straightforward — go to Account Settings, click Manage Subscription, and cancel. Your access continues until the end of the billing period.---OPTION 3 — CRUNCHYROLL MOD APKThis is the option most people search for.APK stands for Android Package Kit — the file format every Android app ships in. A modified APK is the original app file with a targeted code change applied. For Crunchyroll, that change is specific: the subscription verification layer is bypassed. The code that checks for an active paid account before unlocking premium content simply doesn't run.Everything else in the app is untouched. Same interface, same video player, same search. Streams come from Crunchyroll's own servers — content, licensing, and delivery quality are identical to what paying subscribers receive. The current stable version is 3.113.2.WHAT THE MOD UNLOCKS:- Zero ads — pre-roll, mid-roll, and post-roll all removed- Full catalog — every title on the platform, no playback walls- Same-day simulcast — no seven-day delay- HD and 4K quality — the SD cap is gone- Offline downloads — officially a $9.99 Mega Fan exclusive, free here- Manga library and Game Vault — both officially behind the $14.99 Ultimate plan- All language tracks — Japanese, English, Hindi, Portuguese, Arabic, German, Spanish and more with no regional locksGet CRUNCHYROLL MOD APK’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inHOW TO INSTALL IT:Step 1 — Enable unknown sourcesSettings → Security → Unknown Sources. On Android 8 and above this is a per-app permission; your phone will prompt you automatically when you open the APK file.Step 2 — Download from a verified sourceOnly download from sources with active community discussion, where users are tracking specific version numbers and confirming working builds. Skip sites with no visible community, surveys before the download link, or aggressive pop-up redirects.Step 3 — Scan with VirusTotal firstGo to virustotal.com, upload the APK before opening it. Free service, 70+ antivirus engines, under a minute. Do not skip this step regardless of how trustworthy the source looks.Step 4 — Uninstall the official Crunchyroll appThe MOD and the official app conflict during installation.Step 5 — Install and verifyOpen the file, confirm the permission prompt, done in under a minute. If the full catalog is accessible and no ads appear, the install worked.IMPORTANT: The file itself is not the risk — the source is. Anyone can attach malicious code to an APK and redistribute it under the same name. VirusTotal scanning and community-verified sources are both non-negotiable.ACCOUNT AND BAN RISK:Full catalog access works without signing into any account. If you want watch history and cross-device sync, use a secondary Google account — not your primary Crunchyroll profile. Crunchyroll's systems can flag accounts accessing premium content without active subscriptions, and bans have been reported consistently enough to take seriously.RUNNING IT ON PC:Install BlueStacks from the official BlueStacks site, use the Install APK sidebar option, and select the MOD file. Apple Silicon Macs (M1, M2, M3) are natively supported. For low-RAM machines, LDPlayer is a lighter alternative with the same installation process.---OPTION 4 — FREE ALTERNATIVES TO CRUNCHYROLLIf the MOD route feels like too many steps, these platforms cover a lot of ground for free:- Zoro.to / Aniwatch — Browser-based, no account needed, large catalog, genuinely ad-free. The lowest-friction free option and works on any device including PC.- 9anime — Broader regional coverage, more ads than Zoro, solid for filling catalog gaps.- Anime Pahe — Built for slow connections and older devices. Smaller catalog but reliable where bandwidth is limited.- Tubi — Fully licensed, ad-supported, completely free. Better anime selection than most people expect, weighted toward completed series.- Funimation — Merging into Crunchyroll but still operational. Strong English dub library.None of these match Crunchyroll's

When the costs started rising, of course we noticed – and realized that we simply didn’t know how to control them systematically. We didn’t know because our developers don’t just use the AI tools we build. They decide for themselves which ones will best help them get their jobs done. Most of them use between three and five AI tools in a given month. They’re using our IDEs as much as ever – it’s just that now they’ve added more CLI agents, agentic development environments (for running several AI agents in parallel), and IDE-integrated AI tools into the mix. Most JetBrains devs use at least three AI tools.They’re using all those tools in and alongside our IDEs. One way to address the problem of ballooning costs would be to limit the number of AI tools our developers can use. In discussions with people from other companies, we often hear about decisions to use just one or two options. That would potentially reduce entropy and limit the overhead of managing everything. However, limiting ourselves in this way would likely cause us to miss out on the best options at any given time. This week the best setup is Claude Code on Opus models, tomorrow it’s Codex, and next week it might be Claude Code on a mix of GLM and Opus. Ideally there should be a balance between developer freedom and managing this “tooling zoo” in terms of cost, efficiency, budgeting, compliance, and security. Here’s how we’ve tried to strike that balance. Initial pain pointsCopy heading link Skyrocketing costs. Starting in January 2026, we saw a sharp rise in the adoption of AI tools, along with an increase in token consumption. We attribute this spike to the release of the Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6 models, which significantly improved agent performance. JetBrains developers began using these models in various places, like Claude Code CLI, the AI chat in JetBrains IDEs, and Junie. After that, usage started almost doubling every month. Soon enough, we hit 150 Claude Code seats and moved onto the Enterprise plan with rates based on API usage. That’s when costs really took off. Our AI spend increased roughly 10x in the first half of 2026. Admin headaches. Average consumption per developer was rising. So was the number of developers who wanted access to different tools – to compare Claude Code to Codex or to try third-party agents, for example. Several people needed to sign off on each request. The tickets piled up for administrators, and the wait times slowed down developers. Experimenting our way to a solutionCopy heading link Manual spreadsheet work → unsustainable Copy heading link Our tooling zoo had grown to include the various agents available through the AI сhat in JetBrains IDEs, as well as Junie CLI, the CLI and desktop versions of Claude Code and Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and a long tail of other tools. To start forecasting and managing this growth – as well its costs – we manually opened up different consoles, downloaded data, and grouped it across several dimensions by department and business unit. This one-time exercise took four days. We had a snapshot of the situation and not much else when it came to setting organizational usage or managing them on an ongoing basis. This was a reasonable start, but that time commitment obviously made it an unsustainable approach moving forward. Internal dashboards → ongoing expenses read-only Copy heading link Most AI tools, including JetBrains ones, have centralized APIs that allow you to pull per-user usage data. We put together a couple of quick-and-dirty solutions that did so (and tried a few more polished third-party ones) and combined the results into dashboards mapped to our organizational structure. This allowed us to drill down into ongoing expenses, but we still couldn’t set or enforce spending limits conveniently. Internal console and a CLI wrapper → the winning prototypeCopy heading link For our own AI tools, we already had a management console with analytics for consumption and efficiency baked in.
