content: AidlBinder IpcAndroidAndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentMaster Android Binder IPC & AIDL with a Hands-On Jetpack Compose ExampleD I N E S HFollow5 min read·6 days ago48ListenShareHave you ever wondered how your Android app communicates with system services like LocationManager or CameraManager under the hood? Or how two completely separate Android apps can talk to each other securely?In Android, process isolation is a core security boundary: every app runs in its own Linux process with a dedicated sandboxed Process ID (PID). One app cannot directly access another app’s memory space. To bridge this gap, Android provides Binder IPC (Inter-Process Communication) and AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language).Press enter or click to view image in full sizeIn this article, we’ll break down Android Binder IPC and AIDL in a friendly, practical, step-by-step format. We’ll explore an my project reference implementation, Android-Binder-IPC-AIDL-Example, which demonstrates cross-process communication between a Jetpack Compose client app and a remote background service app.💡 What is AIDL?AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language) is an IDL syntax used to define the programming interface that both the client and service agree upon for inter-process communication.Get D I N E S H’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inBecause processes cannot share memory, objects must be broken down into primitives that the OS can understand and marshal across process boundaries.How AIDL Works Under the HoodYou write a .aidl file defining interface methods.The Android SDK compiler (aidl) reads this file and auto-generates a Java/Kotlin interface.Inside this generated interface, the compiler creates two key components:Stub: An abstract inner class that extends Binder and lives on the Server process. It unmarshals incoming data packets (Parcels) and executes the actual method implementation.Proxy: A client-side representation created when calling Stub.asInterface(IBinder). It marshals method calls and arguments into Parcels and sends them to the kernel Binder driver.🛡️ Why Binder IPC MattersWhy does Android use Binder instead of standard Linux sockets, shared memory, or local HTTP servers?Security & Identity Verification: Binder operates inside the Linux kernel. The kernel injects sender UID (User ID) and PID metadata into every transaction. A client cannot forge its identity when invoking a service.Performance (Single-Copy Transmission): Binder uses mmap() to map shared memory between process user spaces and kernel space. Data is copied only once from the sender process into kernel memory mapped to the receiver.Reference Counting & Lifecycle: Binder automatically tracks process references. If a client app crashes, the service receives a BinderDeathRecipient notification to clean up resources.Microkernel Architecture: Android’s system architecture relies on decoupled services (WindowManager, ActivityManager, AudioService) running in isolated processes while exposing Binder endpoints to client applications.🏗️ How This Repo WorksThe reference repository Android-Binder-IPC-AIDL-Example is structured as a clean Gradle multi-module project:SampleBinderIPC/├── :shared --> Holds the common .aidl contract├── :server --> Background service providing random color generation└── :client --> Jetpack Compose UI consuming remote service callsLet’s dive into the code implementation across these three modules.1. The Common Contract (:shared)The shared module contains the AIDL file IAIDLColorInterface.aidl. This file defines the contract between the server and the client.// IAIDLColorInterface.aidlpackage com.fierydinesh.binderipc.shared;interface IAIDLColorInterface { // Generates a random color integer int getColor();}Both the :client and :server modules include :shared as a dependency so they inherit the generated interface.2. The Remote Service (:server)The server process exposes the service via AIDLColorService.kt. It implements IAIDLColorInterface.Stub() and returns this Binder reference in onBind().class AIDLColorService : Service() { override fun onBind(intent: Intent): IBinder { Log.d("AIDLColorService", "onBind() called") return binder } // Server-side implementation of the generated Stub private val binder = object : IAIDLColorInterface.Stub() { override fun getColor(): Int { Log.d("AIDLColorService", "getColor() executed on server") return Color.rgb( Random.nextInt(256), Random.nextInt(256), Random.nextInt(256) ) } }}In the server’s AndroidManifest.xml, the service is exported with an explicit <intent-filter> action so foreign processes can discover and bind to it:<service android:name=".AIDLColorService" android:enabled="true" android:exported="true"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="AIDLColorService" /> </intent-filter></service>3. The Jetpack Compose Client (:client)The client application’s MainActivity.kt binds to the remote service, converts the returned IBinder object into the AIDL interface proxy using IAIDLColorInterface.Stub.asInterface(), and triggers remote calls when the user interacts with the UI.class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() { var iaidlColorInterface: IAIDLColorInterface? = null // Handles connection lifecycle callbacks private var connection = object : ServiceConnection { override fun onServiceConnected(name: ComponentName?, service: IBinder?) { // Convert remote IBinder reference to typed Proxy interface iaidlColorInterface = IAIDLColorInterface.Stub.asInterface(service) Log.d("CLIENT_APP", "Connected to remote AIDL service") } override fun onServiceDisconnected(name: ComponentName?) { iaidlColorInterface = null } } override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) { super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) // Bind to remote server process using explicit package intent val intent = Intent("AIDLColorService").apply { setPackage("com.fierydinesh.binderipcserver") } bindService(intent, connection, BIND_AUTO_CREATE

title: ReTect: A Two-Layer Model for Protecting Android Apps Against Reverse Engineering
excerpt: Every Android app you ship can be taken apart. The APK is not a locked box — it’s a readable archive. With tools like jadx and Frida, an… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidReverse EngineeringKotlinSoftware DevelopmentSoftware EngineeringReTect: A Two-Layer Model for Protecting Android Apps Against Reverse EngineeringFarman Ullah MarwatFollow8 min read·6 days ago10ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeEvery Android app you ship can be taken apart. The APK is not a locked box — it’s a readable archive. With tools like jadx and Frida, an attacker pulls out your keys, your URLs, your logic, and your business rules in an afternoon. This isn’t a rare, advanced threat. It’s the default condition of shipping on Android, and it applies to your app right now.The instinct is to fight this by hiding better — more obfuscation, stronger client-side encryption, one clever check. That instinct is a trap. Anything the app can read, an attacker can eventually read too, because the key and the logic sit in the same binary you handed them. You cannot win by hiding a secret inside something you gave away.So stop trying to make the app un-crackable. Make it not worth cracking.That’s the idea behind ReTect — from Reduce & Detect — a two-layer model:Reduce — shrink the attack surface so that even a fully cracked APK yields nothing usable. No live keys, no free compute, no logic worth stealing. The vault is empty before anyone breaks in.Detect — RASP, Runtime Application Self-Protection. Assume the device is already compromised and make the runtime hostile: catch emulators, root, hooking, and tampering, and respond quietly.The reason it’s two layers and not one is that each covers the other’s failure. Detect will eventually be bypassed — every runtime check can be. But if Reduce did its job, that bypass buys the attacker nothing, because there was never anything valuable on the device to begin with. Reduce guarantees the payoff is zero; Detect raises the cost of even trying.For a team, this reframes the whole conversation. The question stops being “is our app secure?” — no client is — and becomes “if this APK is fully cracked tomorrow, what do we actually lose?” ReTect is how you make the honest answer to that question: nothing that matters.Layer 1 — Reduce: don’t ship what you can’t afford to loseThe rule for this layer is one sentence: the client is untrusted. Treat every value in the APK as already public, and every request from the app as something a script can forge. Then design so none of it matters.Never ship an API key. Proxy it.This is the single most abused mistake in Android apps. You’re given a third-party key — say a Gemini key for AI — and the fast path is to drop in their SDK, or fetch their API straight from the app, with the key sitting in the code.Don’t. That key is now in the APK, and the APK is readable. Someone greps your binary, pulls the key, and runs your paid AI quota into the ground on their own project — billed to you.The fix is not to hide the key better. It’s to never put it on the device. Stand up your own backend, keep the key server-side, and let the app call your server. Your server calls Gemini and passes the result back.App → Your Server (holds the key) → Gemini → back to AppThe device never sees the key, never talks to the provider directly, and you now have one choke point where you can rate-limit, revoke, and monitor. A key in the APK is a key that’s already leaked.Never give free, anonymous access to expensive operations“If you can see it, you can steal it.”A free, no-login trial feels generous. To an attacker it’s an unlocked door left open on purpose. Anonymous access is unattributable and can’t be throttled per user — so it’s the first thing they hit, because there’s no cost to trying.The moment something expensive — AI inference, downloads, any real compute — is reachable without an account, it stops being a trial. It’s free resources for whoever finds it, running through the proxy you just built in the step above.Put a login in front of anything that costs you money. Auth isn’t about billing convenience; it converts “anyone on the internet” into “a named account you can rate-limit, flag, and ban.” Even a cracked client is useless if every valuable call needs an authenticated account behind it.Authenticate is not authorizeLogin proves who is calling. It does not prove they’re allowed to touch what they asked for — and that gap is where apps bleed. Every request that names a resource (/user/1043/profile, /order/88) must be ownership-checked on the server, every time. If the backend returns record 1044 just because the client asked for it, login bought you nothing. Sequential IDs plus "the server trusts the ID the client sent" is the classic IDOR hole.Same rule for entitlements: the client never decides “is this user premium.” That verdict lives on the server. The client asks; the server decides.Return only the minimumThe server sends only the fields the screen needs — not the full user object with internal flags, roles, or other users’ data the UI happens not to render. A cracked client reads the raw JSON, not your layout.Don’t leave landmarks in the binaryAn attacker doesn’t read your whole app — they grep the decompiled output for api_key, token, gemini, https://. Whatever surfaces is where they start digging. Remove the easy targets:Turn on R8: minifyEnabled, resource shrinking, renaming, dead-code stripping. Set debuggable false. Strip any Log calls that leak tokens or PII.Store config/preference keys under encoded or encrypted names, not "user_api_key".Keep endpoint URLs out of plaintext — build or decrypt them at runtime.Be clear-eyed about what this buys you: it is not hiding a secret — you already can’t. It’s removing signposts so finding the point of interest costs real effort instead of one grep. Friction, not a wall — which is exactly what Reduce is about.Verify the caller, and break the easy MITMA stolen token can still be replayed from a script or an emulator farm. Two server-side checks close that gap:Play Integrity API — the app requests a signed verdict; your backend verifies it before serving the

title: Thinking Like the Compose Runtime — Part 4: When Compose Decides to Do Nothing
excerpt: In Part 3, we discovered how the runtime never loses its place. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Jetpack ComposeAndroid App DevelopmentAndroidAndroid DevelopmentKotlinThinking Like the Compose Runtime — Part 4: When Compose Decides to Do NothingNeeraja GandlaFollow4 min read·6 days ago1ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeIn Part 3, we discovered how the runtime never loses its place.Using identity and the Slot Table, the Composer can recognize a composable across recompositions and retrieve everything associated with it.So now the runtime can always find a composable.But here’s an interesting question.Does finding a composable automatically mean it has to execute it again?Our intuition says yes.After all, recomposition literally means running composable functions again.So once the runtime reaches a composable, shouldn’t it simply execute it?Surprisingly…No.One of the biggest performance optimizations in Compose is knowing when not to do any work.A Small ExampleImagine a simple screen.@Composablefun ProfileScreen(user: User) { Header() UserCard(user) Footer()}Now suppose some state change causes ProfileScreen() to become invalid.The runtime begins recomposition.It reaches UserCard(user).Should it execute UserCard()?Maybe.Maybe not.That depends on a simple question.Has anything that UserCard() actually depends on changed?The Goal Isn’t RecompositionThis is an important shift in perspective.Many developers think Compose tries to make recomposition fast.That’s true.But it’s not the ultimate goal.The runtime has an even better optimization.Avoid recomposition entirely whenever possible.Doing no work is always cheaper than doing fast work.When Is Skipping Safe?Imagine this composable.@Composablefun Greeting(name: String) { Text("Hello $name")}Suppose the previous composition received:name = "Neeraja"During recomposition, it receives:name = "Neeraja"Exactly the same value.Would running Greeting() produce a different UI?No.The output would be identical.So why execute it again?The runtime simply skips it.Nothing changed.Nothing needs updating.But How Can Compose Trust That?Now things become interesting.Imagine a different composable.data class User( var name: String)@Composablefun UserCard(user: User) { Text(user.name)}Suppose the runtime sees the exact same User object during recomposition.Can it safely skip?Not necessarily.Someone might have changed:user.name = "Rahul"The object reference is still the same.But the UI should now be different.If the runtime skipped recomposition, it would display stale information.Get Neeraja Gandla’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThis is why checking object identity isn’t enough.The runtime needs to know whether a type can change without Compose noticing.Enter StabilityThis is exactly the problem stability solves.A stable type makes a promise to the Compose Runtime.It says,“If something that affects my UI changes, Compose will know.”That promise gives the runtime confidence.If a stable parameter hasn’t changed, recomposition can be skipped safely.If that promise cannot be trusted, the runtime takes the safer path.It recomposes.Not because it wants to.Because correctness always comes before performance.Stable Doesn’t Mean ImmutableThis is one of the biggest misconceptions.Many developers think stable means the object never changes.That’s actually immutable.A stable object can change.The important difference is that those changes happen through observable state.For example,class Counter { var count by mutableStateOf(0)}count changes.But every change is visible to the runtime.So Compose never misses an update.That’s why stability is about predictability, not unchangeability.What About @Stable and @Immutable?The compiler tries to infer stability automatically.Many common types already have known stability.Sometimes, however, developers know something the compiler cannot infer.That’s where annotations like @Stable and @Immutable come in.Notice what these annotations are doing.They aren’t making your app faster by themselves.They’re giving the runtime more confidence about the promises your types make.The reward for keeping those promises is simple.More opportunities to skip recomposition.Putting It All TogetherLet’s connect the ideas from the last four articles.A state change happens.↓The Snapshot System marks readers as invalid.↓The Composer finds those composables again using identity and the Slot Table.↓Before recomposing, the runtime asks,“Can I safely skip this?”If every relevant parameter is stable and unchanged…It skips.Otherwise…It recomposes.The runtime isn’t trying to execute composables.It’s trying to produce the correct UI while doing the least amount of work possible.Coming Up NextWe’ve now seen how the runtime decides whether recomposition is even necessary.But another question remains.Throughout this series, we’ve casually talked about state changes.Where does that state actually live?How can multiple composables read it safely while other parts of the app are updating it?The answer lies in one of the most elegant pieces of the Compose Runtime.Snapshots.And once you understand snapshots, you’ll realize they’re the invisible foundation that makes everything we’ve learned so far possible.

title: MVI architecture in Jetpack Compose
excerpt: The last two posts were about picking the right tool for a single line of code — a scope, a coroutine builder. This one is bigger: how do… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidJetpack ComposeKotlinAndroid DevelopmentSoftware ArchitectureMVI architecture in Jetpack ComposeImran AliFollow4 min read·6 days agoListenShareThe last two posts were about picking the right tool for a single line of code — a scope, a coroutine builder. This one is bigger: how do you structure an entire screen so that six months from now, you (or whoever inherits the code) can actually reason about what it does?That’s what MVI gives you. Not a library, not a framework — a small set of rules about where state lives and how it’s allowed to change. Once you’ve built one screen this way, every screen after it follows the same shape, and that predictability is worth more than almost any individual pattern decision you’ll make.The problem MVI solvesMost Compose screens start simple: a few mutableStateOf variables, a couple of callbacks, done. Then the screen grows. Loading states, error states, a snackbar, a dialog, an API call that can fail three different ways — and suddenly you've got state scattered across a dozen variables, some in the Composable, some in the ViewModel, and no single place that tells you "here's everything this screen could possibly look like right now."Get Imran Ali’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inMVI’s answer: one state object, one way to change it.Model — a single, immutable data class representing everything the screen needs to renderIntent — every possible thing the user (or the system) can do, represented as a sealed classView — a Composable that does nothing but render the current Model and forward IntentsThe whole architecture is really just structured discipline around a single rule: the View never mutates state directly. It sends an Intent, the ViewModel decides what that means, and a new Model comes out the other side.Step 1: Define the ModelStart with the state, not the UI. Everything the screen can show should be representable in one data class.data class ProfileState( val isLoading: Boolean = false, val profile: Profile? = null, val errorMessage: String? = null)This alone forces a useful discipline: if a piece of UI needs to change based on something, that something has to live here. No exceptions, no “just one local variable real quick.”Step 2: Define the IntentsEvery user action becomes a sealed class member. This is also where the architecture pays off during code review — you can look at one file and see the complete list of things a user can do on this screen.sealed interface ProfileIntent { data class LoadProfile(val userId: String) : ProfileIntent object Retry : ProfileIntent object DismissError : ProfileIntent}Step 3: The ViewModel — the only place Model changesThe ViewModel exposes the current state and a single entry point for intents. This is the piece that actually does the “reducing” — taking an Intent and the current State and producing a new State.class ProfileViewModel( private val repository: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() { private val _state = MutableStateFlow(ProfileState()) val state: StateFlow<ProfileState> = _state.asStateFlow() fun onIntent(intent: ProfileIntent) { when (intent) { is ProfileIntent.LoadProfile -> loadProfile(intent.userId) is ProfileIntent.Retry -> _state.value.profile?.let { loadProfile(it.id) } is ProfileIntent.DismissError -> { _state.update { it.copy(errorMessage = null) } } } } private fun loadProfile(userId: String) { viewModelScope.launch { _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true, errorMessage = null) } try { val profile = repository.getProfile(userId) _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = false, profile = profile) } } catch (e: Exception) { _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = false, errorMessage = e.message) } } } }}Notice there’s exactly one function that writes to _state: onIntent and the private functions it calls. Nothing else in the codebase can touch this state. That constraint is the entire value proposition — when a bug report says "the profile screen shows the wrong thing," you know exactly where to look.Step 4: The Composable — render State, emit IntentThe View layer’s job shrinks down to almost nothing interesting, which is exactly the point.@Composablefun ProfileScreen(viewModel: ProfileViewModel = viewModel()) { val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() ProfileContent( state = state, onIntent = viewModel::onIntent )}@Composableprivate fun ProfileContent( state: ProfileState, onIntent: (ProfileIntent) -> Unit) { when { state.isLoading -> LoadingIndicator() state.errorMessage != null -> ErrorView( message = state.errorMessage, onRetry = { onIntent(ProfileIntent.Retry) }, onDismiss = { onIntent(ProfileIntent.DismissError) } ) state.profile != null -> ProfileDetails(profile = state.profile) }}ProfileContent is a pure function of state. Give it the same ProfileState, get the same UI, every time — which also makes it trivial to preview and test without touching a real ViewModel at all.The building blocks, side by sidePieceTypeResponsibilityRuleModelImmutable data classEverything the screen can renderSingle source of truth — no state outside itIntentSealed interface/classEvery possible user/system actionExhaustive — the when should never need an elseViewModelHolds State, exposes onIntentThe only place State is allowed to changeOne entry point in, one StateFlow outComposablePure function of StateRendering onlyNever mutates State directly, only emits IntentThe one-paragraph mental modelState flows down, Intents flow up, and there is exactly one function allowed to turn an Intent into a new State. Once that rule holds for one screen, it holds for all of them — and that’s what makes a codebase predictable at scale instead of just “organized for now.”What’s nextThis is also where the series starts to compound: next week I’m taking this exact same MVI structure and rebuilding it in SwiftUI, then the week after that, sharing the shared logic between both platforms with Kotlin Multiplatform.What’s

title: Mutex vs Semaphore in Kotlin Coroutines
excerpt: Concurrency is one of the most challenging aspects of software development. As applications become increasingly asynchronous, multiple… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin CoroutinesKotlinKotlin MultiplatformAndroid DevelopmentAndroidMutex vs Semaphore in Kotlin CoroutinesNematFollow5 min read·6 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Louis Tsai on UnsplashConcurrency is one of the most challenging aspects of software development. As applications become increasingly asynchronous, multiple coroutines often attempt to access the same shared data simultaneously. Without proper synchronization, applications suffer from race conditions, inconsistent state, crashes, and unpredictable behavior.Kotlin Coroutines provide two primary synchronization primitives to solve these problems:MutexSemaphoreAlthough both are synchronization mechanisms, they solve fundamentally different problems. Many developers mistakenly use them interchangeably, which often leads to unnecessary complexity or performance bottlenecks.This article explores everything you need to know about Mutex and Semaphore, including their internal behavior, differences, real-world use cases, performance considerations, interview questions, and best practices.Understanding the ProblemImagine multiple coroutines updating the same bank account balance.var balance = 1000repeat(1000) { launch { balance += 10 }}At first glance, the final balance should be:1000 + (1000 × 10) = 11000Instead, you may get:104501072010910Every execution produces a different answer.This is called a race condition.It occurs because multiple coroutines are reading and writing the same variable simultaneously.Synchronization primitives prevent these situations.What is a Mutex?Mutex stands for Mutual Exclusion.A Mutex ensures that only one coroutine can execute a critical section at any given time.If another coroutine tries to enter while the lock is held, it waits until the lock becomes available.Think of it as a bathroom with a single key.Coroutine A │ ▼Acquire Lock │ ▼Critical Section │ ▼Release LockCoroutine B │ ▼Wait...Only one coroutine owns the key.Everyone else waits.Mutex in Kotlinval mutex = Mutex()var counter = 0coroutineScope { repeat(1000) { launch { mutex.withLock { counter++ } } }}println(counter)Output1000Every execution produces the same answer because only one coroutine modifies the counter at a time.How Mutex Works InternallySuppose five coroutines attempt to acquire the same Mutex.Coroutine 1 ---> Lock AcquiredCoroutine 2 ---> WaitingCoroutine 3 ---> WaitingCoroutine 4 ---> WaitingCoroutine 5 ---> WaitingWhen Coroutine 1 releases the lock:Coroutine 2 acquires itCoroutine 3 waitsCoroutine 4 waitsCoroutine 5 waitsOnly one coroutine executes inside the protected block.What is a Critical Section?A critical section is any code that accesses shared mutable state.Example:counter++Although it looks like one operation, it actually performs three operations.Read counterIncrement valueWrite value backIf another coroutine interrupts in the middle, data becomes inconsistent.Mutex guarantees these three operations execute atomically.Real Android ExampleSuppose multiple API requests update a local cache.Without Mutex:cache[user.id] = userTwo requests may overwrite each other unexpectedly.With Mutex:mutex.withLock { cache[user.id] = user}Now updates occur sequentially.What is a Semaphore?A Semaphore controls how many coroutines can access a resource simultaneously.Unlike Mutex:Mutex allows1 coroutineSemaphore allowsN coroutineswhere N is configurable.Example:Semaphore(3)Only three coroutines may execute simultaneously.The fourth waits.Semaphore in Kotlinval semaphore = Semaphore(3)repeat(10) { launch { semaphore.withPermit { println("Running") delay(1000) } }}Only three coroutines execute simultaneously.How Semaphore Works InternallySuppose Semaphore has 3 permits.Available Permits = 3Coroutine AAcquire PermitPermits Left = 2Coroutine BAcquire PermitPermits Left = 1Coroutine CAcquire PermitPermits Left = 0Coroutine DMust WaitOnce any coroutine finishes,Permit ReleasedPermits = 1Coroutine D StartsThe Biggest MisconceptionMany developers believe Semaphore prevents race conditions.This is not always true.Example:val semaphore = Semaphore(3)var counter = 0repeat(1000) { launch { semaphore.withPermit { counter++ } }}Three coroutines may execute simultaneously.Therefore:Coroutine Acounter++Coroutine Bcounter++Coroutine Ccounter++Race conditions can still occur.Semaphore limits concurrency.It does not guarantee exclusive access.Get Nemat’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inIf only one permit is configured:Semaphore(1)It behaves similarly to a Mutex from a concurrency perspective, but it still has different semantics and is generally not a replacement for a Mutex.Common Use Cases for MutexProtecting Shared Variablesmutex.withLock { counter++}Updating Room Cachemutex.withLock { dao.insert(user)}Modifying In-Memory Cachemutex.withLock { users[id] = user}Writing to Shared Filemutex.withLock { file.write(text)}Updating Authentication Tokenmutex.withLock { accessToken = newToken}Only one refresh operation updates the token at a time.Common Use Cases for SemaphoreLimiting Parallel Network Callsval semaphore = Semaphore(5)Only five API requests execute simultaneously.Limiting Image DownloadsInstead of downloading 100 images simultaneously,allow only:10 downloadsat once.Database Connection PoolSuppose only 20 database connections exist.Semaphore ensures no more than 20 coroutines use them simultaneously.File ProcessingSuppose processing large files consumes lots of memory.Limit processing to:4 files simultaneouslyExpensive CPU TasksIf you have 8 CPU cores,allow:Semaphore(8)to avoid excessive parallelism.Performance ConsiderationsMutex performs well when:protecting small critical sectionsshared state updatesavoiding race conditionsHowever, avoid holding a Mutex during long-running operations.Bad:mutex.withLock { delay(5000)}Every waiting coroutine remains blocked for five seconds.Instead:val result = api.fetch()mutex.withL

title: Beyond the Acronym — SOLID Principles for Android Developers
excerpt: A practical look at five design principles through real Android examples Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeAndroidKotlinSoftware ArchitectureClean CodeSolid PrinciplesBeyond the Acronym — SOLID Principles for Android DevelopersAdrián LeyvaFollow7 min read·6 days agoListenShareA practical look at five design principles through real Android examplesMost Android engineers can picture the file without needing to see it. One class quietly handling networking, database access, UI state, and analytics all at once, grown large enough that nobody wants to be the one who touches it next. Adding a single feature means reading carefully through logic that has no clear boundaries, hoping the change does not ripple into a screen three taps away. This is not an edge case. It’s what happens, reliably, when a codebase grows without best practices.SOLID refers to five object-oriented design principles introduced by Robert C. Martin: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. They were written well before ViewModels or Jetpack Compose existed, but Android development, with its layered architecture and its habit of changing requirements mid-sprint, turns out to be one of the clearest places to see them in action. This article works through each principle using practical Kotlin examples grounded in patterns from real production code, with the goal of showing not only what each principle states, but why it matters once your app has to keep working through months of change you did not plan for.Single Responsibility PrincipleA class should have one, and only one, reason to change. This does not mean a class should do only one thing in the narrowest sense; it means a class should be answerable to only one actor or concern.Consider a common anti-pattern: a ViewModel that fetches user data, formats it for display, and also handles analytics logging.class UserProfileViewModel( private val api: UserApi, private val analytics: AnalyticsService) : ViewModel() { private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<UserUiState>(UserUiState.Loading) val uiState: StateFlow<UserUiState> = _uiState fun loadUser(userId: String) { viewModelScope.launch { try { val response = api.getUser(userId) val formattedName = "${response.firstName} ${response.lastName}".trim() val formattedJoinDate = SimpleDateFormat("MMM yyyy", Locale.US) .format(response.joinDate) _uiState.value = UserUiState.Success( name = formattedName, joinDate = formattedJoinDate ) analytics.logEvent("user_profile_loaded", mapOf("user_id" to userId)) } catch (e: Exception) { _uiState.value = UserUiState.Error(e.message ?: "Unknown error") analytics.logEvent("user_profile_error", mapOf("user_id" to userId)) } } }}This ViewModel changes if the API contract changes, if the date format changes, if the analytics schema changes, or if the display logic changes. Four reasons to change means four sources of risk every time you touch this file. Splitting responsibilities across a mapper, a dedicated analytics tracker, and a leaner ViewModel isolates each concern.class UserDisplayMapper { fun toDisplayModel(response: UserResponse): UserDisplayModel { return UserDisplayModel( name = "${response.firstName} ${response.lastName}".trim(), joinDate = SimpleDateFormat("MMM yyyy", Locale.US).format(response.joinDate) ) }}class UserProfileAnalyticsTracker(private val analytics: AnalyticsService) { fun trackLoaded(userId: String) = analytics.logEvent("user_profile_loaded", mapOf("user_id" to userId)) fun trackError(userId: String) = analytics.logEvent("user_profile_error", mapOf("user_id" to userId))}class UserProfileViewModel( private val api: UserApi, private val mapper: UserDisplayMapper, private val tracker: UserProfileAnalyticsTracker) : ViewModel() { private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<UserUiState>(UserUiState.Loading) val uiState: StateFlow<UserUiState> = _uiState fun loadUser(userId: String) { viewModelScope.launch { try { val response = api.getUser(userId) _uiState.value = UserUiState.Success(mapper.toDisplayModel(response)) tracker.trackLoaded(userId) } catch (e: Exception) { _uiState.value = UserUiState.Error(e.message ?: "Unknown error") tracker.trackError(userId) } } }}Now each class is testable in isolation, and a change to date formatting no longer risks breaking analytics tracking.Open/Closed PrincipleSoftware entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. In practice, this means you should be able to add new behavior without rewriting existing, already-tested code.A frequent violation shows up in payment processing or notification handling, where a single function grows a new conditional branch every time a new type is introduced.class PaymentProcessor { fun process(payment: Payment) { when (payment.type) { PaymentType.CREDIT_CARD -> processCreditCard(payment) PaymentType.PAYPAL -> processPayPal(payment) PaymentType.GOOGLE_PAY -> processGooglePay(payment) // Every new payment method means editing this function again } } private fun processCreditCard(payment: Payment) { /* ... */ } private fun processPayPal(payment: Payment) { /* ... */ } private fun processGooglePay(payment: Payment) { /* ... */ }}Every new payment provider requires modifying and redeploying this class, along with re-running regression tests on branches you did not touch. An interface-based approach lets you extend behavior by adding new classes instead.interface PaymentStrategy { suspend fun process(amount: BigDecimal): PaymentResult}class CreditCardPayment(private val gateway: CardGateway) : PaymentStrategy { override suspend fun process(amount: BigDecimal): PaymentResult = gateway.charge(amount)}class PayPalPayment(private val client: PayPalClient) : PaymentStrategy { override suspend fun process(amount: BigDecimal): PaymentResult = client.createOrder(amount)}class GooglePayPayment(private val client: GooglePayClient) : PaymentStrategy { override suspend fun process(amount: BigDecimal): PaymentResult = client.charge(amount)}class PaymentProcessor(private val strategy: PaymentStrategy

title: Your Android App Is One Null Away From Crashing — Here’s Why
excerpt: How unboxing, unguarded exceptions, and race conditions silently break production apps Continue reading on CodeToDeploy »
content: AndroidKotlinJavaAndroid App DevelopmentProgrammingYour Android App Is One Null Away From Crashing — Here’s WhyHow unboxing, unguarded exceptions, and race conditions silently break production appsDilipchandarFollow6 min read·6 days ago55ListenShareThree of the bugs I’m about to show you made it past code review, past QA, and straight into production. They didn’t show up during testing. They never do. Here’s what caused them — and the simple fixes that would have prevented each one.Press enter or click to view image in full size💥 Master Any Skills in 3 Months 📚 Up to 50% OFF Premium Courses ⏰ Limited-Time Offer👉 Enroll Now & Start LearningPress enter or click to view image in full sizeBe careful during UnboxingBoxing is the conversion of a primitive type to an object, whereas Unboxing is getting the object back from a primitive type. Let’s take the example below where a boolean value is taken from the Object typeclass Sample { private Map<String, Object> properties;public Sample(Map<String, Object> props) { this.properties = props;}public Map<String, Object> getProperties() { return properties;}}// Putting boolean value into mapclass MainActivity extends Activity {Map<String, Object> map = new HashMap<>();map.put("booleanValue", true);Sample sample = new Sample(map);}// Getting boolean value from mapclass ActivityTwo extends Activity {Sample sample = new Sample();// Casting Object to primitive type booleanboolean value = (boolean) sample.getProperties().get("booleanValue"); }Here’s the catch:What if the value for booleanValue is null?map.put("booleanValue", null);Then if we cast like thisboolean value = (boolean) sample.getProperties().get("booleanValue");We will get an exceptionFatal Exception: java.lang.NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method ‘boolean java.lang.Boolean.booleanValue()’ on a null object referenceSo whenever there is a chance of getting a null value, we will have to use Boolean instead of boolean, as the former can be nullable. So the correct casting will beBoolean value = (Boolean) sample.getProperties().get("booleanValue");Throwing exceptions without guarding can crash the appLet’s take the example belowfun performOperation(op : Char, b : Double, a : Double) : Double { return when (op) { '+' -> a + b '-' -> a - b '*' -> a * b '/' -> if (b == 0.0) throw UnsupportedOperationException("Cannot divide by zero") else a / b else -> throw UnsupportedOperationException("Unknown operator: $op") }}The code snippet above performs mathematical operations based on the input. But here’s the catch'/' -> if (b == 0.0) throw UnsupportedOperationException("Cannot divide by zero") else a / belse -> throw UnsupportedOperationException("Unknown operator: $op")These two lines of code above throw an UnsupportedOperationException without any try/catch. This means when that particular scenario occurs (if b == 0.0 or any other operation like %, the app will crash.val doubleValue = performOperation('%', 2.0, 1.0) // op is different from '+', '-', '*', '/'val doubleValue = performOperation('/', 0.0, 1.0) // b is 0.0 and op is '/'So we have to guard the function with a try/catch block when we are throwing an exception.fun performOperation(op : Char, b : Double, a : Double) : Double { try { return when (op) { '+' -> a + b '-' -> a - b '*' -> a * b '/' -> if (b == 0.0) throw UnsupportedOperationException("Cannot divide by zero") else a / b else -> throw UnsupportedOperationException("Unknown operator: $op") } } catch (e: Exception) { return 0.0 }}The above code works fine, and if any exception occurs, the app won’t crash. Instead, a value of 0.0 is returned, and the app’s execution continues.Or else a better idiomatic solution would befun performOperation(op: Char, b: Double, a: Double): Result<Double> { return runCatching { when (op) { '+' -> a + b '-' -> a - b '*' -> a * b '/' -> if (b == 0.0) throw UnsupportedOperationException( "Cannot divide by zero" ) else a / b else -> throw UnsupportedOperationException( "Unknown operator: $op" ) } }}App crashes due to a race condition or timing issue in broadcast executionLet’s take a look at the example below where a line of code causes an app crash only during production.Fatal Exception: java.lang.NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method ‘int java.util.ArrayList.size()’ on a null object referenceclass DataSelectorActivity extends Activity {private ArrayList<String> stringList;@Override protected void onResume() { super.onResume(); addData(); registerReceiver(dataReceiver, new IntentFilter("com.example.printdata")); }private final BroadcastReceiver dataReceiver = new BroadcastReceiver() { @Override public void onReceive(Context context, Intent intent) { printData(); } };}In the above class, a stringList is created but not yet instantiated or initialized, and a broadcast receiver is created with a function called printData inside. The broadcast receiver is registered in onResume().Get Dilipchandar’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inAnd the method printData has the stringList iteration like below, for example.private void printData() { for (int i = 0; i < stringList.size(); i++) { // code causing app crash if(stringList.get(i).isEmpty()) { System.out.println("Hi"); } } }And a function that initializes the stringList exists like below.private void addData() { stringList = new ArrayList<>(); stringList.add("sample"); stringList.add(""); stringList.add("data");}So the expectation for code execution is like this,class DataSelectorActivity extends Activity {private ArrayList<String> stringList;@Override protected void onResume() { super.onResume(); addData(); registerReceiver(dataReceiver, new IntentFilter("com.example.printdata")); }private final BroadcastReceiver dataReceiver = new BroadcastReceiver() { @Override public void onReceive(Context context, Intent intent) { printData(); } };private void addData() { stringList = new ArrayList<>(); str

title: BoxWithConstraints: When You Actually Need It
excerpt: BoxWithConstraints gets recommended a lot, often as the one-line answer to "how do I make my layout responsive?" It can do that. But it… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Jetpack ComposeAndroid DevelopmentKotlinJetpack Compose LayoutAndroidBoxWithConstraints: When You Actually Need ItChristophy BarthFollow4 min read·6 days agoListenShareBoxWithConstraints gets recommended a lot, often as the one-line answer to "how do I make my layout responsive?" It can do that. But it also gets pulled into plenty of cases where a plain modifier or a window size class would be cleaner and cheaper, and it carries a real cost that its convenient API hides. It's worth knowing exactly what it gives you, what it costs, and being a little suspicious of your own urge to use it.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeA person measuring the width of a doorway with a tape measure before moving furniture through it.What it hands youA normal composable has no idea how much space it has while it’s composing. It composes first, and only later, during the measure pass, does anyone find out the actual size. BoxWithConstraints changes that ordering for its own content: inside its block, you get a scope that exposes the incoming constraints as readable values before the children compose, so you can branch on the space available.BoxWithConstraints { if (maxWidth < 400.dp) { CompactContent() } else { WideContent() }}The maxWidth and maxHeight here are Dp values you can compare against directly, and you can read the raw constraints object too if you need pixels. The important part is that this decision happens during composition, so you can compose entirely different content depending on the size, not merely resize the same content. That's the capability nothing else gives you in the same spot.Why “during composition” matters, and what it costsThat power comes straight from how it works underneath. BoxWithConstraints is built on SubcomposeLayout, which defers composing its children until the measure passes, when the size is finally known. That deferral is the mechanism that lets you read the size before you decide what to show.The cost is that this is more expensive than ordinary composition, and it crosses the phase boundary between composition and layout, which is a hotter, more frequent place to be doing composition work. For a screen-level decision made once, that cost rounds to nothing. Sprinkled inside a list item that appears hundreds of times, it adds up in a way that shows in a profile. It can also complicate things that expect a normal composition, like some animations and state that lives inside the block, because that state now comes to life a step later than usual.Get Christophy Barth’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inSo the honest question before using it is whether you actually need to change what composes based on size, or whether you only need to change how the same thing looks.A worked example: a card that adapts on its ownHere’s the case where I do use it. Say you have a content card that should show its image and text stacked when it’s narrow, and side by side when it’s wide, and its width isn’t tied to the screen size because it sits in a grid whose column count varies. Window size classes can’t answer this, because the card’s width isn’t the window’s width. This is a local decision.@Composablefun AdaptiveCard(item: Item, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) { BoxWithConstraints(modifier) { if (maxWidth < 320.dp) { Column { ItemImage(item, Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) ItemText(item) } } else { Row { ItemImage(item, Modifier.width(120.dp)) ItemText(item, Modifier.padding(start = 16.dp)) } } }}The card measures its own available width and picks a structure, and it does the right thing whether it’s alone on a phone or one of three columns on a tablet. That’s the sweet spot: the decision is about this specific bounded area, and the two branches are structurally different compositions rather than the same tree at different sizes.When you don’t need itMost “responsive” needs don’t call for it at all, and swapping in a cheaper tool keeps your tree simpler.If you only want to cap a width so long lines stay readable, Modifier.widthIn(max = 640.dp) does that with no subcomposition. If you're adapting a whole screen between phone and tablet, window size classes are the better fit, because they read from the window and they're built for exactly that top-level decision. If you just want a child to fill or wrap its space, that's a plain size modifier doing constraint math, and it never needs to know the number. And if you want to animate a size change, animateContentSize handles it without anyone reading a dimension.The tell that you’ve picked the wrong tool is finding yourself inside a BoxWithConstraints only to pass maxWidth into a modifier you could have written directly. If the size is just feeding back into sizing, you didn't need to read it.The rule I settle onTreat BoxWithConstraints as a precise instrument, not a default. When the choice is really about what to compose in a specific bounded area, and that area's size isn't the same as the window's, it's exactly right and there's no cheaper substitute. For everything else, a modifier or a size class gets you there with less machinery and less cost. Knowing the difference is most of what separates a layout that stays fast from one that ends up doing subcomposition work it never needed to.May your layouts adapt where they must and stay simple everywhere else.

title: StateFlow vs. Flow vs. SharedFlow vs. LiveData: A Simple Guide for Android Developers
excerpt: Four names, one confusing question: which one do I actually use? Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android App DevelopmentKotlinKotlin FlowJetpack ComposeKotlin StateflowStateFlow vs. Flow vs. SharedFlow vs. LiveData: A Simple Guide for Android DevelopersDev_PratixaFollow5 min read·Aug 3, 2026ListenShareFour names, one confusing question: which one do I actually use?Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThis image was generated using an AI-based image creation toolIf you are new to Android development, you have probably come across a confusing situation where you need to pass some data from your ViewModel to your UI, and you realise there are four different tools that all look like they do the same work. The official documentation doesn’t clearly say which one to choose, tutorials often contradict each other, and it is tempting to just use whatever approach the last tutorial you watched used without really understanding the reasoning behind it.Let’s understand it now. No complicated jargon just straightforward examples showing what each tool actually does and when you should use it.Think of it like a group chatHere is a simple way to picture the difference between all four:Flow is like a phone call that only happens when someone actually picks up. If nobody is listening, nothing happens. And if two people call in separately, it is like two separate calls happening not one shared call.StateFlow is like a whiteboard with today's status written on it. Anyone who walks up to the whiteboard immediately sees the latest value, even if they just arrived. It always has something written on it.SharedFlow is like a text message. If you are not looking at your phone when it arrives, you might miss it, because it would not be saved for you like a note on a whiteboard.LiveData is an older tool, kind of like StateFlow's predecessor, built back when Android screens (Activities/Fragments) worked a bit differently than they do now with Jetpack Compose.Keep this one rule in your head, and 90% of the confusion goes away:Use StateFlow to hold the current UI state. Use SharedFlow for notify one-time events like showing a toast.Let’s go through each one with beginner-friendly examplesFlow - the basic building blockA Flow is just a stream of values over time. On its own, it doesn't remember anything, and it doesn't do anything until something collects it (starts listening to it).fun getNumbers(): Flow<Int> = flow { emit(1) emit(2) emit(3)}Nothing happens when this function is called. It only starts running when something collects it:getNumbers().collect { number -> println(number) // prints 1, 2, 3}Think of Flow as the raw pipe that data flows through. You will rarely expose a plain Flow directly to your UI usually you will turn it into a StateFlow first (more on that below).StateFlow - for things your screen needs to always knowUse StateFlow when you are representing state something your screen should always have an answer for, like "is the user logged in?" or "what's in the shopping cart right now?"class LoginViewModel : ViewModel() { private val _isLoggedIn = MutableStateFlow(false) val isLoggedIn: StateFlow<Boolean> = _isLoggedInfun onLoginSuccess() { _isLoggedIn.value = true }}The key thing: isLoggedIn always has a value; it starts at false, and anyone who checks it later immediately gets the current answer, even if they didn't see the exact moment it changed. That's why it's great for state.Get Dev_Pratixa’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inBeginner tip: if you rotate your phone screen and your data resets or disappears, you are probably using the wrong tool StateFlow is usually the fix, because it remembers its last value for new screens that just started watching it.SharedFlow - for things that happen onceUse SharedFlow when you are representing an event something that should happen exactly once, like showing a popup message or navigating to another screen.class LoginViewModel : ViewModel() { private val _showError = MutableSharedFlow<String>() val showError: SharedFlow<String> = _showErrorfun onLoginFailed() { viewModelScope.launch { _showError.emit("Incorrect password, try again") } }}Unlike StateFlow, SharedFlow doesn't have to remember a value. That's actually the whole point you don't want an error message popping up again just because the screen restarted (like after rotating the phone). It should only show up once, right when it happens.Common beginner mistake: using StateFlow for a popup message. Since StateFlow always remembers its last value, rotating the screen can cause the same error message to pop up again, even though the user already saw and dismissed it. If you only want something to happen once, SharedFlow is the safer choice.LiveData - the older tool you will still see in a lot of codebasesLiveData came before StateFlow and works in a similar way it holds a value, and your UI can observe it.class LoginViewModel : ViewModel() { private val _isLoggedIn = MutableLiveData(false) val isLoggedIn: LiveData<Boolean> = _isLoggedInfun onLoginSuccess() { _isLoggedIn.value = true }}LiveData is still common in older Android projects, and it’s completely fine to use. However, for modern apps especially those using jetpack compose and StateFlow is the preferred choice because it integrates seamlessly with Kotlin coroutines and Compose, making state management simpler and more consistent.Bonus: Compose State a 5th option, just for the UI layerIf you are building screens entirely in Jetpack Compose, there is actually a fifth tool worth knowing: mutableStateOf. This one isn't for your ViewModel it is for state that lives directly inside a composable, like whether a dropdown is expanded:@Composablefun ExpandableCard() { var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }Column { Button(onClick = { expanded = !expanded }) { Text(if (expanded) "Collapse" else "Expand") } if (expanded) { Text("Here's the extra content!") } }}Simple rule: if the state only matters to this one screen this one screen and doesn’

title: Musicolet Is My New MP3 Playing Best Mate
excerpt: Like millions of Android owners who use their phone to play MP3 music, I went down the de facto Poweramp route for many years. Continue reading on Medium »
content: MP3AndroidPowerampMusicoletMusicolet Is My New MP3 Playing Best MateKevin TeaFollow3 min read·6 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeLike millions of Android owners who use their phone to play MP3 music, I went down the de facto Poweramp route for many years. After all, I was in good company with the app being downloaded more than 50 million times. I did go off piste on occasions with Winamp and Pulsar, but always returned to the fold. Until now.Earlier this year I spent three weeks on a Greek island bowing to my wife’s request for a beach holiday. She adores lounging on a sunbed and taking a dip in the sea to cool off. This bores me shitless, but I passed the time reading musicians’ biographies on my Kindle and listening to my Grateful Dead, Little Feat and other sixties and seventies bands. So, I got pretty up close and personal with Poweramp playing through earbuds.Recently, we spent a weekend in an Airbnb in North Yorkshire and I was scrolling through my newsfeeds when I came across a review of Musicolet. Normally I would scan read and move on, but the review piqued my interest so I downloaded the app and fired it up.I am over 70, always listened to music and spent three years working on a music magazine in London, going to numerous gigs, so my hearing is probably not the most reliable gauge of music quality via MP3s and ear buds..Get Kevin Tea’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inHowever, firing up the Grateful Dead’s American Beauty on the opening track Ripple I could hear sounds that I didn’t pick up on a Greek Beach. Garcia’s and Weir’s guitar work was clearly defined and separate, as was Lesh’s bass.That’s the background, now for some of the finer points. First, the app is free and the features at this level will suit 95% of users. I upgraded to the premium, not necessarily for the extra features, but to support development. Unlike other MP3 players, Musicolet is totally offline, so you can be confident it is not feeding your listening habits to external third parties, trying to update cover art and loading is instantaneous.The GUI is an example of understated beauty and usefulness and the navigation bar puts everything in a single row, making features instantly available. No more moving out of what’s playing the dipping into nested folders. Everything you need is a simple swipe away. Sometimes I feel that developers make accessing features to difficult by trying to be clever rather than relying on simplicity. This is something I always struggled with in Poweramp.I have never used queues, but might be tempted to explore as the reviewer wrote: “Musicolet is jam-packed with useful features. Multiple queues is the crown jewel of Musicolet. Most players give you one ‘Now Playing’ list; if you want to listen to something else, you lose your spot in the current one. Musicolet lets you have up to 20 independent queues. I can hop between different lists without breaking a sweat. Musicolet also comes with a decent collection of widgets to choose from.”Musicolet’s tag editing is straightforward compared to Poweramp’s and has an easy to use sleep timer if you want to drift off to sleep listening to music. Cut off can be by time or number of tracks played. If the time module hits the cut off point, the app plays the current track to its end and then closes everything down.Apart from coughing up cash for the premium version, the real test of sticking with my new MP3 playing mate is that I have removed Poweramp from my two Android devices. You can’t say better than that.

title: AI in Mobile App Development: Lessons from 14+ Years of Building Products at Scale
excerpt: Every week, a new article claims that AI is redefining mobile applications. Continue reading on Medium »
content: AIMobile App DevelopmentAndroidIOSMehul PatelAI in Mobile App Development: Lessons from 14+ Years of Building Products at ScaleMehul PatelFollow5 min read·6 days ago51ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeEvery week, a new article claims that AI is redefining mobile applications. Most of them discuss possibilities. Very few discuss production realities.The difference between experimenting with AI and delivering AI to millions of users is measured in architecture, not headlines.Over the last 14+ years, I’ve had the opportunity to architect Android platforms, lead distributed engineering organizations, and deliver mobile products used by more than 14 million users worldwide. My journey has evolved from writing Android code to leading engineers across Android, iOS, AI, and backend teams, building products where artificial intelligence isn’t a marketing feature — it is part of the core product experience.I’ve worked on everything from on-device machine learning and smart home intelligence to video streaming platforms, IoT ecosystems, camera SDKs, and AI-powered security applications.One thing has become increasingly clear:Building AI-powered mobile products is fundamentally different from building traditional mobile applications.It requires a different mindset, different architecture, and different engineering discipline. Here are the lessons that years of shipping production software have taught me.1. AI Doesn’t Start with Models. It Starts with Architecture.Most discussions begin with machine learning models.In reality, AI projects begin months earlier.Long before data scientists train a model, engineering teams must design:reliable event collectionscalable telemetry pipelinesclean data contractsprivacy-compliant analyticssynchronization strategiesoffline capabilitiesWithout these foundations, even the most sophisticated model becomes ineffective. On one of our large-scale smart-home platforms, the challenge wasn’t deciding whether personalization should exist.The challenge was architecting a system capable of processing millions of device events, user interactions, notification preferences, and sensor updates without compromising responsiveness, scalability, or battery life. By the time AI entered the conversation, most of the difficult engineering decisions had already been made.AI succeeds or fails on the quality of the platform beneath it.2. On-Device AI Changes EverythingPerhaps the biggest misconception about AI in mobile is the assumption that intelligence always lives in the cloud.Increasingly, it doesn’t.Modern smartphones possess dedicated NPUs capable of running sophisticated neural networks locally. I’ve led implementation of TensorFlow Lite based features where inference happens entirely on-device. This completely changes architectural priorities.Instead of asking:“How accurate is the model?”Engineering teams begin asking:Can this model execute within 20 milliseconds?What happens on lower-end chipsets? How much battery does continuous inference consume? What thermal impact does this create? Can inference continue offline? Is the APK size still acceptable? These aren’t data science questions. They’re mobile engineering questions.When AI runs locally, architecture becomes a balancing act between:latencybattery efficiencythermal performancememory consumptionmodel accuracyapplication sizeFinding that balance is where real engineering begins.3. Mobile AI Is More Than ChatbotsGenerative AI has made conversational interfaces dramatically more capable.But chat experiences are often the easiest component.Get Mehul Patel’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe harder engineering challenge is everything happening underneath. In products involving live camera feeds, WebRTC, RTSP, and HLS streaming, AI depends on infrastructure capable of delivering frames reliably despite:unstable networksvariable bandwidthcodec differenceshardware fragmentationedge device limitationsObject detection.Motion analysis.Person recognition.Smart alerts.None of these matter if the streaming architecture isn’t resilient. The visible AI experience is only as good as the invisible engineering supporting it.4. AI Introduces a New Security ModelSecurity discussions often focus on what AI can improve.Fraud detection.Behavioral analysis.Anomaly detection.Intelligent authentication.All valuable.However, AI also creates an entirely new attack surface. Shipping machine learning models inside an application introduces concerns such as:model extractionadversarial inputsreverse engineeringinference manipulationintellectual property exposureEngineering teams now need to perform threat modelling not only for authentication systems but also for ML pipelines.Security is no longer limited to APIs and encryption.It extends into the intelligence layer itself.5. The Highest ROI from AI Often Happens Before ReleaseIronically, the fastest return on AI investment frequently comes from development — not production.Across engineering organizations I’ve managed, AI has accelerated:code reviewsdocumentationregression testingtest generationbug identificationdeveloper onboardingThese improvements compound quickly across multiple teams.But there is one rule we’ve consistently followed.AI produces drafts. Engineers produce software.Senior engineers remain accountable for architecture, maintainability, performance, security, and production readiness.AI accelerates execution.It does not replace engineering judgement.6. Predictive Analytics Depends on Engineering DisciplineOrganizations often ask,“Can AI predict user behaviour?”Usually, yes.But only if the application has been instrumented correctly.Poor analytics cannot be rescued by better machine learning.I’ve seen teams attempt predictive initiatives without consistent event tracking, meaningful telemetry, or reliable historical data.The result is almost always disappointing.Before inv

title: Everyone Can Generate Code. Few Can Build Great Software.
excerpt: Why the next generation of AI won’t be measured by how much code it writes — but by how effectively it helps turn ideas into successful… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeAISoftware DevelopmentIOSAndroidMobile App DevelopmentEveryone Can Generate Code. Few Can Build Great Software.QicAppFollow7 min read·6 days agoListenShareWhy the next generation of AI won’t be measured by how much code it writes — but by how effectively it helps turn ideas into successful products.The AI Revolution Is Real. But So Is the Reality.Artificial Intelligence has transformed software development at a pace few could have imagined.A few years ago, building software required months of planning, a team of designers, architects, backend engineers, frontend developers, QA specialists, DevOps engineers, and project managers. Today, with a single prompt, AI can generate application code, create database schemas, write documentation, suggest APIs, and even produce working prototypes within minutes.It’s nothing short of revolutionary.Naturally, an entirely new generation of AI development tools has emerged. Every week, another platform claims to build your application automatically. The message is almost always the same:“Describe your idea in one prompt, and AI will build your software.”For founders, entrepreneurs, and businesses looking to launch products quickly, it sounds almost magical.And to be fair, these tools are incredibly impressive.They’ve dramatically reduced the barrier to entry.They’ve made software development faster.They’ve improved developer productivity.They’ve enabled more people than ever before to experiment with ideas.But after years of building software for startups, enterprises, and growing businesses, we’ve realized something important.The biggest challenge in software development has never been writing code. The biggest challenge has always been building the right product. And that’s a problem AI alone still cannot solve.The Biggest Myth About AI DevelopmentThere’s one misconception that has become increasingly common over the past two years.People assume software development begins with coding. It doesn’t. Professional software development begins with understanding. Before a single line of code is written, countless decisions must already be made.Questions like:What problem are we solving?Is this problem worth solving?Who exactly are the users?What are they struggling with today?Which features belong in Version 1?Which features should wait until later?What should the onboarding experience look like?Which technology stack is appropriate?Should this be a mobile app, a web platform, or both?How will the database scale?What security standards are required?How will authentication work?What APIs are needed?How will the product evolve six months after launch?These aren’t coding questions.They’re product questions.And they determine whether software succeeds or fails. AI can generate code. But code without direction is simply automation.Code Is Becoming a CommodityFor decades, writing code was considered one of the most valuable technical skills in the world.Today, AI has fundamentally changed that equation.Whether you’re using ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, or another AI assistant, generating code is no longer the bottleneck.In many cases, AI writes clean, efficient, and production-quality code. That’s extraordinary progress.But here’s what has changed:Code is no longer the competitive advantage.The competitive advantage is understanding the problem better than everyone else.Because every AI model has access to similar programming knowledge.What differentiates successful companies isn’t the ability to generate code.It’s the ability to make better product decisions.Software Is Much Bigger Than DevelopmentWhen most people imagine software development, they picture something like this:Idea -> Code -> LaunchProfessional software engineering looks very differentCoding is only one stage. Everything before development determines what gets built. Everything after development determines whether it succeeds.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeWhy So Many AI-Generated Products Never Reach ProductionEvery day, social media is filled with posts saying:“I built this SaaS in just three hours using AI.”That’s impressive.But the real question isn’t:Can AI build it?The real question is:Will anyone use it?Software doesn’t succeed because it compiles. Software succeeds because it solves meaningful problems. Many AI-generated applications never move beyond prototypes because they skip the difficult work.They skip:User researchProduct validationCustomer interviewsFeature prioritizationScalability planningCost estimationDocumentationLong-term architectureSecurity planningBusiness strategyThe result? A functional application. But not necessarily a successful product.AI Is Excellent at AnswersBut Businesses Need Execution. Today’s AI excels at answering questions.Ask it to write code. It writes code.2. Ask it to create documentation.It creates documentation.3. Ask it to design a database.It designs one.But successful companies aren’t built from answers.They’re built through execution.Execution means making hundreds of interconnected decisions over months — not generating isolated outputs.The future of AI isn’t simply answering prompts.The future of AI is guiding execution.Imagine AI asking questions instead of immediately providing answers.Get QicApp’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inQuestions like:Why are customers paying for this?Is this actually an MVP?Which feature delivers the highest business value?What technical debt are we creating?Will this architecture support one million users?Is this solving a symptom or the root problem?That’s a completely different experience. title: AQARION: A Mathematical Framework for Exact and Approximate Observable Quotients of Finite…
excerpt: AQARION-ARITHMETIC Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidTechEducationMathWritingAQARION ACADEMY & QUANTARION AIFollow5 min read·6 days agoListenShareAQARION: A Mathematical Framework for Exact and Approximate Observable Quotients of Finite Deterministic Dynamical SystemsVersion: August 2026 Public Research Manifesto---AbstractAQARION is a mathematical framework for the study of exact and approximate observable quotients of finite deterministic dynamical systems.Rather than studying trajectories or spectra directly, AQARION studies how coarse observations of a dynamical system interact with its evolution.Its primitive mathematical object is the triple\[(X,T,\Pi),\]where\(X\) is a finite state space,\(T:X\rightarrow X\) is a deterministic evolution map,\(\Pi\) is an observable partition of \(X\).Every observable partition induces an observable subspace, and AQARION investigates when this subspace is preserved exactly—or approximately—under the Koopman operator.The central invariant is the observable defect operator\[D_\Pi=(I-P_\Pi)KP_\Pi,\]which provides an exact certificate of observable invariance and quantitative measures of observable leakage.AQARION unifies operator theory, finite dynamics, quotient systems, algorithmic refinement, computational verification, and formal proof into a single mathematical framework for observable dynamics.---1. MotivationClassical finite dynamical systems begin with\[(X,T).\]The fundamental questions concerntrajectories,attractors,cycles,graph structure,entropy,spectral properties.AQARION introduces a different perspective.Suppose the observer cannot distinguish individual states.Instead, the observer sees only equivalence classes determined by an observable partition\[\Pi.\]The central question becomes> Does the observable itself evolve consistently under the dynamics?This shifts the focus from state evolution to observable evolution.---2. Primitive Mathematical ObjectsAQARION is built from the following primitives.Finite State Space\[X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}.\]---Deterministic Evolution\[T:X\rightarrow X.\]---Observable Partition\[\Pi=\{B_1,\ldots,B_k\}.\]Each block represents states that are observationally indistinguishable.---Observable ProjectionEach partition induces a projection\[P_\Pi.\]The associated observable space is\[V_\Pi=\operatorname{Im}(P_\Pi).\]---Koopman OperatorDynamics act on observables through\[(Kf)(x)=f(T(x)).\]---3. The Central QuestionAQARION asks:Is the observable space invariant?That is,\[K(V_\Pi)\subseteq V_\Pi?\]If yes,the observable defines an exact quotient dynamics.If no,the dynamics leak information outside the observable space.---4. The Observable Defect OperatorThe defining object of AQARION is\[\boxed{D_\Pi=(I-P_\Pi)KP_\Pi.}\]This operator measures precisely the component of the evolved observable lying outside the observable subspace.---Exactness CriterionThe fundamental equivalence is\[\boxed{D_\Pi=0\iffK(V_\Pi)\subseteq V_\Pi.}\]Thus,\[D_\Pi\]is an exact certificate of observable invariance.---5. Exact Observable QuotientsAn observable partition satisfying\[D_\Pi=0\]defines an exact observable quotient.The induced quotient dynamics evolve without observable ambiguity.These exact observables form the structural core of AQARION.---6. Approximate Observable QuotientsMost observables are not exactly invariant.AQARION therefore introduces quantitative defect measures.Define\[\epsilon_\Pi=\|D_\Pi\|.\]Then\[\epsilon_\Pi=0\]corresponds to exact invariance,while\[\epsilon_\Pi>0\]measures observable leakage.This naturally produces a hierarchy of approximate observable quotients.---7. Observable Defect GeometryBinary exactness is only the first invariant.AQARION develops a geometry of observable defects.Important quantities includeRank\[\operatorname{rank}(D_\Pi).\]---Get AQARION ACADEMY & QUANTARION AI’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inNullity\[\dim\ker(D_\Pi).\]---Operator Norm\[\|D_\Pi\|.\]---Frobenius Norm\[\|D_\Pi\|_F.\]---Singular Spectrum\[\sigma(D_\Pi).\]---Spectral EntropyNormalize singular values\[p_i=\frac{\sigma_i}{\sum_j\sigma_j}\]and define\[H_D=-\sum_ip_i\log p_i.\]These invariants measure the geometry of observable leakage.---8. Observable Lattice TheoryDefine\[\operatorname{Obs}(X,T)=\{\Pi:D_\Pi=0\}.\]This is the collection of exact observable partitions.AQARION studiesrefinement,joins,meets,maximal chains,minimal generators,canonical quotients,lattice invariants.One major open problem is whether\[\operatorname{Obs}(X,T)\]forms a complete lattice under suitable assumptions.---9. Classification ProblemsThe mature objective of AQARION is classification rather than computation.Representative questions include:Which observable partitions are exact?Which families always occur?Which systems admit unique minimal observable quotients?How large can observable lattices become?How does refinement interact with dynamics?These are structural mathematical problems.---10. AlgorithmsAQARION also develops constructive algorithms.Topics includepartition refinement,observable minimization,exactness certification,defect computation,canonical representatives,exhaustive enumeration,reproducible verification.The computational program serves the mathematical theory rather than replacing it.---11. Computational VerificationEvery computational claim follows a verification ladder:Conjecture │ ▼Counterexample Search │ ▼Exhaustive Enumeration │ ▼Independent Reproduction │ ▼Mathematical Proof │ ▼Formal Lean Verification │ ▼Peer ReviewComputational evidence is distinguished from formal proof at every stage.---12. Benchmark SystemsAQARION is not defined by any single example.Instead, benchmark systems serve as mathematical laboratories.Examples include:Kaprekar dynamical systemsFibonacci recurrence systemsBoolean networksCellular automataTransformation semigroupsRandom mappingsSymbolic dynamical systemsFinite linear systemsDiscretized complex mapsThese examples test the framework across diverse dynamica
