You can adjust or withdraw your consent at any time by visiting the Opt-Out.Accept AllDeny AllManage Settings <iframe src="https://www.googletagmanager.com/ns.html?id=GTM-5P98" height="0" width="0" style="display:none;visibility:hidden"></iframe> Skip to content Topics Search Burger menu icon IDEs CLion DataGrip GoLand IntelliJ IDEA PhpStorm PyCharm RustRover Rider RubyMine WebStorm Plugins & Services JetBrains Platform Scala Toolbox App JetBrains AI Junie JetBrains for Data Air Team Tools Datalore TeamCity YouTrack Qodana Databao .NET & Visual Studio .NET Tools ReSharper C++ Languages & Frameworks Kotlin Ktor MPS Amper Education & Research JetBrains Academy Research Company Company Blog Security Community Programs Life at JetBrains IntelliJ IDEA IntelliJ IDEA – the Leading IDE for Professional Development in Java and Kotlin Follow Follow: Linkedin Linkedin Bluesky Bluesky X X Facebook Facebook Youtube Youtube RSS RSS Download All News Releases Livestreams Tips & Tricks Early Access Program Plugins News IntelliJ IDEA Goes LSP: Java and Kotlin Intelligence Comes to VS Code, Cursor, and Agentic Flows Marco Behler August 4, 2026 It’s no secret that agentic development is changing how developers build software. As agents take on more and more of the implementation work, developers spend less and less time manually editing code. For this manual work, they might only need a basic, narrow set of features that IDEs provide, like navigating to declarations, finding references, some simple code completion, or renaming. These features are generally covered by the Language Server Protocol (LSP), which allows programming language support to be implemented once and then reused by any LSP-capable IDE or editor. Even agents can make use of LSP servers today, leading to faster and more deterministic results and, eventually, reduced token consumption. In response to these changes, we’ve been working hard at JetBrains to offer IntelliJ IDEA’s smart language features for Java and Kotlin in an LSP format. Today, we’re happy to announce that IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin intelligence is available in a preview extension for third-party editors, starting with VS Code and its forks (such as Cursor). We have also been running internal trials and experiments with a select few external customers, and the results have shown that the same LSP functionality can significantly improve terminal-based agentic workflows, like with Claude Code or Codex. We will share the very promising results of these experiments soon. Introducing the VS Code extensionCopy heading link The Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension is now available, powered by IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin language technology. It brings a focused set of capabilities to VS Code-based editors, including: Java, Kotlin, and mixed-language project support. Debugging (DAP-based). Smart code completion, navigation, and code analysis. Refactorings and editor assistance. Support for Maven, Gradle, and Bazel. Fast and reliable performance, even for large projects and monorepos. You can find the full list of features in our documentation. Getting startedCopy heading link You can install the Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace and the Open VSX registry. Install from Visual Studio Marketplace Install from Open VSX registry After installation, open your Java or Kotlin projects in VS Code or Cursor. The extension will start analyzing your projects, import the ones that have Maven, Gradle, or Bazel build files, and then enable Java and Kotlin language features in the editor for you. Compatibility notice Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA includes code analysis features and quick-fixes that overlap with Red Hat’s and Oracle’s extensions for Java. To avoid confusion, we recommend disabling those extensions while testing. LicensingCopy heading link During the preview phase, the extension is free to use. Each build renews the evaluation period and is limited to 30 days. After the preview period, using the extension will require an IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate subscription. The same license will let you use IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin capabilities whether you are working in the IntelliJ IDEA desktop IDE, in VS Code-based editors, or in other supported environments. You can review the pricing options here. Note: For pure Kotlin projects, you can use the Kotlin LSP, which we continue to develop and maintain. The Kotlin LSP’s source code is Apache 2.0 licensed. You can use it for free, either directly or via its extensions (Visual Studio Marketplace, Open VSX registry), with no subscription required. What’s nextCopy heading link The VS Code extension is just one milestone in a longer development journey to bring the intelligence of IntelliJ IDEA to our users wherever they are. We strongly believe the best way to do Java and Kotlin development is inside IntelliJ IDEA. At the same time, we recognize that teams may have practical reasons to work in other environments, with other editors and tools. Wherever you choose to work, we want you to benefit from IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin intelligence. To this end, we’re already working on supporting fully agentic, terminal-based workflows. In the near future, we’ll share our initial results (think: reduced token consumption), and we’ll give you a chance to try out our agent plugins when they’re ready. content: Jetpack ComposeSoftware ArchitectureAndroidAndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentFrom God ViewModel to Composed Screen LogicYves KalumeFollow6 min read·5 days ago20ListenShareoriginally published on yvesandmobile.substack.comWhen building a Compose UI, passing a ViewModel deep into the UI makes components less reusable because they become tied to one ViewModel type, and therefore to one screen. It also makes them harder to test in isolation and can break previews because previews are not meant to recreate the real runtime environment of the app.So instead, we keep the ViewModel at the route level.This is generally the recommended shape with state hoisting : move state up to the lowest common owner, expose immutable state down, and send events back up when the UI wants something to change.That model gives us many real benefits.But as the screen grows, the same pattern starts showing its pressure points.Why This StartedThe first pressure point is the composable API itself. If every piece of state is hoisted and every user action becomes a callback, the screen function can quickly grow.@Composablefun HomeScreen( state: HomeUiState, onRefresh: () -> Unit, onRetry: () -> Unit, onSourceSelected: (SourceItem?) -> Unit, onSearchQueryChanged: (String) -> Unit, onClearSearch: () -> Unit, onLoadMore: () -> Unit, onArticleClicked: (ArticleItem) -> Unit, onErrorDismissed: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier,) { //...}One common solution is to group all user actions into a sealed class or sealed interface, then expose one method from the ViewModel to handle them.sealed interface HomeAction { data object Refresh : HomeAction data class SourceSelected(val source: SourceItem?, ) : HomeAction data class SearchQueryChanged(val query: String, ) : HomeAction //...}The screen API becomes much smaller :@Composablefun HomeScreen( state: HomeUiState, onAction: (HomeAction) -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier,)And the route becomes cleaner too:@Composablefun HomeRoute( viewModel: HomeViewModel = viewModel(),) { val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() HomeScreen( uiState = uiState, onAction = viewModel::onAction, )}This solves one problem.The composable no longer exposes a long list of callbacks. The screen has one state parameter and one action entry point.But the pressure does not disappear. It usually moves into the ViewModel.class HomeViewModel( //...) : ViewModel() { fun onAction(action: HomeAction) { when (action) { HomeAction.Refresh -> refresh() HomeAction.ClearSearch -> clearSearch() is HomeAction.SourceSelected -> { selectSource(action.source) } is HomeAction.SearchQueryChanged -> { updateSearchQuery(action.query) } //... } }}For some screens, this is a good tradeoff. The UI API becomes simple, and all possible user actions are explicit in one place.But the issue appears when the screen keeps growing.After a while, the when statement starts to become the new version of the long parameter list. The callbacks are no longer visible in the composable signature, but every small interaction still ends up in the same ViewModel.My “God ViewModel Trauma”I have also worked on codebases with very large ViewModels. Sometimes, the real issue is the fact that the rest of the app architecture is not doing enough.Business rules that should live in use cases and data decisions that should live in repositories end up in the ViewModel. Mapping, validation, filtering, formatting, and orchestration all get mixed together because the ViewModel is the easiest place to put things.But even when repositories and use cases are well separated, I still had this feeling that we could handle large Compose screens better. Compose encourages us to break UI into smaller composables. We do not build one huge composable that renders the entire screen. We split the UI into smaller pieces, give each piece a clear responsibility, and compose them together.What if we could apply the same idea to screen behavior?What if we could compose not only composables, but also the logic behind those composables ?Instead of having one huge ViewModel that handles every small component interaction, could we keep one screen owner while giving each part of the screen its own focused behavior.That was the direction I wanted to explore.Thanks for reading Yves and Mobile! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.Composing the Logic Behind the UILet’s build our small news app, that supports source selection, pagination, search, and pull to refresh.Get Yves Kalume’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inIn this approach, the screen still has one ViewModel, it still exposes the UiState, But it no longer needs to contain every piece of behavior directly.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeComponent controllerThe screen is built from smaller behavior units. we call them controllers (but the name is not the most important part).Each controller is a segregated interface that owns the behavior of a composable or screen section.interface SourcesController { fun selectSource(source: SourceItem?)}interface ArticlesController { fun loadMore() fun retry()}interface SearchController { fun onQueryChanged(query: String) fun clearSearch()}interface RefreshController { fun refresh()}Screen state store.One of the biggest challenges with this kind of architecture is sharing data between different components without creating duplicated requests or race conditions.If each controller owns its own independent state or loads its own version of the data, the screen can easily become inconsistent. That’s why all controllers communicate through one shared screen state store.class HomeStateStore { private val _state = MutableStateFlow(HomeUiState.initial()) val state: StateFlow<HomeUiState> = _state.asStateFlow() fun update(reducer: HomeUiState.() -> HomeUiState) { _state.update { current -> current.reducer() } }}The StateStore is the mutable source of

content: AndroidGeminiAIAndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentAI, Meet App: Testing Android App FunctionsMake sure you are calling the right app and getting the right responseKatie BarnettFollow6 min read·5 days ago191ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeImage generated by GeminiThe new App Functions API is the next frontier for Android. It essentially turns your app into an on-device data provider for AI agents. Instead of relying on generic web searches, AI can now talk directly to your app to fetch highly personalised, user-specific information.It is easy to implement, there is even a dedicated AppFunctions agent skill that will help you integrate it faster but how do you test it?App Functions Testing ChallengesAs of writing this article (early August 2026), the App Functions API is in a private preview with trusted testers, so you can’t just add it to your app and test it out immediately with Gemini or any other AI apps on your device or emulator. But if, like me, you want to stay ahead of the AI curve (and your competitors!), you can prepare your app right now. That way, when it does roll out to users, your app will be ready to start chatting with Gemini!There are a few methods you can use. First up, let’s see what Gemini sees…For my demonstrations, I am using a small app, Game Night Guru, that queries a local database of boardgames and will recommend what the user should play based on their group size and interests and will also allow them to keep track of what they have played and enjoyed.Test App Functions Integration via ADBBefore we bring AI into the mix, let’s verify that the Android OS has successfully registered the App Functions that have been built.The first step is to install Android Debug Bridge (adb) if you haven’t already so you can communicate with your device.Note: For App Functions to work, you will need to use a System Image of 36.0 (codename Baklava) or a device running Android 16 and above.Also, you need to ensure your device has USB debugging enabled which requires Developer Options to be enabled.Run this command in your terminal to list all App Functions currently registered on your device:adb shell cmd app_function list-app-functionsYou will get back a long list of all the app functions available on the device from every app!To make it easier to find your app, you can filter it specifically using grep:adb shell cmd app_function list-app-functions | grep -A 20 dev.katiebarnett.gamenightguruNote: Make sure to replace the package name with your own application package name. You can also modify the number after -A in the grep command (the --after-context flag) to see more or less of the function definition.Now, you will get back the full specification of your available App Functions!Press enter or click to view image in full sizeHere is just one of the App Functions that my app exposes. As you can see, all the detail is there!Be aware — if you are writing your own App Functions, anyone else with a device connected to adb or an app that acts as an agent can see all your function definitions/schemas, so don’t include language or proprietary information that you don’t want others to see!Okay, now that we know that Android sees our function, how can we test if the prompting actually works?Get Katie Barnett’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inTime to try the Testing Agent.Download & Install the Testing AgentGoogle provides a privileged Testing Agent app that acts as a stand-in for Gemini. This allows us to test end-to-end workflows without needing a full production system.To use the testing agent, make sure you have enabled Developer Options on your emulator or deviceDownload or clone the source code from the App Functions Github repositoryOpen your terminal (or use the Android Studio Terminal) and change to the agent directory from wherever you saved the App Functions repository source code: cd appfunctions/agentBuild and install the agent to your connected device using the provided script: ./run_privileged.sh --buildImportant Note for Windows Users: Because this is a .sh shell script, it will not run in standard Command Prompt or PowerShell. You must run this command using Git Bash (which is installed automatically if you have Git for Windows) or WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux).Using the Testing AgentThe first thing we can do is check that the agent sees the App Functions. Using the dropdown, check which apps have app functions. You can enter parameters and get back the exact results the function returns (no AI involvement yet) and execute functions that update the data.Now we know it can see our app and the available App Functions, let’s hook it up to Gemini!Get a Gemini API KeyTo give our Testing Agent a brain, we need a Gemini API key. We will be using the free tier so no need to add a credit card or sign up to a pro plan.Go to the Google AI Studio API Keys page.Sign in with your Google account.Click Create API key at the top rightCreate or choose a project and name your key. Click Create keyCopy the generated key using the copy icon or the Copy key buttonTest it Live!This is where the magic happens. We are going to ask the agent a natural language question and watch it trigger our app’s specific function.Open the AppFunctions Testing Agent app on your Android device/emulator.Navigate to the Settings screen. Paste your Gemini API key into the settings/configuration screen of the agent.3. Navigate to the Agent Demo, type a natural language prompt that targets the function you want to test. For example:“I have 4 friends coming over for 2 hours and we love strategy games. What should we play?”4. content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeAndroidDevAI AgentAndroidAIAndroid App DevelopmentAndroid AppFunctions: Teaching AI Agents How to Use Your AppCedric FerryFollow6 min read·6 days ago38ListenShareIntroductionFor most of Android’s history, we have built applications for people. A user opens an app, looks at a screen, finds a button, navigates through a menu, enters some data, and finally performs an action. This model works well when the user is a human.It works much less well when the user is an AI agent.An agent that wants to interact with an application can try to understand what is displayed on the screen, identify UI elements, navigate through them, and reproduce the same steps as a human. But this turns a simple operation into a fragile sequence of visual interactions.Android AppFunctions introduce a different model.Instead of asking an agent to understand how to use your UI, your application can describe what it can do. That is a significant change. We are moving from: Show me the correct screen to Execute this functionThe digital island problemMost applications are effectively islands of business logic surrounded by a user interface.A news application knows how to retrieve articles. A banking application knows how to transfer money. A shopping application knows how to add products to an order.But these capabilities are usually accessible through screens designed for humans.From the perspective of an AI agent, the functionality is hidden behind navigation, buttons, text, images, scrolling, dialogs, and other UI elements.Consider a simple request: “Give me the latest food recipes from New York Times.”An agent operating only through the UI might have to find the application, launch it, wait for it to load, locate the food section, scroll through the content, interpret what appears on screen, and extract the relevant information.This is particularly important with LLM-based agents. The model may be good at reasoning about what it sees, but repeatedly asking a probabilistic model to navigate a UI is not an ideal interface between software systems. and can lead to mistakes.If an application already knows how to retrieve the information, there should be a more direct way to ask it.From guessing to structured executionPrevious generations of assistants were often based around predefined intents, keywords, and integrations.Modern LLMs have changed one part of the problem significantly: understanding what the user is trying to achieve.A user can say: “Add some milk to my shopping list.” or “Can you put milk on the list?” or “I forgot milk. Add it for me.”A language model can often infer that these requests represent the same underlying action.But understanding the request is only half of the problem.The model still needs a reliable way to discover which application can perform that action, understand the parameters it requires, execute it, and interpret the result.This is where AppFunctions become interesting.AppFunctions as a capability layerInstead of expecting the agent to understand your buttons and layouts, your application exposes structured capabilities that the system can discover and call.Conceptually, an application might expose functions such as:getHeadlines()addItemToShoppingList(item)playMatch(matchId)createNote(content)transferMoney(account, amount)The important part is not the exact function names.The important part is that the application is exposing capabilities rather than screens.The UI remains valuable for humans. AppFunctions provide an additional interface for software acting on the user’s behalf.The agentic flow: Retrieve, Match, ExecuteFirst, the agent retrieves available AppFunctions metadata.Next, a model interprets the user’s request and matches it against the available functions and their schemas.Finally, Android invokes the selected function and the application performs its normal business logic.For example:User:"Create a note that says buy milk." ↓Agent:understands the request ↓AppFunction discovery:finds createNote(content) ↓Android:executes createNote("buy milk") ↓Your application:validates → stores → returns resultThe interesting architectural point is that the AI does not need to implement your application’s business logic. Your application still owns that logic.Get Cedric Ferry’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe agent decides which capability to request. Your code remains responsible for executing it correctly.How the pieces are connectedAn agent application can retrieve function metadata, use a function-calling model to select the appropriate function, and then ask the Android platform to execute it.Your app therefore participates by exposing clearly defined capabilities. This separation is important.The agent handles interpretation.Android handles discovery and invocation.Your application handles business logic, permissions, data and persistence.That is a much cleaner boundary than giving an AI model control of a sequence of buttons and hoping it reaches the correct result.Prepare your app for AppFunctionsAs usual you need to import the right dependencies.KSP at the top of your gradle file: alias(libs.plugins.ksp)AppFunctions dependency:implementation(libs.androidx.appfunctions)implementation(libs.androidx.appfunctions.service)ksp(libs.androidx.appfunctions.compiler)KSP at the bottom of your gradle file:// Configure AppFunctions KSPksp { arg("appfunctions:aggregateAppFunctions", "true") arg("appfunctions:generateMetadataFromSchema", "false")}toml file:androidx-appfunctions = "1.0.0-alpha08"ksp = "2.3.6"androidx-appfunctions = { module = "androidx.appfunctions:appfunctions", version.ref = "androidx-appfunctions" }androidx-appfunctions-compiler = { module = "androidx.appfunctions:appfunctions-compiler", version.ref = "androidx-appfunctions" }androidx-appfunctions-service = { module = "androidx.appfunctions:appfunctions-service", version.ref = "androidx

title: 60 Android Interview Questions for Mid-Level Developers (2–5 Years)
excerpt: What Separates a Developer From an Android Engineer Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android DevelopmentKotlinMobile DevelopmentSoftware EngineeringInterview60 Android Interview Questions for Mid-Level Developers (2–5 Years)Sohaib AhmedFollow6 min read·5 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhat Separates a Developer From an Android EngineerAfter interviewing Android developers at different experience levels, I noticed one interesting pattern.Junior developers usually struggle with fundamentals.Senior developers are evaluated on architecture, leadership, and decision-making.But mid-level developers are different.At this stage, companies are no longer only looking for someone who can build screens and consume APIs. They expect developers to understand why things are designed in a certain way.A mid-level Android developer should be able to take ownership of features, make technical decisions, debug complex issues, and write code that other developers can maintain.This article covers the Android interview questions that reveal whether someone has moved beyond implementation and started thinking like an engineer.1. Android ArchitectureArchitecture is usually the first area where I differentiate between a developer who has experience and someone who has only worked on tasks.A mid-level developer should understand how applications are structured and why those decisions matter.QuestionsWhat architecture pattern have you used in your projects?A good answer should not only mention MVVM, MVI, or Clean Architecture.The important part is explaining:Why you selected that architecture.What problem it solved.What trade-offs it introduced.For example:“We used MVVM because we wanted to separate UI logic from business logic and make ViewModels easier to test.”That shows understanding.Why should business logic not live inside Activities or Fragments?A common mistake is creating large Activities containing:API calls.Database operations.Validation logic.Navigation decisions.This creates code that becomes difficult to test and maintain.A better approach separates responsibilities:UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → Data SourceThe exact structure can change, but responsibilities should remain clear.Explain Clean Architecture.A good mid-level developer should understand the purpose:Separation of concerns.Independent business logic.Easier testing.Better scalability.They should understand concepts like:Domain layer.Data layer.Presentation layer.Dependency direction.2. MVVM and MVIModern Android applications heavily depend on state management.QuestionsWhat is the difference between MVVM and MVI?A simple explanation:MVVM:View observes state.ViewModel prepares data.UI reacts to changes.MVI:UI is driven by a single state.User actions become intents/events.State changes happen through a predictable flow.Neither pattern automatically creates a good application.The important thing is consistency.How do you handle UI state?A strong answer includes concepts like:Loading state.Success state.Error state.Empty state.For example:sealed interface UiState { data object Loading : UiState data class Success(val data: List<Item>) : UiState data class Error(val message: String) : UiState}The interviewer is checking whether you think about all possible UI scenarios.3. Kotlin Advanced ConceptsAt the mid-level, Kotlin knowledge becomes important.QuestionsDifference between CoroutineScope and lifecycleScope?What are structured concurrency principles?Difference between Flow and StateFlow?Difference between SharedFlow and StateFlow?What are inline functions?What are reified types?Explain extension functions.What are sealed classes used for?Difference between List, Set, and Map?How does Kotlin handle null safety?4. Coroutines and Asynchronous ProgrammingMany developers use coroutines daily but cannot explain how they work.QuestionsWhat happens when a coroutine is suspended?A good answer:Suspending does not block the thread.The coroutine releases the thread while waiting and resumes later when the operation completes.Difference between launch and async?launchUsed when you don’t need a result.Example:Saving data.Sending analytics.asyncUsed when you need a returned value.Example:Fetching two APIs simultaneously and combining results.How do you handle coroutine exceptions?A good developer should mention:try/catch.CoroutineExceptionHandler.SupervisorJob.Proper scope management.5. Flow and Reactive ProgrammingQuestionsWhat is Kotlin Flow?Difference between Flow and LiveData?What is StateFlow?What is SharedFlow?How do you collect Flow safely?What happens when a collector is cancelled?A strong answer should explain that Flow provides a cold asynchronous stream, while StateFlow represents a hot state holder.6. Dependency InjectionDependency injection becomes important as applications grow.QuestionsWhy use Dependency Injection?What problems does DI solve?Explain dependency inversion.Difference between constructor injection and field injection.Have you used Hilt or Koin?How would you manage different environments?Examples:Development API.Production API.Testing dependencies.7. Room DatabaseMid-level developers should understand local persistence deeply.QuestionsDifference between Room and SQLite?What are Entities?What are DAOs?What are Relations in Room?How do migrations work?How do you handle database schema changes?What happens if a migration fails?8. Networking and API DesignQuestionsHow do you structure API calls?How do you handle API errors?How do you implement retry logic?How do you handle token expiration?How do interceptors work?Difference between authentication and authorization?A good developer understands that network failures are normal.Get Sohaib Ahmed’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inApplications should gracefully handle:Timeout.No internet.Server errors.Invalid responses.9. PaginationLarge data sets require proper handling.QuestionsHow would you load thousands of records efficiently?Have you used

title: Your MVI is probably MVVM with extra steps
excerpt: Start here. If your ViewModel looks like this, you’re writing MVVM. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeYour MVI is probably MVVM with extra stepsAndroidKotlinSoftware ArchitectureYour MVI is probably MVVM with extra stepsNguyenkhacphucFollow12 min read·5 days agoListenShareIf your ViewModel looks like this, you're writing MVVM.sealed interface Intent { data class Search(val q: String) : Intent data object Retry : Intent}class SearchViewModel(private val repo: Repo) : ViewModel() { private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SearchState()) val state = _state.asStateFlow() fun onIntent(i: Intent) = when (i) { is Intent.Search -> search(i.q) Intent.Retry -> search(_state.value.query) } private fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { _state.update { it.copy(loading = true, error = null) } try { val items = repo.search(q) _state.update { it.copy(loading = false, items = items) } } catch (e: Exception) { _state.update { it.copy(loading = false, error = e.message) } } }}Sometimes it's fancier. A Result hierarchy, a genuinely pure reduce:fun reduce(s: SearchState, r: Result): SearchState = when (r) { Result.Started -> s.copy(loading = true, error = null) is Result.Loaded -> s.copy(loading = false, items = r.items) is Result.Failed -> s.copy(loading = false, error = r.message)}private fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { _state.update { reduce(it, Result.Started) } val items = repo.search(q) _state.update { reduce(it, Result.Loaded(items)) } // <-- still here}That version earns partial credit. A pure (State, Result) -> State is worth having wherever you call it from.But look at where it's called from. _state.update sits inside the coroutine that did the async work. Type three characters, get three of them.Two properties, not one, and they're independent:1. A pure reducer — transitions are testable.2. A single writer — transitions are atomic, stale results are droppable.Dispatch-style MVI can have the first. Never the second, because the second is about where the write happens.Renaming search() to handleIntent() doesn't move the write. Neither does wrapping it in reduce().Two greps:grep -rn '_state\.update\|_state\.value =' src --include=*.ktgrep -rn 'fun reduce.*State.*):.*State' src --include=*.ktMore than one hit in the first, outside a single collector, and you don't have property 2.Three architectures, not two// 1. Honest MVVMfun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) } _state.update { it.copy(items = repo.search(q)) }}// 2. Dispatch MVI — identical, with a router in frontfun onIntent(i: Intent) = when (i) { is Intent.Search -> search(i.q)}// 3. Reducer MVI — the write movedfun onIntent(i: Intent) { intents.tryEmit(i) }The gap between 2 and 3 is real. The gap between 1 and 2 is vocabulary.The problem MVI solvesNot "unidirectional data flow" — MVVM has that. It's this:// 1. OUT OF ORDER// user types "a", "ab", "abc" — three coroutines alive_state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }val items = repo.search(q) // "ab" resolves last_state.update { it.copy(items = items) }// field says "abc", list shows results for "ab"// 2. READ-MODIFY-WRITE ACROSS A SUSPENSIONval cart = _state.value.cartval priced = pricing.quote(cart) // suspends; state moves_state.value = _state.value.copy(cart = priced) // stale write// 3. INTERLEAVED TRANSITIONS// flow A_state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }// flow B, concurrently_state.update { it.copy(error = "failed") }// emitted: loading = true AND error != null// a state your UI never expectedupdate {} gives you atomicity per mutation. Not consistency per transition.Why MVVM breaks this naturallyIt isn't sloppiness. Follow the value:fun onClick() { search(query) } // returns Unit. drops the Job.private fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { val items = repo.search(q) // <-- a value nobody is awaiting _state.update { it.copy(items = items) } // so it delivers it itself}The async producer has no consumer. There's exactly one thing that coroutine can do with its result: write it. And it writes from inside the async region, because that's where it lives.MVVM doesn't break the boundary. It never established one.Dispatch MVI puts a sealed class in front of that and changes nothing.What Dispatch MVI does not fixNo cancellation handle:private fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { ... }// ^ Job returned, immediately dropped// nothing to cancel when "abc" arrives. "ab" still lands.Nowhere to put a stale guard:private fun search(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { val items = repo.search(q) // is `q` still what the user wants? no reliable way to know. // the closure captured it before suspending. _state.update { it.copy(items = items) }}Transition logic has no address. "When a search fails, clear the spinner" is a statement inside a catch block. You can't call it — you have to provoke it:@Test fun `failure clears loading`() = runTest { Dispatchers.setMain(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) val repo = mockk<Repo>() coEvery { repo.search(any()) } throws IOException("timeout") val vm = SearchViewModel(repo) vm.onIntent(Intent.Search("kotlin")) advanceUntilIdle() assertFalse(vm.state.value.loading) Dispatchers.resetMain()}Five pieces of machinery to test one if.Reducer MVIASYNC repo.search(q) → Loaded(items) ─────────────────────────────SYNC reduce(state, Loaded) → state'The suspend function returns a result object, not a state mutation.private val intents = MutableSharedFlow<Intent>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)private val results = Channel<Result>(Channel.UNLIMITED)private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SearchState())fun onIntent(i: Intent) { intents.tryEmit(i) } // non-suspendinit { // async region: owns every coroutine, produces Results only intents.filterIsInstance<Intent.Search>() .map { it.q } .debounce(300) .distinctUntilChanged() .flatMapLatest { q -> flow { emit(Result.Started) emit(Result.Succeeded(q, repo.search(q))) }.catch { emit(Result.Failed(q, it.message)) } } .onEach { results.send(it) } .launchIn(viewModelScope) // sync region: one collector, o

title: Deep Linking in Android: The One Feature Every App Needs in 2026
excerpt: You receive a delivery notification saying: Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidMobile DeeplinksKotlinJetpack ComposeAndroid App DevelopmentDeep Linking in Android: The One Feature Every App Needs in 2026SupsabhiFollow6 min read·5 days ago11ListenShareYou receive a delivery notification saying:“Delivery for your order has started. Track it now.”You tap the notification, and instead of opening the app’s home screen, it directly opens the Order Tracking page.How does this happen? The answer is Deep Linking.It feels like magic. It’s not. It’s a few lines of XML and Kotlin, and by the end of this article, you’ll know exactly how to add it to your own app.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeDeep linking is one of those features that makes an Android app feel smooth, modern, and connected to the web. It improves user experience by taking users directly to the screen they need instead of making them navigate through multiple pages.This is useful for product pages, blog posts, offer screens, profile pages, and more. For developers, it improves user experience, engagement, and conversion. So let’s explore it in more detail.What is this Magical Deep Linking?At its core, a deep link is a URL that takes a user straight to a specific page or piece of content inside your app, bypassing the app’s main home screen.For example :When user taps on https://myshoppingapp.com/product/125instead ofPress enter or click to view image in full sizeIt directly opens Product Details (Product ID = 125)That’s Deep Linking.You’ve seen this everywhere:Clicking a WhatsApp link opens a specific chatTapping an Instagram link opens a specific profileClicking a password reset email opens your banking app on the reset screenThat’s deep linking in action.Types of Deep Links1. Standard Deep LinksThese use custom URI schemes or standard HTTP routes (http, https, or custom schemes like myapp://).Example: myapp://product/10Only your application understands this custom URL.They take users to specific screens in your app. If the app isn’t installed, the device might prompt the user to choose a browser or show a broken link unless handled.2. Android App Links (Verified Deep Links)A special type of Android deep link verified against your actual website domain. If the app is installed, it opens immediately without showing an “Open with…” choice dialog.Get Supsabhi’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inAndroid recommends App Links for production because they provide a better user experience and are more secure. For a production app, App Links are the gold standard and Google’s recommended approach.How Deep Linking WorksThe process is simple.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeStep-by-Step Implementation in KotlinLet’s build a working example. Imagine we are building a store app, and we want links like [https://myawesomeapp.com/product/42]to open our app’s MainActivity directly to the DetailsScreen.Step 1: Configure AndroidManifest.xmlTo let Android know your app handles specific URLs, add an <intent-filter> inside the activity tag in your AndroidManifest.xml.<activityandroid:name=".MainActivity"android:exported="true"><intent-filter><action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" /><category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" /></intent-filter><! - Deep Link Intent Filter →<intent-filter android:autoVerify="true"><action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" /><category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" /><category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" /><! - Accepts URIs that begin with "https://myawesomeapp.com/product" →<dataandroid:scheme="https"android:host="myawesomeapp.com"android:pathPrefix="/product" /></intent-filter></activity>Key Attributes Explained:android.intent.action.VIEW: Required so the filter can respond to search results or link clicks.android.intent.category.BROWSABLE: Required for the link to be clickable from a web browser.android.intent.category.DEFAULT: Allows the app to handle implicit intents.android:pathPrefix=”/product”: Ensures only URLs starting with /product match this activity.Step 2: Define the NavGraph with navDeepLinkAttach the navDeepLink builder to the composable destination inside your NavHost. Compose Navigation automatically parses the route parameter from the deep link URL.package com.example.deeplinkdemoimport androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Boximport androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxSizeimport androidx.compose.material3.Textimport androidx.compose.runtime.Composableimport androidx.compose.ui.Alignmentimport androidx.compose.ui.Modifierimport androidx.navigation.NavTypeimport androidx.navigation.compose.NavHostimport androidx.navigation.compose.composableimport androidx.navigation.compose.rememberNavControllerimport androidx.navigation.navArgumentimport androidx.navigation.navDeepLinkconst val BASE_URL = "https://myawesomeapp.com"@Composablefun AppNavigation() {val navController = rememberNavController()NavHost(navController = navController,startDestination = "home") {// Home Screencomposable(route = "home") {HomeScreen()}// Details Screen with Deep Linkcomposable(route = "details/{itemId}",arguments = listOf(navArgument("itemId") {type = NavType.StringType}),deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink {// Match URI pattern: https://myawesomeapp.com/product/42uriPattern = "$BASE_URL/product/{itemId}"})) { backStackEntry ->// Extract argument parsed directly by Compose Navval itemId = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("itemId") ?: "Unknown"DetailsScreen(itemId = itemId)}}}@Composablefun HomeScreen() {Box(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(), contentAlignment = Alignment.Center) {Text(text = "Home Screen")}}@Composablefun DetailsScreen(itemId: String) {Box(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(), contentAlignment = Alignment.Center) {Text(text = "Loaded Item Details for ID: $itemId")}}Step 3: Handle Optional Query Parameters (Optional)If your link format includes query parameters (e.g., [https://myawesomeapp.com/product?itemId

title: LinkedIn made a career plan for me. Does it work?
excerpt: I started to use my free month of LinkedIn Premium and after some quick questions it created a learning plan for me. I will share with you… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeKotlinMobileMobile App DevelopmentKotlin MultiplatformSoftware DevelopmentLinkedIn made a career plan for me. Does it work?Saidel LópezFollow3 min read·5 days ago1ListenShareI started to use my free month of LinkedIn Premium and after some quick questions it created a learning plan for me. I will share with you my experience as an Android Developer and my search to learn properly Kotlin Multiplatform.LinkedIn LearningTurns out, LinkedIn now offers multiple courses and certifications from different topics with well stablished instructors. Instead of blindly moving everywhere, there’s this feature that generates a custom plan. So I took the chance to follow a learning path to master Kotlin Multiplatform.How hard is it to create a plan for KMP?Consider that Kotlin Multiplatform is an ambitious plan of Google to create applications for different platforms in order to reuse code, business logic and even UI for Android, iOS and Web. It doesn’t only include a full and deep knowledge of Kotlin language, but Jetpack Compose, OOP and even some topics such as frontend, styles, Swift, SwiftUI and architecture of iPhone apps. So my expectation is a mix of all those topics together.How does LinkedIn create your plan?The experience is a very basic one. There’s this form that ask you what your current job is and ask you for some keywords to start to search between the available courses. It creates modules that encapsulates the courses and the order to take this courses. Establishes a goal of half an hour per week in order to keep trace of you advances. There are certifications programs for commons stacks topics as AWS, Google Services or Data Science where the learning path is already pre-defined.What was the proposed career plan?It is hard to say by now. My first impression was that not all the topics were touched in there given the name of the courses and how much time it takes to finish them (around 3 hours each). It created a plan of three modules. The first one dedicated to Kotlin basics (2 courses); the second one on Java Threads and Concurrency (1 Course); and the third one finally dedicated to Kotlin Multiplatform basics and relevant libraries.Although not my original expectation, turns out that the information is quite condensed with a lot of information per minute. It covers a lot of ground all of a sudden. From my point of view, the jump between knowing the very basics of Kotlin to fixing issues in Swift UI is not trivial. It will make people struggle with the learning curve.Get Saidel López’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inIn general:I think is a good general view of complex topics. It requires certain level of knowledge before starting this path.I should consider the courses quite informative but it requires you to give an extra to practice by your end. The easiest path is just to see the videos, download the project and run the examples. But you’ll feel empty this way.LinkedIn doesn’t ask for your current level to create the learning plan. It assumes that you’re a mid level revisiting the basics. Maybe it took the info from my profile and assume my level. That’s blurry to me since it didn’t ask me.I truly think that more courses are required in between to get the whole knowledge and don’t feel that you pass from baby steps to command a nuclear submarine in 5 hours.ConclusionsThis is a good initiative that I’m certain it will evolve through the time. Having LinkedIn integrated with courses and certifications is a great idea since basically it updates your CV in real time. Even so, I still don’t believe a hiring manager will take this info blindly and hire you because of your path. At least not yet.I strongly suggest you to take some courses and check it yourself. In the Links section you’ll see the courses it proposed to me so you can go on and check yourself. Maybe you can process all this info better than me.LinksKotlin Essential Training: Object-Oriented and Async Code (2h 51m)Kotlin Essential Training: Functions, Collections, and I/O (4h 42m)Advanced Java: Threads and Concurrency (2h 59m)Kotlin Multiplatform Development (2h 33m)Kotlin Multiplatform Libraries (1h 39m)

title: Android System Design: Building a Production-Ready Authentication Flow
excerpt: A secure authentication system is more than simply storing a token after login. It must handle token expiration, concurrent API requests… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidAndroid DevelopmentSystem Design InterviewKotlinMobile System DesignAndroid System Design: Building a Production-Ready Authentication FlowNematFollow6 min read·5 days ago41ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Sasun Bughdaryan on UnsplashA secure authentication system is more than simply storing a token after login. It must handle token expiration, concurrent API requests, app restarts, network failures, and logout scenarios without interrupting the user.The following implementation pattern is widely used in production Android applications because it is reliable, scalable, and easy to maintain.Step 1: Store Tokens SecurelyAfter a successful login, the backend typically returns two tokens:Access Token — A short-lived token included with every authenticated API request.Refresh Token — A long-lived token used only to obtain a new access token when the current one expires.These tokens should never be stored in plain SharedPreferences or an unencrypted DataStore.Instead:Store them using encrypted local storage.Protect the encryption keys with the Android Keystore.Keep persistence responsibilities inside a dedicated TokenDataStore.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe rest of the application should never know where or how these tokens are stored.Step 2: Introduce a SessionManagerInstead of allowing every component to read and write tokens directly, introduce a SessionManager as the single source of truth for the application’s authentication state.The SessionManager is responsible for:Saving a new session after loginRestoring the session when the app startsProviding the current access tokenClearing the session during logoutBroadcasting authentication state changesAll authentication-related components communicate with the SessionManager, not with TokenDataStore directly.Prevent Concurrent RefreshesOne important responsibility of the SessionManager is ensuring that only one token refresh happens at a time.Consider this scenario:Request A → 401Request B → 401Request C → 401Without coordination, all three requests may attempt to refresh the token simultaneously, resulting in:Refresh Request 1Refresh Request 2Refresh Request 3This wastes network resources and can even invalidate refresh tokens on some backend implementations.Instead, the SessionManager should serialize refresh operations (for example, using a Mutex). The first request performs the refresh while the others wait for the result.Step 3: Isolate the Refresh APIRefreshing a token is a special operation.The refresh request:should not include the expired access token,should not pass through the authentication interceptor,should not trigger another refresh attempt.Otherwise, a failed refresh request could trigger another refresh, creating an infinite loop.A clean solution is to use two Retrofit/OkHttp clients.Authenticated Client │ ├── AuthInterceptor ├── TokenAuthenticator └── All protected APIsPlain Client │ ├── Refresh Token API └── Login/Register APIStep 4: Attach the Access Token AutomaticallyEvery authenticated request requires an Authorization header.Instead of adding it manually on every API call, use an OkHttp Interceptor.This keeps networking concerns out of the UI and repository layers.Some applications also check the token’s expiration time here. If the token is close to expiring, the app can refresh it proactively before the server returns a 401 Unauthorized response.Step 5: Handle Token Expiration TransparentlyEventually, every access token expires.When the backend responds with 401 Unauthorized, the application should:Pause the failed request.Ask the SessionManager to refresh the token.Retry the original request using the new access token.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeFrom the user’s perspective, this entire process happens automatically.To avoid infinite retry loops, ensure each request is retried only once. If the retry also fails with 401, treat the session as invalid.How OkHttp Authenticator WorksWhen an API request receives a 401 Unauthorized response, OkHttp invokes the application’s Authenticator.Unlike an Interceptor, which runs before a request is sent, an Authenticator runs after the server rejects a request due to authentication.Get Nemat’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe responsibility of the Authenticator is simple:Detect that authentication has failed.Obtain a valid access token.Rebuild the original request with the new token.Return the rebuilt request to OkHttp.OkHttp then automatically retries the request. The calling code remains completely unaware that a refresh occurred.This separation of responsibilities keeps the networking layer clean:Interceptor → attaches tokens to outgoing requests.Authenticator → replaces expired tokens after a 401.The sequence looks like this:Request │ ▼AuthInterceptor │ ▼Server │ ▼401 Unauthorized │ ▼Authenticator │ ▼Refresh Access Token │ ▼Create New Request │ ▼Retry OnceStep 6: Distinguish Authentication Failures from Network FailuresNot every refresh failure means the user should be logged out.Refresh token rejected (HTTP 4xx)If the backend rejects the refresh request, the refresh token is no longer valid.The application should:clear the local session,remove stored tokens,navigate the user back to the login screen.Network timeout or connectivity issueIf the refresh request fails because of:no internet connection,timeout,temporary server outage,the session should remain intact.Logging the user out in this situation would create a poor user experience, as the authentication credentials are still valid.Step 7: Centralize Session Expiration HandlingThe SessionManager should expose the authentication state as a StateFlow or Flow.When a session becomes invalid, it emits a “session expired” state.Step 8: Restore the Session on App StartupWhen the application launches, determine whether a valid session already exists before decidi

title: Five Years of Jetpack Compose: Five Things I Love About It
excerpt: 1. Lists stopped being a project Continue reading on Medium »
content: Jetpack ComposeKotlinCompose MultiplatformKotlin MultiplatformAndroidFive Years of Jetpack Compose: Five Things I Love About ItKevin Desai3 min read·5 days ago----ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeJetpack Compose Logo1. Lists stopped being a projectA RecyclerView list was four files: the XML row layout, the ViewHolder, the Adapter, and a DiffUtil callback. Every one of them was boilerplate, and the DiffUtil callback was where the bugs lived. Get the item comparison subtly wrong and rows would flicker or recycle into the wrong state.LazyColumn is three lines, and the key parameter replaces DiffUtil entirely.LazyColumn { items(listOfItems, key = { it.id }) { item -> ItemRow(item, onTap = { doSomething(item.id) }) }}The key does the diffing. Compose uses it to track identity across recompositions, so reorders animate correctly and state stays attached to the right row.2. Animations are easyFading a view in and out took two code paths and a callback. You couldn’t flip visibility and animate at the same time, because GONE takes effect immediately and cuts the animation off mid-frame. So you animated alpha, set visibility in an end action, and remembered to reset alpha on the way back in.// hidingview.animate().alpha(0f).setDuration(200) .withEndAction(() -> view.setVisibility(View.GONE));// showingview.setAlpha(0f);view.setVisibility(View.VISIBLE);view.animate().alpha(1f).setDuration(200);AnimatedVisibility is one boolean. Compose keeps the content in the tree until the exit animation finishes and then removes it, which is the bookkeeping that end action was doing by hand.AnimatedVisibility( visible = isExpanded, enter = fadeIn() + expandVertically(), exit = fadeOut() + shrinkVertically()) { DetailPanel()}Press enter or click to view image in full size3. Layouts got boring, in the good wayMost screens are a Row, a Column, and a Box, nested. There's no ConstraintLayout ID graph to maintain and no wondering which constraint is fighting which.Get Kevin Desai’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inNesting is also cheap here in a way it wasn’t with Views. Compose measures each child once by design, so you don’t pay the double-measure penalty that made nested LinearLayout with weights something you avoided.Row(verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically) { Icon(painterResource(profileIcon), null) Column(Modifier.weight(1f).padding(start = 12.dp)) { Text(firstName, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium) Text(lastName, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodySmall) } Switch(checked = profile.isSignedIn, onCheckedChange = onToggle)}I can read that and figure out how the screen would look easily. Something that was doable with ConstraintLayout/LinearLayout as well just a lot more tedious and verbose.4. It stopped being Android-onlyCompose Multiplatform took the same composable functions to desktop, iOS, and web. The parts that are genuinely shared are the ones you’d want to share anyway: layout, state handling, design system. Platform specifics stay behind expect/actual.@Composablefun ProfileCard(profile: UserProfile) { Card { /* identical on Android, desktop, iOS */ }}Compose Multiplatform has come a long way and it’s performance on non Android platforms is increasing with every single release.5. The Compose mental model is portableCompose isn’t an Android idiom you learn and then leave at the door. Describing a screen as a function of state, instead of mutating a hierarchy, is how SwiftUI, Flutter and React all work. Compose previewed at Google I/O in May 2019 and SwiftUI landed at WWDC three weeks later, both downstream of React in 2013 and Flutter in 2018.The overlap is close enough to read across without a translation layer:@Composablefun Greeting(name: String) { Column { Text("Hello, $name") Button(onClick = { greet() }) { Text("Tap me") } }}struct Greeting: View { let name: String var body: some View { VStack { Text("Hello, \(name)") Button("Tap me") { greet() } } }}Column and VStack, Text and Text, Button and Button. The machinery underneath is different: SwiftUI's body returns some View and the compiler types that tree statically, while a composable returns Unit and emits nodes as a side effect. But I can read a SwiftUI screen without looking anything up, and that was never true of UIKit. UI writing skills are now portable.Compose isn’t perfect. Recomposition still surprises me, and I’ve spent real time in the layout inspector working out why something recomposed more often than it should have. But writing Compose is fun like XML never was. Building complex UIs is much easier now and so are animations. Here is to another five years!

title: Kotlin Coroutine Exception Handling: The Mental Model That Made It Click for Me
excerpt: Exception handling and cancellation were among the most confusing parts of Kotlin coroutines for me. Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinKotlin CoroutinesException HandlingStructured ConcurrencyKotlin Coroutine Exception Handling: The Mental Model That Made It Click for MeDima DanilovFollow16 min read·5 days ago2ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeException handling and cancellation were among the most confusing parts of Kotlin coroutines for me.There are plenty of good articles and discussions about this topic, but I rarely find one explanation that is enough on its own. I usually need to read several versions before the idea clicks. Knowing the rules is not enough. I want to understand why they produce the behavior I see.One source that helped me was Marcin Moskała’s Kotlin Coroutines: Deep Dive. After reading it for the second time, I tried to connect the individual rules into one mental model.Running the examples:Every runtime-behavior example includes the required imports, a fun main(), and its expected output. It can be copied directly into the Kotlin Playground or an IntelliJ IDEA Kotlin project with the kotlinx-coroutines-core dependency and run as written. Shorter snippets without main() are conceptual fragments that assume the declarations shown by their context.The difficulty does not come from one complicated rule. It comes from several simple behaviors interacting:A coroutine can complete successfully, be cancelled, or fail.The direct parent Job determines how a child's failure affects the hierarchy.The coroutine builder determines how we can observe the result or failure.Suspending scope functions determine where child coroutines are awaited and where failures can be caught.This is the shortcut I use:builder = how can I observe the failure?direct parent = who is affected by the failure?scope function = where do we wait, and where can the failure be caught?Let us build that model one layer at a time.1. Failure and cancellation are not the sameA coroutine may finish in three relevant ways:It returns normally.It is cancelled with a CancellationException.It fails with another exception that escapes its body.Cancellation and failure can both leave a Job with isCancelled == true, but coroutine machinery treats their causes differently.When a regular child created with launch or async fails with an exception other than CancellationException, it fails its regular parent Job. The parent then cancels its other children.Cancellation follows a different rule. When a parent is cancelled, cancellation propagates downward to all of its children. However, when one child is cancelled independently with CancellationException, that cancellation does not cancel its parent or siblings.The relationship can be summarized like this:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeA parent still tracks its children and cannot complete until they reach a final state. But normal child cancellation is not reported as a failure of the parent.Here is an independently cancelled child:import kotlinx.coroutines.*// Expected output:// Child cancelled: true// Parent is still active: truefun main() = runBlocking<Unit> { val parent = launch { val child = launch { delay(1_000) } child.cancelAndJoin() println("Child cancelled: ${child.isCancelled}") println("Parent is still active: $isActive") } parent.join()}The child finishes in the cancelled state, but the parent continues normally.Can the parent react to an independently cancelled child?Yes. Independent child cancellation does not automatically propagate upward, but the parent can observe the child’s final state and apply its own policy. For example, an operation may require the second child to be cancelled when the first child is independently cancelled:import kotlinx.coroutines.*// Expected output:// First child cancelled: true// Second child cancelled: true// Parent is still active: truefun main() = runBlocking<Unit> { coroutineScope { val first = launch { delay(1_000) } val second = launch { delay(1_000) } first.invokeOnCompletion { cause -> if (cause is CancellationException) { second.cancel( CancellationException("First child was cancelled") ) } } first.cancel(CancellationException("No longer needed")) joinAll(first, second) println("First child cancelled: ${first.isCancelled}") println("Second child cancelled: ${second.isCancelled}") println("Parent is still active: $isActive") }}About this example: This shows that a parent can observe child cancellation. It is not a general coordination pattern. When several production tasks share one lifetime, cancelling their owning scope is usually easier to reason about.invokeOnCompletion observes completion, it does not catch an exception propagating from the child. The callback runs whenever the child completes, and its cause describes how:null means the child completed successfully.CancellationException means the child was cancelled.Any other exception means the child failed.Here, the if body runs only for cancellation. If first fails with another exception, the callback still runs, but the regular coroutineScope rule already cancels second. Explicit handling is needed only because independent cancellation does not propagate to the sibling.The direction shortcut is therefore:parent cancellation → downward to childrenregular child failure → upward through regular parentsindependent child cancellation → does not cancel parent or siblings2. The direct parent comes from the scopeBoth launch and async are extension functions on CoroutineScope:fun CoroutineScope.launch(...): Jobfun <T> CoroutineScope.async(...): Deferred<T>This matters because the receiver scope provides the coroutine context used by the builder. That context normally contains the parent Job, a dispatcher, a coroutine name, and other context elements.Conceptually:CoroutineScope└── provides a context containing a Job └── launch or async creates a new child JobFor example:val scope = CoroutineScope(Job() + Dispatchers.Default)val child = scope.launch { // This coroutine has its own Job. // Its direct parent is the Job from `scope`.}Nested builders create anoth

title: The Android Overlay Shortcut We Almost Overbuilt (Until We Remembered What We Already Had)
excerpt: Picture a locked-down tablet — a hotel check-in kiosk, a warehouse scanning terminal, any device running one app full-screen with nothing… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidReact NativeAndroid App DevelopmentKotlinThe Android Overlay Shortcut We Almost Overbuilt (Until We Remembered What We Already Had)Subhadeep DasFollow3 min read·5 days agoListenSharePicture a locked-down tablet — a hotel check-in kiosk, a warehouse scanning terminal, any device running one app full-screen with nothing else allowed to touch it. Now imagine you need to show a small popup on top of it. Nothing fancy. Just “here’s what was just scanned,” visible for a second, then gone.The obvious way to float something on an Android screen is the “Draw over other apps” permission. Every floating chat bubble and screen-recorder button uses it. So we almost went that route. But building it out meant walking through the whole checklist: declare the permission, check at runtime whether it’s actually granted, send the user to a Settings screen to turn it on manually, handle them backing out without granting it, and re-check every time the app opens because they can revoke it whenever they want. A lot of scaffolding for one small popup.We Already Had a Simpler DoorHere’s the context that made this easy: our app wasn’t picking an Accessibility Service just to get a popup. It already needed one for something unrelated — reading scanned data and typing it directly into whatever field is focused in another app. On Android, that’s not a “nice to have” implementation choice; without root access, an Accessibility Service is basically the only supported way to reach into another app’s focused field and set its text. So the service existed for a real, load-bearing reason, and it was already alive and connected by the time the popup idea came up.It turns out Accessibility Services get their own way of drawing on screen: TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY. And it skips the entire checklist above. No permission declaration. No runtime check. No settings redirect. No "what if they say no" branch. If your service is connected, you just grab the window manager and add the view. Done.Get Subhadeep Das’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inIt’s not a trick or a loophole — it’s genuinely documented as a separate, trusted window type available specifically to connected accessibility services, precisely because tools like screen readers need to draw over anything, reliably, without asking permission every time. It’s also more capable than the normal overlay in one interesting way: it can draw over places a regular “draw over other apps” overlay explicitly can’t touch anymore, like the status bar or lock screen — those got locked down for everyone else back in Android 8.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeAndroid Accessibility shortcut toggleWhy This Is the Real LessonThe point isn’t “accessibility services are a secret bypass for locked-down devices.” We checked, and Android’s own kiosk-mode documentation says the opposite of what would make a tidier story: overlays from other apps aren’t blocked by default in kiosk (lock task) mode at all — an administrator has to explicitly opt in to blocking them. So the “it gets past kiosk restrictions” angle isn’t the honest reason this worked.The real reason is simpler and, honestly, more useful to remember: if you already have an Accessibility Service running for a legitimate purpose, adding an overlay on top of it is nearly free. No extra permission flow, no extra user friction, no extra failure states to design around. The moment you’re already paying for that access, the popup is a few lines of code, not a feature.Where This Shows UpAny single-purpose kiosk or terminal device where a background tool occasionally needs to say something to the person using it.Warehouse or field-scanning apps that already inject data into another app’s fields and want instant “got it” feedback.Any app that already has an accessibility service for a real reason and is about to reach for SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW out of habit, without noticing it doesn't need to.The Honest CaveatNone of this is a reason to spin up an Accessibility Service just to get an easier overlay. That permission is heavy for good reason — it can technically see and interact with almost everything on the device, and Google reviews its use closely. The savings here only kick in when the service already exists for a genuine purpose. In your case, it did — the wedge/typing feature needed it regardless of the popup. In that case, this is one of those rare moments where the simpler implementation and the more capable one are the same choice.

title: Samsung One UI 9: Why It Skips the Redesign
excerpt: Why the biggest update in years isn’t really about how it looks. Look at it from a UI/UX angle and you’ll notice Samsung isn’t trying to… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Mobile Ui DesignUX DesignProduct DesignSamsung One UiAndroidWhat’s New in One UI 9 | Samsung USDesign Studio UI/UXFollow9 min read·5 days ago1ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhy the biggest update in years isn’t really about how it looks. Look at it from a UI/UX angle and you’ll notice Samsung isn’t trying to make One UI 9 look different, it’s trying to make it think ahead. AI handles more of the small decisions for you now, foldables finally get layouts that adjust instead of just stretching awkwardly, and privacy stops hiding in some settings menu nobody checks.Almost every Galaxy device runs on Samsung One UI, your phone, your tablet, that foldable if you’ve got one. Nobody really sits and thinks about it, but it’s the thing deciding how you tap, scroll, and lately, talk to AI, every day without you noticing. Something changed with this version though. Samsung stopped trying to make things look different and started trying to make things work smarter. Less redesign, more automation. Less “notice this new icon” and more “the phone just handled that for you.Here’s what we’re getting into: what’s actually new, what still bugs people, how One UI 9 testing has gone across different devices, and what any of this means if you’re the one building apps for Galaxy phones.What Is Samsung One UI, and Why Did Samsung Ditch TouchWiz?Anyone who owned a Samsung phone before 2018 remembers TouchWiz. Menus everywhere, navigation that made no sense, and forget using it one handed unless your thumb had unusual reach.Samsung One UI fixed that with one basic idea: put the stuff people actually tap within thumb’s reach. Menus moved down, content moved up, and suddenly big phones stopped feeling like they needed two hands just to open an app. That’s the thumb zone design in its purest form, put the important stuff where fingers naturally land, not where a designer thinks it looks good.That single fix grew into something bigger over the years. Samsung One UI isn’t just about reachability anymore. It’s the layer holding together Galaxy AI, DeX, foldable multitasking, and more customization than most Android skins even attempt. Icons, widgets, lock screens, system sounds, you can mess with almost all of it, and somehow Samsung still keeps the basics simple enough that someone who just wants their phone to work doesn’t feel lost.One UI 9 Features: What’s New in the Android 17 UpdateOne UI 9 runs on Android 17. Samsung confirmed the beta details on its own newsroom well before the stable version landed on July 22, 2026, alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Z Flip 8. This is really the first release built around that Android base from the ground up, so here’s what actually changed, and why it matters from a design standpoint.Gemini AI Integration in One UI 9The biggest change is how deep Gemini now sits inside Samsung’s software. The partnership with Google has clearly moved forward, and you get Gemini Intelligence, a system wide AI layer that helps with searches, content, and everyday tasks without needing to dig through five different apps. There’s also Gemini Notebook, which works like one shared space for notes and research instead of having everything scattered around.Now Nudge got noticeably sharper too. It used to wait for you to ask something. Now it just suggests things on its own, like realizing your day’s packed and nudging you to head out a little earlier.Here’s the design tension worth naming though: proactive suggestions only work if they’re right often enough to feel helpful instead of intrusive. A nudge that’s wrong three times in a row stops feeling like intelligence and starts feeling like noise you have to dismiss. Samsung hasn’t published failure rates or how Nudge handles being wrong, and that’s the actual UX question that matters here, not just “does it exist” but “does it know when to shut up.”This shift, where the interface acts before you even reach for it, isn’t unique to Samsung. It’s part of a broader design direction our team has written about in Zero UI Design: Examples & Trends, which looks at how interfaces are increasingly built to respond to context rather than wait for a tap. Now Nudge is basically Zero UI thinking applied to a phone you already own, minus the polish that makes Zero UI actually trustworthy.New One UI 9 Features Beyond AINot everything here revolves around AI. A few practical touches deserve some credit too:My FanCam automatically tracks and crops action shots in your Gallery, so you’re not stuck zooming in every time you want a decent photo from a concert or your kid’s football game.Customizable Quick Settings can finally be arranged the way you’d actually use them, not the way Samsung guessed you would. This is a small but real fix to a common IA mistake: designing for an assumed user instead of letting the real user define priority.Blue Dot location indicator pops up whenever an app is quietly using your location, and tapping it tells you exactly who’s responsible. This is a just-in-time disclosure pattern, showing information at the exact moment it’s relevant instead of front-loading it in a permissions screen nobody reads carefully.Upgraded DeX multitasking lets you move windows between virtual desktops now and preview them right from Recents.One UI 9 vs One UI 8.5: What ChangedOne UI 8.5 went big on visuals. New icons, redesigned panels, a fresh look basically everywhere. One UI 9 goes the opposite way. SamMobile’s breakdown of the update notes that since One UI 8.5 already delivered the major visual overhaul, One UI 9 wasn’t expected to bring similarly big design changes, and that’s exactly how it played out. Animations feel smoother, transitions snap a bit quicker, and most of what’s new just works quietly in the background instead of showing off. It’s less about reinventing and more about refining, and for software this old, that’s probably the smarter move anyway.Designing for Foldables: One UI 9’s Adaptive Layout

He and his team develop and maintain an Android-based platform that gives parents control over apps, contacts, screen time, messaging, and browsing through a web-based interface. As the company and its engineering organization have grown, maintaining consistent code quality, security visibility, and policy enforcement – across multiple repositories and language ecosystems – has become increasingly important. In this interview, we spoke with Drew about introducing Qodana into the team’s workflow, the challenges they were trying to solve, and what they’ve learned during rollout. Can you tell us about your role and your team?I’m a career full-stack software engineer, currently working as a DevSecOps engineer. My day-to-day sits between the engineering teams and the systems they ship through: CI/CD, pipelines, developer tooling, and the security and quality controls that run alongside them. Alongside that, I’ve built several internal services that support our DevOps work, done a lot of PR and code review, mentored other engineers, and dug into time and space complexity and other performance issues across the codebase. I drove the Qodana adoption directly, from evaluation through to rollout. What were your biggest challenges around code quality before Qodana?We already had written standards for code style, pull request reviews, and QA. Style guides existed for TypeScript, Kotlin, and React. Every PR required two reviewers. What was missing was consistent enforcement of any of it. ESLint ran in some places, sometimes locally, sometimes during a build, but it was not a formal CI step. Prettier and tests were reliable; but static analysis was not. Across several language ecosystems and a growing repo count, that meant standards were applied unevenly, depending on which repo a developer was working in and who reviewed their PR. There was no single place to see whether quality was getting better or worse over time. How did you manage code reviews and quality checks previously?Reviews were manual, with two reviewers per PR, against the written style guides. Automated checks in the pipeline were limited to formatting and tests. Linters ran inconsistently across repos, and there was no shared static analysis layer enforcing the same rules everywhere. Anything that needed deeper inspection (security issues, license problems, dependency risks) was caught case by case, rather than as a pipeline step. Were there any specific compliance or security requirements you needed to meet?Yes. The product we sell goes on kids’ devices, so security and dependency posture matter to us. We’re working toward alignment with CIS Controls v8 and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. Those frameworks shape how we think about the development pipeline. Several of the controls land directly on the kind of work Qodana supports. CIS v8 Control 7 covers continuous vulnerability management, and Control 16 covers application software security, which calls out static analysis and secure coding practices specifically. CSF 2.0’s Protect and Identify functions cover similar ground: knowing what’s in your software, knowing where the risk is, and keeping controls between vulnerable code and production. For us, these frameworks lead to the same practical requirement: automated checks that run on every change, with results we can audit later. Drew’s take on Qodana Copy heading link What made you start looking for a solution like Qodana?A few things lined up at once. The pipeline itself was being modernized, and we wanted to fold static analysis, SCA, and license checks into it. Our Dependency Update Policy needed enforcement tooling, and the inconsistency across repositories was getting harder to ignore as the codebase grew. We needed a single tool that could provide coverage across our languages and run in both CI and the IDE. What other tools did you consider?We looked at SonarQube, ESLint-only setups, and standalone software composition analysis tools. Each covered part of the problem. None covered the full surface area without significant operational overhead or a patchwork of tools to integrate. What stood out about Qodana?Qodana fit the requirements better than the alternatives.
