excerpt: Turn code guidelines into automated guardrails to prevent footguns and fragile tests. Every growing codebase accumulates “dangerous” APIs: methods that are easy to misuse, cause flaky tests, or break architecture boundaries. Initially, teams rely on PR reviews or wiki pages: “Don’t use spyk in tests," or "Use custom scopes instead of GlobalScope." Eventually, human vigilance fails. Guidelines get ignored, code reviewers miss things, and dangerous patterns spread across pull requests. The fix? St
content: KontureAndroidCode QualityAndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentHow to Ban a Class or Method in Code (And Why You Should)Turn code guidelines into automated guardrails to prevent footguns and fragile tests.Bao LeFollow3 min read·4 days ago461ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeEvery growing codebase accumulates “dangerous” APIs: methods that are easy to misuse, cause flaky tests, or break architecture boundaries.Initially, teams rely on PR reviews or wiki pages: “Don’t use spyk in tests," or "Use custom scopes instead of GlobalScope."Eventually, human vigilance fails. Guidelines get ignored, code reviewers miss things, and dangerous patterns spread across pull requests.The fix? Stop relying on memory. Automate the ban.What Does “Banning an API” Mean?Banning an API means setting up automated static checks or compiler rules that trigger build errors or linter failures whenever forbidden classes, functions, or imports appear in source code.Get Bao Le’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inInstead of catching bad patterns during manual code review or worse, after an outage or flaky test run in production, the feedback loop shrinks to milliseconds inside the developer’s IDE or local build.Why Should You Ban APIs?Code Reviews Don’t Scale: As engineering teams grow and PR velocity increases, human reviewers cannot reliably catch every forbidden import or anti-pattern. Banning APIs shifts enforcement from subjective human vigilance to deterministic build checks.Eliminate Subtle Footguns: Certain methods are design anti-patterns by nature (spyk(), GlobalScope). Banning them prevents developers from shooting themselves in the foot before code even reaches CI.Prevent Test Flakiness & Runtime Leaks: Unsafe concurrency calls or blocking sleeps introduce non-deterministic race conditions and thread starvation that waste hours of debugging time.Enforce Architectural Boundaries: Banning cross-layer imports prevents domain modules from referencing implementation details or framework dependencies, stopping architecture drift before it starts.3 Real-World APIs You Should Ban1. MockK’s spyk (The Partial-Mock Footgun)spyk() creates a partial mock where un-stubbed methods execute real code.Why ban it? Spies obscure tight coupling and introduce fragile, non-deterministic test failures when internal class logic changes.Use instead: Pure mocks (mockk<T>()), fakes, or dependency injection.2. GlobalScope & runBlocking (The Concurrency Traps)GlobalScope launches top-level coroutines that bypass structured concurrency, while runBlocking blocks execution threads.Why ban them? GlobalScope causes memory and coroutine leaks. runBlocking starves threads and triggers UI freezes or ANRs.Use instead: Inject a lifecycle-managed CoroutineScope or use coroutineScope {}.3. Thread.sleep() (The Flaky Test Anti-Pattern)Thread.sleep(1000) is often used to hack around async test race conditions.Why ban it? It slows down CI pipelines and creates hardware-dependent, flaky tests.Use instead: Coroutine testing utilities (runTest, advanceUntilIdle()) or explicit await conditions.How to Enforce the Ban: 3 Automated ApproachesApproach 1: Static Analysis (Detekt)Configure built-in linter rules in detekt.yml using Detekt:style: ForbiddenMethodCall: active: true methods: - value: 'io.mockk.spyk' reason: 'Use pure mocks (mockk) or fakes instead of spyk.' - value: 'java.lang.Thread.sleep' reason: 'Use coroutine delay() or virtual time in tests.' ForbiddenImport: active: true imports: - value: 'kotlinx.coroutines.GlobalScope' reason: 'Inject a scoped CoroutineScope instead.'Approach 2: Architecture Unit Tests (Konture)Write executable architecture rules in standard Kotlin unit tests using Konture. By default, Konture inspects production code, but you can explicitly specify sourceSets = SourceSets.tests() when banning APIs inside test code:class ForbiddenApiTest { @Test fun `test code should not use MockK spyk`() { Konture.files(sourceSets = SourceSets.tests()) { should().notCall("io.mockk.spyk") } } @Test fun `production code should not use GlobalScope`() { Konture.files { should().notContainImport("kotlinx.coroutines.GlobalScope") } }}Approach 3: Kotlin @Deprecated with ERROR LevelFor internal methods in your own modules, enforce compiler-level errors:@Deprecated( message = "BaseActivity is banned. Use ComposeActivity instead.", replaceWith = ReplaceWith("ComposeActivity()"), level = DeprecationLevel.ERROR // Fails compilation!)class BaseActivitySummaryCode reviews shouldn’t be spent playing “API police.” Automate your rules with linters like Detekt, architecture tests with Konture, or compiler errors to keep your codebase clean and deterministic.

title: Is SOLID Really Solid? The Android Edition
excerpt: What several real Android and Kotlin codebases taught me about the five principles everyone quotes in interviews. Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidKotlinSoftware DevelopmentMobileGoogleIs SOLID Really Solid? The Android EditionAmitFollow9 min read·4 days ago23ListenShareWhat several real Android and Kotlin codebases taught me about the five principles everyone quotes in interviews.Every Android interview eventually gets to SOLID. You recite the five principles, maybe give the textbook example with the rectangle and the square, and everyone nods. Then you go back to work and write a 900-line ViewModel.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThat gap bothered me. So I went through several independent Android and Kotlin codebases — single-module apps, multi-module Clean Architecture, and two Compose Multiplatform projects — and actually looked. Not to grade anyone. I wanted to know which of these principles survive contact with production code, and whether the violations actually hurt.Everything below is what I found in that sample, described generically.What SOLID Is Actually SolvingSkip the definitions; you can get those anywhere. Every one of the five principles is a different angle on the same question: when something changes, how much else has to change with it, and can you make that change confidently?Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThat’s the whole thing. Coupling and blast radius. Worth knowing that the acronym is younger than the ideas — Robert C. Martin wrote these up across the late 1990s, Michael Feathers noticed the initials spelt a word around 2004, and Liskov’s substitution rule goes back to 1987. So when people call SOLID “Java-era dogma,” they’re half right about the vocabulary and mostly wrong about the problem.The God Repository: ISP Is the Most Underrated PrincipleThis was the most consistent finding in the whole exercise, and it wasn’t close.Across multiple unrelated codebases, built by teams who had never seen each other’s work, I kept finding one repository interface with dozens of methods. In the worst cases, over a hundred. Authentication sitting next to booking logic sitting next to payments sitting next to a dozen report types, all in one contract. Then every screen in the app depends on it.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe cost lands in two places. Tests first: a screen that calls three methods still has to satisfy the whole interface to compile a test, so setup becomes ceremony. The tell was sitting in these teams’ own test files — they stubbed three methods out of seventy. That ratio is the ISP violation, already written down. Change safety second: touch any signature on that interface, and you’ve potentially triggered a recompile and a review for every unrelated consumer. The person renaming a parameter in a reporting method now technically affects the login screen.What got me was that this wasn’t one team’s mistake. It appeared independently, which means it isn’t carelessness — it’s the natural end state of a completely reasonable habit. You need a new endpoint; there’s already a repository, you add the method. Nobody in that moment is making a bad call. The interface just grows one method at a time until it’s the largest coupling point in your app, and no single commit is the one you’d flag in review.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeTreat “just add a method to the existing repository” as a decision point, not a default.Breaking Them Up Without Breaking the AppSpotting one is easy. Fixing it while it backs a shipping screen is the actual problem. The two shapes come apart in opposite directions.For a god ViewModel, work inward. List the distinct responsibilities as plain bullets first — that step alone usually reveals the seams. If coverage is thin, write characterisation tests: not good tests, just enough to pin what the thing currently does so you’d notice if you changed it. Then extract one responsibility into a small class behind a narrow interface and have the original delegate to it. Run tests, ship, repeat. The original stays alive the whole time, getting thinner. You’re not rewriting it, you’re strangling it.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeFor a god repository, invert the order: add the new interfaces before you remove the old one. Group the existing methods by feature domain — the way a product person would describe them, not by which table they hit. Define a narrow interface per group, then have your existing implementation class satisfy all of them alongside the fat one. Nothing breaks, no consumer notices. You’ve added smaller doors into the same room. Now migrate consumers one at a time, each shipping on its own, and delete the fat interface when nothing references it.The common thread is sequence, not scope. The eventual diff is the same size; you’re delivering it as twenty safe steps instead of one terrifying one. These classes got built one small addition at a time, and that’s exactly how they come apart.Dependency Inversion Carried EverythingDIP was the clear winner in this sample. The pattern that kept working: a DI container binds every repository interface to exactly one implementation, and in the better codebases those implementations were marked internal — invisible outside their own module. Business logic and UI reference the interface, never the concrete type.Get Amit’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThat’s the entire reason fast unit tests existed here at all. Every codebase with a test suite worth running had this; every codebase without it had tests that touched real infrastructure, or no meaningful tests at all. And it’s cheaper now than when the principle was written — Kotlin makes interfaces cheap, and Hilt (compile-time, so a missing binding is a build error) or Koin (runtime resolution) make binding them two lines.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe way I watched it get undermined connects straight back to the god repository. You can depend on an abstraction perfectly correctly and still be cou

title: 14/28: The Journey of a Single Touch, From Driver to Your View
excerpt: InputReader, InputDispatcher, and event delivery Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidAndroid InternalsAospKotlinAndroid App Development14/28: The Journey of a Single Touch, From Driver to Your ViewPramod PatelFollow8 min read·4 days ago1ListenShareInputReader, InputDispatcher, and event deliveryPress enter or click to view image in full sizeA single touch crosses three layers (kernel, native system service, and your app process) before dispatchTouchEvent ever fires.By the time dispatchTouchEvent hits your root view, the event has already crossed a process boundary, survived a dispatcher timeout check, and been queued, classified, and routed in native code running inside system_server.That routing is where most touch-handling confusion actually comes from. The bugs that feel like guesswork (why does onInterceptTouchEvent fire twice, why does a child steal the event from the parent, why does fast scrolling sometimes drop a touch) are explainable once you see the journey from hardware to hierarchy. App developers are handed the last hop. The system did most of the work before you had a chance to override anything.Where does a touch actually begin?Not in Java. Not even close.Your finger lands on the glass and the touch controller fires a raw position reading. The Linux kernel picks it up through an evdev (event device) driver, a generic kernel interface for input hardware. Every touchscreen, button, and sensor exposes itself as a /dev/input/eventN node. The kernel writes raw input_event structs (type, code, value triples) to that node in a tight loop. Nobody in your app process has read permission on /dev/input. That layer is entirely off-limits to you.The first Android component to touch those events is InputReader, a native C++ thread running inside system_server's inputflinger service. InputReader wraps a component called EventHub, which epoll-watches all /dev/inputnodes simultaneously. When the kernel signals a new event, EventHub wakes InputReader's thread, which reads the raw evdev data and runs it through a mapper pipeline:For a touchscreen, MultiTouchInputMapper handles the raw ABS_MT_* axis codesIt classifies finger slots, computes pointer IDs, applies per-device calibration (pressure curves, size normalization)It translates kernel codes into Android-layer MotionEvent semantics: ACTION_DOWN, ACTION_MOVE, ACTION_UPAfter classification, InputReader enqueues the cooked event into a QueuedInputListener and notifies InputDispatcher (another native thread in the same process).What does InputDispatcher actually decide?InputDispatcher is the routing brain. It holds a snapshot of all registered windows (their bounds, their flags, their focus state) and for each touch event it must decide: which window gets this?For a finger landing at screen coordinates (x, y), InputDispatcher walks the window list in z-order (topmost first) and hit-tests each window’s touchable region. The winner is the window that owns the touch stream for the duration of the gesture. This decision happens in native code, in system_server, before your process wakes up at all.Once the target window is chosen, InputDispatcher sends the MotionEventthrough a per-window input channel.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe process boundary crossing: InputDispatcher (system_server) sends the event through a Unix socket pair to your app process. The input channel is established when your window is registered with WindowManager.How does the event cross the process boundary?The input channel is a socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_SEQPACKET, 0), a bidirectional Unix socket pair where InputDispatcher holds one end (server) and your app process holds the other (client). When your window is added via WindowManager.addView, the framework creates this pair and hands the client fd to your app's ViewRootImpl.Your app’s main thread watches that socket fd through a WindowInputEventReceiver, an InputEventReceiver whose native half registers the channel fd directly on the Looper's epoll set. When InputDispatcher writes a serialized InputMessage to its end of the socket, the epoll in your app's Looper wakes, the receiver reads the bytes, deserializes them back into a MotionEvent, and feeds it into the dispatch pipeline.This is the process boundary crossing: a real IPC hop, not a shared memory read. There is no zero-copy magic here for touch events; the serialized event bytes go through the kernel’s socket buffer. The round-trip acknowledgment (your app sending back a “finished” signal) is part of the same channel, and that acknowledgment is what InputDispatcher is waiting for to start its timeout countdown.What happens inside ViewRootImpl before your View sees it?Your app’s main thread receives the raw MotionEvent from the socket, but ViewRootImpl does not immediately hand it to your View tree. It runs the event through an InputStage pipeline, a chain of handlers, each of which can consume, transform, or pass the event forward.Here’s the actual stage chain from ViewRootImpl.java in setView():// frameworks/base/core/java/android/view/ViewRootImpl.javamSyntheticInputStage = new SyntheticInputStage();InputStage viewPostImeStage = new ViewPostImeInputStage(mSyntheticInputStage);InputStage nativePostImeStage = new NativePostImeInputStage(viewPostImeStage, "aq:native-post-ime:" + counterSuffix);InputStage earlyPostImeStage = new EarlyPostImeInputStage(nativePostImeStage);InputStage imeStage = new ImeInputStage(earlyPostImeStage, "aq:ime:" + counterSuffix);InputStage viewPreImeStage = new ViewPreImeInputStage(imeStage);InputStage nativePreImeStage = new NativePreImeInputStage(viewPreImeStage, "aq:native-pre-ime:" + counterSuffix);mFirstInputStage = nativePreImeStage;mFirstPostImeInputStage = earlyPostImeStage;The event enters at nativePreImeStage and propagates forward. For a touch event (not a key), the IME stages pass it through quickly. The stage your touch event actually cares about is ViewPostImeInputStage, the one that calls mView.dispatchPointerEvent(event) on your root view, which ultimately routes into ViewGroup.disp

title: From Android MVVM to Kotlin Multiplatform: Evolving SignalBrief for Android and iOS
excerpt: How a focused Jetpack Compose news app became an offline-first Kotlin Multiplatform project with shared domain, data, presentation, and UI Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin MultiplatformAndroid DevelopmentJetpack ComposeKotlinMobile DevelopmentFrom Android MVVM to Kotlin Multiplatform: Evolving SignalBrief for Android and iOSRecipes For SoftwareFollow11 min read·4 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeHow a focused Jetpack Compose news app became an offline-first Kotlin Multiplatform project with shared domain, data, presentation, and UIA few weeks ago, I published an article about building a focused Android news application with Jetpack Compose, MVVM, StateFlow, Hilt, Retrofit, and a deliberately proportional architecture.That version had a narrow goal: fetch top headlines, represent the screen with explicit UI states, isolate networking behind a repository, and keep the codebase understandable without adding layers that the problem did not yet require.The original article is available here:https://medium.com/@recipesforsoftware/building-a-modern-android-news-app-with-jetpack-compose-best-practices-without-overengineering-89442c895de9The application did not remain Android-only.As the project evolved, the requirements changed:the same product should run on Android and iOS;business rules should behave identically on both platforms;the app should continue showing useful content when the network is unavailable;presentation logic should not be duplicated;the core interface should share one design language;platform-specific responsibilities should remain explicit.That evolution became SignalBrief: a Kotlin Multiplatform news reader with a shared domain and data layer, shared Compose Multiplatform UI, Room KMP persistence, Ktor networking, typed failures, cross-platform onboarding, and independent Android and iOS hosts.Source code:https://github.com/recipesforsoftware-pl/signalbriefThis article focuses on the migration: what became shared, what deliberately stayed platform-specific, and how the architecture changed once the application had two real clients.Where the project startedThe first version was a native Android application built around a straightforward MVVM flow:Compose UI ↓ViewModel ↓Repository ↓Retrofit service ↓NewsAPIThe project intentionally did not contain a dedicated domain module, offline cache, multiple data sources, or shared presentation layer.At that stage, those additions would have increased structure without solving an immediate problem.The Android app already demonstrated:unidirectional state flow;explicit loading, success, and error states;dependency injection with Hilt;repository-based isolation of networking;defensive handling of incomplete API data;unit tests around state transitions;release-oriented build configuration;a Compose UI built from reusable components.The original architecture was appropriate for the original scope.The important lesson was not that it had been wrong. It was that architecture should respond to changing requirements.Once iOS became a real target and offline behaviour became part of the product, several abstractions that had previously been unnecessary became justified.Why Kotlin Multiplatform became the right next stepThe goal was not to maximise the percentage of shared code.The goal was to share code where duplication would create real maintenance risk.For SignalBrief, that included:domain models;repository contracts;networking;JSON serialization;local persistence;offline-first behaviour;typed failures;presentation state;onboarding;design tokens;most of the user interface.Some responsibilities remained platform-specific:Android dependency injection;Android DataStore preferences;the Android dark-mode menu;iOS application hosting;iOS NSUserDefaults;Xcode configuration;platform lifecycle integration.This distinction matters. Kotlin Multiplatform works best when the shared boundary is intentional.The architecture evolved around four modules::app:shared:shared-uiiosAppDefining the module boundaries:sharedThe :shared module contains the reusable domain and data layers.It owns:Article, Source, and TopHeadlinesFeed;typed failures;the NewsRepository contract;Ktor networking;kotlinx.serialization DTOs;DTO-to-domain mapping;Room KMP persistence;local and remote data-source interfaces;the offline-first repository implementation;platform HTTP engines and database factories;common tests.It does not depend on Android UI, Hilt, SwiftUI, or Compose.:shared-uiThe :shared-ui module contains presentation logic and Compose Multiplatform UI.It owns:TopHeadlinesPresenter;TopHeadlinesUiState;the shared TopHeadlinesScreen;article cards;loading skeletons;empty and error states;the cached-headlines banner;shared design tokens;light and dark themes;the onboarding flow;the top-level SignalBriefApp shell;the iOS MainViewController bridge.:appThe Android app remains the Android composition root.It owns:SignalBriefApplication;MainActivity;Hilt modules;Android DataStore preferences;Android ViewModels;the Android dark-mode action;launcher icons and the platform splash screen.iosAppThe iOS app is a small SwiftUI host.It owns:the Xcode project;the SwiftUI lifecycle;the app icon and launch screen;local xcconfig-based secret injection;embedding the Kotlin frameworks.This keeps the shared code substantial without pretending Android and iOS are identical platforms.Replacing Retrofit and Gson with Ktor and kotlinx.serializationThe Android-only version used Retrofit and Gson. That was appropriate for a native Android application, but not for a shared KMP network layer.The migration replaced it with:Retrofit + Gson→Ktor Client + kotlinx.serializationThe shared Ktor client configures:content negotiation;JSON serialization;timeouts;response validation;the API base URL;the API-key header.Only the engine is platform-specific:Android → Android Ktor engineiOS → Darwin engineTests → MockEngineThe remote data source is also the only part of the application that understands transport DTOs:JSON response→ DTO→ mapper→ domain modelThe rest of the app works with domain types rather than API response objects.Why a domain bounda

title: Mutability and Immutability in Kotlin: Why val Is the Default Choice
excerpt: One of the first concepts you’ll learn in Kotlin is the difference between val and var. At first glance, it may seem like a simple choice… Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinProgrammingSoftware DevelopmentAndroid DevelopmentClean CodeMutability and Immutability in Kotlin: Why val Is the Default ChoiceJamersomfabricioFollow4 min read·4 days agoListenShareOne of the first concepts you’ll learn in Kotlin is the difference between val and var. At first glance, it may seem like a simple choice between a variable that can change and one that cannot. In practice, however, this decision directly impacts your application's safety, maintainability, and even concurrency.In this article, you’ll learn why the Kotlin community recommends using immutability by default and how this principle is applied in real-world projects.What Are Mutability and Immutability?In Kotlin, mutability is controlled directly when declaring variables and collections.The language provides two keywords for this purpose:val (value): creates a reference that cannot be reassigned after it receives its initial value.var (variable): creates a variable whose value can be reassigned whenever necessary.The Kotlin community follows a simple recommendation:Use val by default. Switch to var only when the value truly needs to change.This small decision helps reduce bugs and makes your code much more predictable.val vs varval (Immutable Reference)A variable declared with val can only be assigned once.val name = "John"// Compilation errorname = "Alice"Once initialized, the reference cannot point to another objectvar (Mutable Variable)A variable declared with var can be reassigned multiple times during the application's execution.var age = 20age = 21age = 22This behavior is useful whenever the value is expected to change.An Important Detail About valThis is one of the most common misconceptions among beginners.Many developers believe that val makes an object immutable.In reality, val only makes the reference immutable.Consider the following example:val numbers = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)numbers.add(4) // Works normally// Compilation errornumbers = mutableListOf()What happened?The reference numbers still points to the same object.However, since the object itself is a MutableList, its contents can still be modified.In other words:val prevents reassigning the reference, but it does not make a mutable object immutable.These are two different concepts.Benefits of ImmutabilityUsing immutable objects provides several advantages.SafetyImmutability prevents accidental modifications to your data.Imagine a financial application where any part of the system could modify an account balance.The fewer places that can change your data, the lower the chance of introducing bugs.PredictabilityWhen an object never changes, understanding your application’s behavior becomes much easier.Its state remains consistent throughout its lifetime.ConcurrencyModern applications often execute multiple tasks simultaneously.Get Jamersomfabricio’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inImmutable objects can safely be shared between threads without synchronization, reducing issues such as race conditions.Mutable and Immutable CollectionsBesides variables, Kotlin also distinguishes between mutable collections and read-only collections.Read-Only Collectionsval fruits = listOf( "Apple", "Banana", "Orange")The List interface does not expose methods such as:add()remove()clear()This means consumers of the list can only read its elements.Mutable Collectionsval fruits = mutableListOf( "Apple", "Banana")fruits.add("Orange")fruits.remove("Banana")In this case, the collection’s contents can be modified freely.Another Important DetailTechnically, List in Kotlin represents a read-only collection.This means it does not expose methods that modify the collection through that reference.Internally, however, the implementation may still be mutable.That’s why you’ll often see code like this:private val items = mutableListOf<Product>()fun getItems(): List<Product> { return items}The caller only sees a List, without access to modification methods.Even so, many projects still prefer returning a copy using toList() to ensure that no one shares the internal collection.How Is This Used in Real Projects?Most modern applications follow a simple pattern:Immutable data.Mutability isolated in a single place.This means only one class is responsible for changing the application’s state.Every other part of the system simply reads that data.This approach improves maintainability, simplifies testing, and prevents unexpected side effects.A shopping cart is a great example.Practical Example: Shopping Cart// Immutable productdata class Product( val id: String, val name: String, val price: Double)// Immutable cart statedata class ShoppingCartState( val items: List<Product>, val total: Double)// Class responsible for state changesclass ShoppingCartManager { private val _items = mutableListOf<Product>() fun getState(): ShoppingCartState { return ShoppingCartState( items = _items.toList(), total = _items.sumOf { it.price } ) } fun addProduct(product: Product) { _items.add(product) } fun removeProduct(productId: String) { _items.removeIf { it.id == productId } }}Why Use toList()?This line often raises questions:_items.toList()The toList() function creates a new list containing the same elements.As a result, consumers of the shopping cart state cannot access the manager’s internal collection.Imagine returning the mutable list directly.Someone could attempt to do this:state.items.add(...)This would bypass the business rules defined by the ShoppingCartManager.By returning a read-only copy, we ensure that every modification goes through the class responsible for managing the state.This is a practical example of encapsulation.SummaryConclusionImmutability is one of the core principles of modern Kotlin development.Although var and mutable collections are still essential in certain scenarios, they should only be used when mutation is actually required.Whenever possible:Prefer val over var.Expose collections as Li

title: Shipping OneSignal for Shipaton
excerpt: Have you ever noticed how much of your push notification code has nothing to do with your product? Token tables, refresh callbacks… Continue reading on Medium »
content: ShipatonKotlinOnesignalFirebaseShipping OneSignal for ShipatonBehzod HalilFollow6 min read·4 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeHave you ever noticed how much of your push notification code has nothing to do with your product? Token tables, refresh callbacks, stale-token pruning, a separate iOS pipeline-none of it is the feature, yet all of it needs maintaining.Stock+ is a Kotlin Multiplatform app whose core product is price alerts, delivered as push notifications. This blog post describes how we migrated it from direct Firebase Cloud Messaging to OneSignal for the Shipaton hackathon: what actually changed architecturally, and the four silent failures I had to go hunting for along the way.Addressing users, not devicesDirect FCM builds a message around a registration token. One token, one device. That sounds simple, but it quietly generates a lot of server-side work: a table of tokens per user, a refresh callback because tokens rotate, pruning on UNREGISTERED because they go stale, a hand-written fan-out loop because a phone and a tablet are two rows, and an entirely separate iOS pipeline with separate credentials.OneSignal inverts the unit of addressing. The client declares an identity:OneSignal.login(userId)The server then addresses that identity instead of a device:mapOf( "app_id" to appId, "target_channel" to "push", "include_aliases" to mapOf("external_id" to listOf(userId)), "headings" to mapOf("en" to title), "contents" to mapOf("en" to body), "data" to data,)One HTTP call reaches every device where that user is logged in, on both platforms, and the server holds no device state at all.Hang on, isn’t OneSignal just a nicer FCM wrapper? I hear you ask. I thought so too, but the real change is the unit of addressing, not the vendor. The migration’s diff removed more lines than it added, which is always a good sign-deleted code doesn’t have bugs, and doesn’t need tests either.No flag dayThe pipeline was already live, and price alerts are the product, so I didn’t want a big-bang cutover. The new channel went in beside the old one, selected purely by configuration:val isEnabled: Boolean get() = appId.isNotBlank() && restApiKey.isNotBlank()// Yamlexternal: onesignal: app-id: ${ONESIGNAL_APP_ID:} # unset => legacy FCM path rest-api-key: ${ONESIGNAL_REST_API_KEY:}This gives us some nice properties. Deploying the code is not the cutover -the binary behaves exactly as before until the credentials are set. Rollback is an environment variable rather than a revert. Local dev and CI have no credentials, so they transparently use the legacy path and nothing ever accidentally sends from a laptop. And note which way the default points: doing nothing gets you the old, proven behaviour.One thing to be careful of: the legacy path needs to stay fully functional-retries, backoff, stale-token pruning, all of it. A fallback which has quietly rotted isn’t really a fallback at all.Durable first, push secondHere’s the design decision I’d defend hardest, and it applies whichever vendor you pick: a push notification is not the notification. It’s an announcement that a notification exists.Every send path persists a durable inbox row first, then attempts the push:fun sendAlertTriggered(fcmToken: String?, ticker: String, alertType: AlertType, price: BigDecimal?, userId: UUID) { val (title, body) = buildAlertMessage(ticker, alertType, price) // Inbox is the source of truth; the push below is best-effort. notificationRepository.save(userId, title, body, alertType.name, ticker) deliverPush(fcmToken, userId, title, body, mapOf(/* ... */))}Push delivery is genuinely unreliable, and not because the vendors are bad at it: denied permissions, offline devices, OS throttling, rotated tokens, guest users. On iOS, best-effort delivery is the explicit platform contract. Ordering it durable-first turns each of those failures from lost product data into a missed buzz-the alert is sitting in the inbox when the user next opens the app. It also lets the whole push layer be best-effort all the way down: no retries blocking a request, no transaction spanning an HTTP call, no error a user can ever see.One interface, opposite directionsShared code depends on a plain interface. You might reach for expect class here, but whilst that works, a plain interface does the same job and stays mockable in tests for free:interface PushIdentityBinder { fun login(userId: String) fun logout()}Android is the easy one: the OneSignal SDK is a Gradle dependency, so the implementation calls it directly. Note that it never throws-any vendor surprise degrades to “no push”, never to “sign-in crashed”:class AndroidPushIdentityBinder : PushIdentityBinder { override fun login(userId: String) { runCatching { OneSignal.login(userId) } } override fun logout() { runCatching { OneSignal.logout() } }}iOS is where it gets interesting. The OneSignal iOS SDK is a Swift package, and Kotlin cannot see it-Swift sees Kotlin through the generated framework, but not the reverse. So on iOS we invert control: Kotlin holds closures, and Swift fills them in at startup:object IosPushIdentityBridge { var onLogin: ((String) -> Unit)? = null var onLogout: (() -> Unit)? = null}// iOSIosPushIdentityBridge.shared.onLogin = { OneSignal.login(externalId: $0) }IosPushIdentityBridge.shared.onLogout = { OneSignal.logout() }One wrinkle cost me a confusing hour: shared is an implementation dependency of the iOS framework, not exported, so its symbols don’t appear in the framework header at all. Swift literally cannot see the bridge. The fix is a thin re-export in the exported module, called from AppDelegate before the root component spins up-a cold start with a saved session binds identity immediately, and getting the order wrong silently no-ops on exactly the launch that matters most: a returning, logged-in user.Get Behzod Halil’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inDesktop sim

title: How Much Does It Cost to Build a POS System?
excerpt: Walk into any retail store, restaurant, or service business today and you will find a point of sale system quietly running the entire… Continue reading on Medium »
content: PosPos SystemWeb DevelopmentAndroidHow Much Does It Cost to Build a POS System?Alexmercer TechoFollow13 min read·4 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWalk into any retail store, restaurant, or service business today and you will find a point of sale system quietly running the entire operation behind the counter. It processes payments, tracks inventory, manages staff shifts, and generates the sales reports that owners rely on to make decisions. Yet when business leaders start exploring the idea of building their own POS system instead of licensing one, the first question that comes up every single time is about cost.This guide is built for exactly that conversation. We are not going to throw a random number at you and call it a day. Instead, we are breaking down every layer of POS development, from the software architecture to the physical hardware, from the payment gateway fees to the long term maintenance you will need to budget for. Business leaders deserve a real answer, and that is what this article delivers.By the end of this piece, you will understand what separates a basic POS build from an enterprise grade system, which technologies drive the cost up or down, and how to plan a budget that actually reflects your business reality. Let us begin by understanding why so many businesses are choosing to build custom POS systems instead of buying one off the shelf.The Business Case for Building Your Own POS SystemReady made POS platforms like Square, Toast, or Lightspeed work well for small operations, but they come with limitations that start to hurt as your business scales. Transaction fees eat into your margins on every single sale, customization options are often locked behind expensive tiers, and your data lives on someone else’s servers under someone else’s terms. For a growing business, these limitations eventually become expensive in ways that are hard to reverse.A custom built POS system flips this equation entirely. You own the platform, you control the fee structure, and you can build workflows that match exactly how your business operates instead of forcing your operations to match a generic template. This is the primary value proposition that pulls mid sized and large businesses toward custom development instead of subscription based tools.There is also a compounding financial argument here that many business owners miss initially. If you are processing a high volume of transactions, even a small percentage saved on transaction fees adds up to a significant amount over a year. A custom POS system paired with a direct payment processor relationship can dramatically reduce the per transaction cost compared to bundled third party platforms that mark up processing fees.Data ownership is another factor that matters more each year as businesses become more analytics driven. When you own your POS system, every transaction, every customer interaction, and every inventory movement becomes data you fully control and can analyze however you want. Off the shelf platforms often restrict or charge extra for deep analytics access, which limits how effectively you can use your own sales data to grow.Understanding the Different Types of POS SystemsNot every POS system serves the same purpose, and the type you choose to build has a direct impact on both features required and total development cost. Let us look at the main categories businesses typically choose from.Retail POS systems designed for stores selling physical products, focusing heavily on inventory management and barcode scanningRestaurant POS systems built for food service businesses, requiring table management, kitchen display integration, and order routingMobile POS systems that run on tablets or smartphones, ideal for businesses like food trucks, pop up shops, or delivery servicesEnterprise POS systems designed for chains with multiple locations, requiring centralized reporting and multi store inventory syncHybrid cloud POS systems that combine offline functionality with cloud based syncing for businesses that cannot afford downtime during internet outagesEach category requires a different combination of features, and this directly shapes how much you will spend during development. A restaurant POS with kitchen display integration and table management will always cost more than a simple retail POS handling basic checkout and inventory tracking.Core Features That Shape Your POS Development BudgetEvery POS system, regardless of industries, needs certain foundational features to function as a real business tool. Understanding these features helps you see exactly where your development budget actually goes.Point of Sale and Checkout FeaturesThis is the heart of the system, the interface your staff uses dozens or hundreds of times every single day to process transactions. title: Cut Android Rebuffers by 70–80%: Ten Fixes, Priced in Dev-Days
excerpt: Smooth Android video in 2026 is the sum of ten coordinated optimizations, not one heroic rewrite. Aligned, they cut video start time by… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Software DevelopmentAndroidVideo StreamingMobile App DevelopmentEngineering ManagementCut Android Rebuffers by 70–80%: Ten Fixes, Priced in Dev-DaysFora SoftFollow4 min read·4 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhat moves video QoE on Android in 2026 — codecs, buffers, protocols, telemetry — and what each fix costs to shipSmooth Android video in 2026 is the sum of ten coordinated optimizations, not one heroic rewrite. Aligned, they cut video start time by 40–60%, rebuffer events by 70–80%, and battery drain by 25–35%. Misaligned, they cook hardware: software-decoded VP9 thermal-throttles a budget Snapdragon 695 in about 90 seconds. At Fora Soft we’ve rebuilt Android video stacks for OTT, telemedicine, fitness, and virtual classrooms, and measured these numbers on real devices and real carrier networks.Four fixes that pay for themselves firstTune Media3’s LoadControl per network class. The single fastest fix in the list. One buffer configuration shared by 5G, LTE, and 3G throws away 20–30% of your rebuffer events, and the library default (50/50/2.5/5 seconds) is wrong for almost every production app. Cost: 4–6 dev-days, including a per-device profiling rig.Ship AV1 + HEVC, skip VP9 on new builds. Hardware AV1 decode now ships on Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 and newer, Pixel 6 and newer, and Dimensity 9200 and newer. That’s still a minority of the active base in 2026, but where it exists AV1 cuts bitrate 40–50% versus H.264, while HEVC stays the workhorse across roughly 70–75% of devices. Don’t trust MediaCodec.getCodecCapabilities() alone: some SoCs claim AV1 support and silently fall back to software decode. Run a 20-frame test decode at session start and cache the verdict per device model.Turn on CMCD telemetry. Media3 has shipped it natively since 1.4; enable it and your CDN logs can finally distinguish a thermal throttle on a flagship from genuine network congestion. Incident triage drops from hours to minutes; skipping it is one of the five pitfalls the guide sees most often.Get Fora Soft’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inBuy low latency only where latency is revenue. Classic HLS delivers 10–15 seconds glass-to-glass. LL-HLS lands at 2.5–3.5 seconds, LL-DASH under 2. For sports, auctions, live tutoring, and surveillance that gap is the product; for VOD it’s a latency tax you don’t need to pay.Hardware AV1 or H.265 decode draws 0.8–1.3 W. Software VP9 draws 3.2–4.5 W — enough to throttle a mid-tier phone in under 90 seconds.The sequencing logic matters more than any single fix. Every extra second of video start time costs roughly 3–5% of retention, and every 1% of rebuffer ratio costs 8–12% of engagement, so you fix the worst number first with the cheapest lever that moves it. The full ten-fix pass runs 70–100 dev-days with a senior Android team, but the guide’s budget framework starts far smaller: with under 10 dev-days, tune LoadControl and add CMCD before touching anything else. This stack runs in production on Perspire.tv, a live fitness platform we built and operate: 30–60-minute sessions, long enough for thermal behavior to matter, on every Android tier. Rebuffer ratio holds under 0.5% on 5G and 0.8% on LTE. The egress side compounds too: in the guide’s worked example — 100,000 monthly Android users at 40 hours each — the AV1 + HEVC ladder alone returns about $3,000–4,000 a month.What the full guide coversDev-day price tags and gotchas for all ten fixes, from 4–6 days for LoadControl tuning to 14–18 for low-latency liveCopy-paste Media3 DefaultLoadControl values for 5G, LTE, and 3G, plus ABR ladder rungs per network classThe five QoE metrics worth tracking — video start time, rebuffer ratio, start failure, exit-before-start, bitrate variance — with 2026 targets from Conviva and Mux benchmarksA protocol decision matrix from classic HLS to WebRTC, including why RTMP ingest should be gone before its 2027 sunsetThe cost model, worked: how $0.36 per 1,000 streams becomes $0.22 on the codec ladderA six-layer reference architecture, from packaging and multi-CDN down to player and telemetryWhen NOT to invest: three situations where vanilla Media3 plus HEVC is the honest answerThe full guide — with the tables, buffer configs, and the worked cost math — is here: 10 Proven Ways to Optimize Android Apps for Smooth Video Streaming in 2026This story is a digest of 10 Proven Ways to Optimize Android Apps for Smooth Video Streaming in 2026, first published on the Fora Soft blog.Fora Soft builds video, real-time communication, and AI software, and has since 2005 - 250+ projects across telemedicine, streaming, e-learning, and security. title: Android Visual Testing: When to Use OCR, Templates, and Screenshots
excerpt: Android visual testing becomes much easier when you stop asking which vision tool is “best” and instead ask what must remain true. A… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidSoftware TestingAutomationOcrAndroid Visual Testing: When to Use OCR, Templates, and ScreenshotskhinmaungthooFollow4 min read·4 days agoListenShareAndroid visual testing becomes much easier when you stop asking which vision tool is “best” and instead ask what must remain true. A release may need to preserve layout, display the correct localized text, keep one icon visible, or move through a known sequence of screens. Each requirement needs different evidence.A practical comparisonUse the narrowest signal that can prove the requirement. Semantic UI state is usually the first choice for behavior. Visual methods become valuable when appearance or pixel-rendered content is part of the contract.UI/accessibility state — for controls, labels, enabled state, and selection; weak for custom-rendered appearance.Screenshot comparison — for layout, spacing, color, typography, and composition; noisy when time, ads, animations, or seeded data change.OCR — for visible text, localization, status messages, and rendered values; pair it with an image when clipping or overlap matters.Template matching — for a known icon, badge, or small visual control; validate themes, density, scaling, and thresholds.Object detection — for a validated object class whose position or size varies; avoid it when a stable selector or template is enough.Four questions that choose the assertion1. Is the requirement semantic or visual?“The Submit button is enabled” is a semantic requirement, so query the UI state. “The Submit button is not clipped after the font change” is visual, so capture the component or screen. A UI query is easier to maintain, but it cannot prove appearance.2. Does the exact text matter?Use OCR when the string is visible but not exposed reliably through the UI tree. Crop to the smallest useful region, select the correct language, and keep the source image. OCR can confirm the words, but a screenshot is still needed to reveal truncation or overlap.3. Is there one stable visual target?Template matching works well for a known icon or compact button. Crop the template tightly, search inside a region of interest, and validate the threshold with both positive and negative samples. Do not lower the threshold until an unrelated shape passes.4. Must the whole composition remain consistent?Use screenshot comparison when relationships between many elements matter. Control locale, fonts, device configuration, system bars, test data, and animations. If one region must stay dynamic, crop or mask that region rather than accepting a permanently noisy test.Make every visual failure usefulA reliable check has five stages: stabilize the screen, capture the relevant region, run one primary assertion, preserve the result, and stop when the screen is outside the reviewed path. A fixed delay is weaker than a real ready condition. Android UI Automator, for example, exposes stability waiting for cases where the UI must settle before capture.Name the starting screen and the expected next screen.Save the screenshot or crop used by the assertion.Record the expected template, text, baseline, class, or UI property.Record the observed OCR result, match score, bounding box, diff, or UI value.Do not perform the next action unless the current-state assertion succeeds.Verify a postcondition after the action; recognition alone is not task completion.A realistic localization exampleConsider a checkout screen in six languages. Use UI state to navigate to the screen, OCR to confirm the localized total and primary action label, and a focused screenshot to show that the label is not clipped. A full-screen golden image is too sensitive to every string-length difference. OCR alone misses damaged layout. The layered test matches the actual requirement.Get khinmaungthoo’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe same principle applies to real-phone smoke tests. Permission dialogs, the keyboard, notifications, device density, and system updates are part of the environment. Good automation reports those states instead of hiding them behind retries.Where LaiCai Flow fitsLaiCai Flow is an automation feature inside LaiCai Screen Mirroring. A Flow can combine screenshot capture, UI checks, OCR, template matching, object detection, actions, and explicit success or failure transitions. That makes the screen a reviewable state instead of treating recognition as an isolated trick.With LaiCai Flow Inside, a compatible Profile can run through LaiCai Android Agent on the phone after deployment. Compatibility still depends on every node, asset, model, and network dependency in that Profile. This is controlled workflow execution, not a promise that every visual test becomes reliable automatically.The evidence checklistApp build, device, Android version, locale, theme, and orientationSource screenshot or cropped regionExpected baseline, template, text, class, or UI stateObserved diff, OCR result, match score, box, or propertyPrevious state, attempted action, expected next state, and stop reasonAsset, model, or baseline versionThe decision is simple once the evidence is clear: UI state for semantics, screenshots for composition, OCR for visible text, template matching for a known visual target, and object detection for a validated class with variable geometry. A longer version with failure examples is available in the Android visual testing guide.Official referencesAndroid screenshot testing explains golden-image comparison.UI Automator documents stability waiting and device-level UI testing.OpenCV template matching explains how a template is located inside a larger image.Tesseract OCR quality guidance covers scale, noise, rotation, and segmentation.These references are useful because they separate implementation details from test intent. Pick the observation first, then choose the library or workflow that can produce repeatable evidence on the devices and app versions you actual

title: Mobile App Development Process: 10 Steps to Ship a Live App
excerpt: A step-by-step guide detailing the complete mobile app development process from idea to live product. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Mobile App DevelopmentSoftware DevelopmentProduct ManagementAndroidIOSMobile App Development Process: 10 Steps to Ship a Live AppA step-by-step guide detailing the complete mobile app development process from idea to live product.AllclonescriptFollow10 min read·4 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeCoding is the first step of mobile app development; this assumption most businesses make. The harsh reality is: the biggest challenges knock much earlier. This includes vague product vision, feature creep, unrealistic timelines, or limited user research, which can derail a project before the first screen is built. These early mistakes lead to unnecessary costs and months of rework businesses have to face.An organized, flexible, and scalable app development process changes everything.Because when every stage is planned, from idea validation and feature prioritization to design, development, testing, and launch, teams can make better decisions. This guide explains the 10 key stages of the mobile app development process and what each one contributes to building a product that users value and businesses can grow.The Mobile App Development Process Is About Making Better DecisionsEvery successful mobile app is shaped by the decisions made before and during development. It is not about how quickly the first line of code is written. Questions like these have a direct impact on the final product:Is there a real market for this idea?Which features should come first?Is the user experience simple enough?Getting these decisions right early saves time, controls costs, and reduces the need for major changes later.That’s why the mobile app development process is more than a technical workflow. It gives businesses a clear path from idea to launch. Teams can validate assumptions, set priorities, and move forward with confidence instead of guesswork.Every stage has a clear purpose before the project moves to the next.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeWhen each stage is completed with a clear purpose, development becomes more predictable and far less risky. Now, let’s start with the first step: validating your app idea before investing in development.Step 1: Validate Your App Idea Before Investing in Development.One of the most expensive mistakes in mobile app development is assuming that a good idea automatically has a market. It doesn’t.Businesses invest in development based on internal opinions, only to discover later that users don’t see enough value to download, pay for, or keep using the app.Validation is about reducing that uncertainty before you commit your budget. Instead of asking, “Can we build this?”, ask, “Should we build this?” The answer comes from understanding your target users, studying competing apps, and identifying where existing solutions fall short.Sometimes the research confirms your idea. Other times, it changes your feature priorities or even your target audience, and that’s a win because those changes are far less expensive before development begins.Start by answering these questions:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe goal is to prove your idea is perfect and gather enough evidence to build with confidence instead of assumptions. That foundation makes every decision in the next stages of the app development more focused and far less risky.Step 2: Define Clear Requirements Before Development Begins.Once you’ve validated your app idea, the next challenge is turning it into a clear development plan. This is where many projects lose momentum. A founder may describe the product in one way, designers interpret it another way, and front-end app developers build something different. The result is endless revisions, shifting priorities, and a budget that keeps growing.A requirement document removes that uncertainty. It defines what the app should do, who it’s built for, and what success looks like before development begins. It also helps everyone, from business stakeholders to developers, work toward the same outcome instead of making assumptions along the way.A well-prepared requirement plan should answer the following:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThink of this stage as creating the blueprint before constructing a building. The clearer the requirements, the fewer surprises you’ll face during development. Once the scope is defined, the next step is deciding which features belong in the first version of the app and which can wait.Step 3: Prioritize Features to Build a Focused First Version.One of the quickest ways to delay an app launch is to keep adding “just one more feature.” What starts as a simple product can easily grow into a long list of ideas, each competing for development time and budget. The result is a delayed launch and an app that’s more complicated than users actually need.Instead of trying to build everything at once, focus on the features that solve the core problem. Your first release should prove that the product works and delivers value. Additional features can always be introduced once you understand how real users interact with the app.A simple way to prioritize features is to group them by business value and urgency.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeLaunching with a focused feature set helps you reach the market sooner, collect real user feedback, and invest in updates that customers actually want. Not features based on assumptions. Once the scope is finalized, the next step is designing an experience that makes those features easy to understand and enjoyable to use.Step 4: Design the User Experience Before Building the Interface.An attractive app may encourage users to open it, but a smooth experience is what keeps them coming back. That’s why experienced product teams focus on user experience (UX) before they think about colors, icons, or animations. If users struggle to complete simple tasks, even the best-looking interface won’t hold their attention.Start by looking at the app fro

In this blog post, I'll address some of the feedback we received, explaining the philosophy and methodology behind the project. Hopefully, this will also help you understand what happens behind the scenes when you install and use skills, allowing you to make better use of tokens and your own time. Why are there so few official skills? Currently, we only consider new skills when there's a verifiable knowledge gap in state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Put simply: you don't need to teach the model what it already knows. (Though there are a few exceptions—read on!) We’ve released around 20 official skills so far, and they intentionally target highly specific, fast-moving areas that standard models aren't fully grounded on yet—things like AGP 9, Navigation 3, advanced Camera APIs, and Perfetto SQL. What about core, more general, skills? Every installed skill injects 100–200 tokens into the baseline context of every task you start. If that skill actually activates, that count can quickly jump into the thousands. In most cases, hoarding basic skills is both counterproductive and expensive. Before installing a skill for writing basic Kotlin or Compose, consider if your LLM of choice really needs it, or if it knows those topics well enough already. Evaluating skills Before their release, each skill is tested against a comprehensive set of evals that prove that the skill delivers clear value. These evals should pass when the skill is active, and fail otherwise. Evals are to skills what integration tests are to code. timeout_s: 1200 repository: url: [redacted - internal git repo] working_dir: wear_compose_m3_empty_app category_ids: - wear prompt: |- Add a horizontal pager to MainActivity.kt.
