title: Garbage Collector (GC) Necə İşləyir: JVM Yaddaşı Dayanmadan Necə Təmizlənir?
excerpt: Əvvəlcə bir cümləlik xatırlatma: Garbage Collector, qısaca GC — Java və Kotlin kimi dillərdə proqramın artıq istifadə etmədiyi obyektləri… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidAndroid DevelopmentKotlinJavaGarbage CollectionGarbage Collector (GC) Necə İşləyir: JVM Yaddaşı Dayanmadan Necə Təmizlənir?Vusal IslamzadaFollow7 min read·3 days agoShareƏvvəlcə bir cümləlik xatırlatma: Garbage Collector, qısaca GC — Java və Kotlin kimi dillərdə proqramın artıq istifadə etmədiyi obyektləri Heap-dən (obyektlərin yaşadığı yaddaş sahəsindən) avtomatik silən mexanizmdir. Proqramçı əl ilə yaddaşı təmizləmir, bunu arxa planda GC edir.Əksər developer GC-ni elə bununla tanıyır və davam etmir: “işə düşür, lazımsız obyektləri silir, mən qarışmıram”. Bu, texniki olaraq yanlış deyil, amma bir neçə sual cavabsız qalır: GC bir obyektin “artıq lazım olmadığını” konkret necə müəyyən edir? Niyə köhnə GC-lər işləyəndə bütün proqram saniyələrlə tamam dayanırdı, halbuki bugünkü default GC olan G1 bunu demək olar hiss etdirmədən edir? Və nə üçün bəzən çox böyük bir obyekt yaratmaq yaddaş kifayət qədər boş olsa belə, GC-ni gözlənilmədən “tez-tez işə salır”?Bu suallara cavab dörd yerdə gizlənib: region-lar, rənglər, referans növləri və kompilyatorun öz gizli optimizasiyaları.Press enter or click to view image in full size1. Heap artıq bir “otaq” deyil, minlərlə kiçik otaqdırAdətən Heap-i iki hissəyə bölünmüş kimi düşünürük: Young Generation (yeni obyektlərin doğulduğu yer) və Old Generation (uzun ömürlü obyektlərin yeri). Bu, köhnə GC alqoritmləri üçün (Serial, Parallel) doğru idi — Heap həqiqətən iki böyük, sabit ölçülü bloka bölünürdü, və Full GC zamanı bu bloklardan hər hansı biri bütövlükdə yoxlanmalı idi.Amma bugünkü standart GC olan G1 (Garbage First) Heap-i tam fərqli təşkil edir. Heap eyni ölçülü, çoxlu kiçik region-lara bölünür — hər biri adətən 1–32 meqabayt arası, cəmi bir neçə min ədəd. Ən maraqlı hissə budur: bir region-un Young yoxsa Old olması sabit, əvvəlcədən müəyyən edilmiş bir yer deyil — bu, dəyişən bir “etiketdir”. Bu gün Young kimi işlədilən region, təmizləndikdən sonra sabah Old kimi işlədilə bilər.Bunun praktiki nəticəsi: G1 heç vaxt bütün Old Generation-ı bir dəfəyə yoxlamır. O, sadəcə ən çox “zibil” olan region-ları seçib, yalnız onları təmizləyir — adı da elə buradan gəlir: “Garbage First”, yəni ən çox qazanc verəcək yerdən başla. Ona görə developer JVM-ə “hər dövrdə tətbiqi ən çox 200 millisaniyə dayandır” kimi bir hədəf verə bilir, G1 isə hər dövrdə bu hədəfə sığacaq qədər region seçib təmizləyir. Dayanma müddəti artıq “Heap nə qədər böyükdür” sualından yox, “sənə nə qədər vaxt lazımdır” sualından asılı olur.Region-lar arası əlaqəni izləmək: Remembered SetBir incə problem var: əgər bir Old region-dakı obyekt, bir Young region-dakı obyektə referans verirsə, GC yalnız Young region-u yoxlayanda (Minor GC) bu referansı necə “görəcək”? Bütün Old Generation-ı hər dəfə yoxlamaq lazım deyilmi?G1 bunu Remembered Set (RSet) adlı bir strukturla həll edir — hər region öz üzərinə “məndən mənə kim referans verir” siyahısını saxlayır. Yəni Old region-dakı obyekt Young-dakı obyektə referans verəndə, bu, həmin Young region-un RSet-inə yazılır. Minor GC işə düşəndə, bütün Old Generation-ı yoxlamaq əvəzinə, GC sadəcə bu kiçik RSet siyahısına baxır. Bu, region-based dizaynın sürətli işləməsinin əsl səbəbidir — “kim mənə referans verir” sualının cavabı əvvəlcədən hazır saxlanılır.Nəhəng obyektlər problemi: Humongous ObjectsBəs böyük bir obyekt — məsələn 10MB-lıq bir massiv — yaradanda nə olur, halbuki hər region cəmi bir neçə meqabaytdır?G1-də əgər bir obyektin ölçüsü region ölçüsünün yarısından böyükdürsə, o, adi qaydada bir region-a yerləşdirilmir — ona Humongous Object (nəhəng obyekt) statusu verilir və o, bir neçə ardıcıl region-u tam tutaraq yerləşdirilir. Problem budur: bu region-lar həmin obyekt üçün “bağlanır”, başqa heç nə üçün istifadə oluna bilmir, obyekt silinənə qədər. Əgər proqram tez-tez çoxlu belə böyük obyekt yaradırsa, bu, Heap-i qeyri-effektiv doldurur və GC-ni gözlənilmədən tez-tez işə salır — bu, “yaddaş kifayət qədər boş görünür, amma GC nədənsə tez-tez işə düşür” tapmacasının çox rast gəlinən səbəblərindən biridir.2. GC bir obyektin hələ lazım olduğunu necə bilir?Bütün GC məntiqinin əsasında duran sual budur, amma çox az yerdə açıq izah olunur.Qayda sadədir: GC root-lardan başlayır — bunlar hazırda aktiv olan, “əlçatan” referanslardır: Stack-dəki lokal dəyişənlər, statik field-lər, aktiv thread-lərin özləri saxladığı referanslar. GC bu root-lardan başlayıb, hansı obyekt hansına referans verir — bu zənciri addım-addım izləyir. Zəncir vasitəsilə çatdığın hər şey canlıdır, çatmayan hər şey zibildir.Bunu effektiv izləmək üçün GC hər obyektə üç rəngdən birini “verir” — diqqət: bu, real yaddaşda saxlanan bir data deyil, sadəcə alqoritmin öz daxili vəziyyətidir:Ağ — hələ ziyarət olunmayıb.Boz — özü ziyarət olunub, amma onun referans verdiyi digər obyektlər hələ yoxlanmayıb.Qara — həm özü, həm referans verdiyi hər şey artıq yoxlanılıb, tam təhlükəsizdir.Proses belə gedir: root-lar Boz olaraq başlayır. Boz qalmayana qədər, hər dəfə bir Boz obyekt götürülür, onun referans verdiyi Ağ obyektlər Boz-a keçirilir, özü isə Qara edilir. Sonda Ağ qalan hər şey — heç yerdən əlçatan olmayan, deməli zibil sayılan obyektlərdir.İndi əsl sual: bu proses proqram işləyərkən, onu dayandırmadan gedirsə, nə olar əgər proqram elə bu anda artıq Qara işarələnmiş bir obyektdən, hələ yoxlanmamış (Ağ) yeni bir obyektə referans yaradarsa? GC artıq Qara obyektə bir daha baxmayacağı üçün, bu yeni obyekt “görünməz” qalır — canlı olduğu halda səhvən zibil sayılıb silinə bilər. Bu, GC dünyasının ən təhlükəli ssenarisidir: hələ istifadədə olan bir obyektin yanlışlıqla itirilməsi.Get Vusal Islamzada’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inG1 bunu SATB (Snapshot-At-The-Beginning — “başlanğıcdakı anlıq görüntü”) adlı bir texnika ilə həll edir. Fikir belədir: yoxlama başlayanda Heap-in məntiqi bir “şəkli” çəkilir — o anda canlı olan hər şey, bu dövr üçün canlı sayılacaq, sonradan referans itsə belə (o obyekt yalnız növ

title: Staff Android Interview Questions: Kotlin & Advanced Language Features
excerpt: The Kotlin questions that separate Senior Android Engineers from Staff Engineers Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinKotlin MultiplatformAndroidAndroid DevelopmentAndroid InterviewsStaff Android Interview Questions: Kotlin & Advanced Language FeaturesNematFollow5 min read·3 days ago21ListenShareThe Kotlin questions that separate Senior Android Engineers from Staff EngineersPress enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Vitaly Gariev on UnsplashIntroductionBy the time you reach a Staff Android interview, interviewers already assume you’re comfortable with Kotlin syntax, null safety, data classes, coroutines, and extension functions.They won’t ask:“What is a data class?”Instead, they’ll ask questions like:“Why would you avoid data classes in this scenario?”“How does Kotlin’s inline keyword improve performance?”“How would you design a type-safe SDK using Kotlin?”“When would you choose composition over inheritance in Kotlin?”At the Staff level, Kotlin is no longer just a programming language — it’s a design tool. Interviewers want to understand how deeply you know the language and whether you can use its advanced features to build scalable, maintainable systems.In this article, we’ll explore common Staff-level Kotlin interview questions along with the reasoning interviewers expect.1. Which Kotlin language features have had the biggest impact on your architecture?What the interviewer wantsThey want to know whether you use Kotlin intentionally rather than simply writing Java in Kotlin syntax.A strong answerDiscuss how features like:Null safetyExtension functionsSealed classesCoroutinesHigher-order functionsDelegationInline functionsReified genericsDSL buildershave simplified architecture, reduced boilerplate, and improved maintainability.For example:“We replaced large utility classes with extension functions, used sealed interfaces to model UI states, and leveraged delegation to share behavior without introducing inheritance.”2. Explain the difference between inline, noinline, and crossinline.This is one of the most common advanced Kotlin interview questions.inlineCopies the function body directly into the caller.Benefits:Eliminates lambda allocationsAvoids function call overheadEnables reified genericsExample:inline fun execute(action: () -> Unit) { action()}noinlinePrevents specific lambda parameters from being inlined.Use it when:Passing the lambda elsewhereStoring the lambdaReturning the lambdacrossinlineAllows inlining but prevents non-local returns.Useful when the lambda executes in another execution context.Staff-level discussionDon’t stop at definitions.Discuss:Performance implicationsBytecode generationTrade-offs between readability and optimizationSituations where excessive inlining increases APK size3. Why are reified type parameters possible only in inline functions?Expected discussion:Normally, generic types disappear because of type erasure.Inlining copies the actual type into the call site, allowing access to:inline fun <reified T> parse(json: String): TInstead of passing:parse<User>()without needing:parse(json, User::class.java)Interviewers expect you to understand why this works rather than memorizing the syntax.4. Explain Kotlin delegation.Delegation is frequently underused but highly valued in Staff interviews.There are two forms:Interface delegationclass Repository( private val logger: Logger) : Logger by loggerAvoids repetitive wrapper methods.Property delegationExamples include:lazyobservablevetoableAlso discuss custom delegates.Example:val token by SecurePreferenceDelegate()Real-world applications include:Feature flagsPreferencesDependency injectionAnalyticsPermissions5. What are value classes, and when would you use them?Value classes wrap a single value without additional runtime allocation in many cases.Example:@JvmInlinevalue class UserId(val value: String)Instead of passing raw strings everywhere:fun loadUser(id: String)Prefer:fun loadUser(id: UserId)Benefits:Type safetyBetter readabilityReduced accidental misuse6. When should you use sealed classes versus sealed interfaces?A Staff Engineer should understand the trade-offs.Sealed classBest when:Sharing common implementationMaintaining stateProviding constructorsSealed interfaceBest when:Multiple inheritance is neededModeling capabilitiesGreater flexibilityExample:sealed interface UiState7. Explain variance in Kotlin.Interviewers often ask:“Explain out and in without memorized definitions.”Example:List<out Animal>ProducerReturns objectsSafe to readConsumer<in Dog>ConsumerAccepts objectsSafe to writeStaff candidates should explain variance using real-world APIs instead of textbook definitions.8. Explain type erasure.Topics expected:JVM genericsRuntime limitationsReflectionReified genericsJava interoperability9. How would you design a type-safe networking library?Interviewers want API design skills.Get Nemat’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inExample:Instead of:fun request(url: String)Prefer:api.get<User>()Discuss:Reified genericsInline functionsExtension functionsSealed resultsDSL builders10. Explain Kotlin contracts.Most candidates have never used them.Example:requireNotNull(value)Contracts help the compiler understand smart casts.Topics:Smart castingPreconditionsLibrary designExperimental status11. What are context receivers?Although still an evolving language feature, interviewers may ask about them to gauge awareness of modern Kotlin.Discuss:Reducing parameter passingCleaner DSLsDependency injectionScope management12. Explain Kotlin DSLs.Example:screen { button { text("Login")}}Discuss:Type-safe buildersReceiversLambdas with receiversCompose as a DSL13. How would you reduce object allocations in Kotlin?Possible answers:Inline functionsValue classesAvoid unnecessary collectionsSequencesLazy evaluationReuse objectsAvoid boxingPerformance discussions are common Staff-level topics.14. Explain lazy initialization.Different approaches:lazy { }lateinitDependency InjectionManual initializationDiscuss thread safety modes.15. Explain hi

title: jsoup 1.23.1 is out: here’s what actually changed
excerpt: jsoup 1.23.1 just dropped and this one is worth paying attention to. Not just a patch release. There are real parser speed gains… Continue reading on Medium »
content: JavaKotlinAndroidOpen SourceProgrammingjsoup 1.23.1 is out: here’s what actually changedRajen TrivediFollow3 min read·3 days agoListenSharejsoup 1.23.1 just dropped and this one is worth paying attention to. Not just a patch release. There are real parser speed gains, meaningful memory improvements, and a security fix that Android and server-side Java devs should know about.Here’s what changed and why it matters.Press enter or click to view image in full sizejsoup 1.23.1 brings real performance gains and a security fix worth knowing about.Add the dependencyGradle (Groovy):implementation 'org.jsoup:jsoup:1.23.1'Gradle (Kotlin DSL):implementation("org.jsoup:jsoup:1.23.1")Maven:<dependency> <groupId>org.jsoup</groupId> <artifactId>jsoup</artifactId> <version>1.23.1</version></dependency>PerformanceThis was clearly the main focus of the release. Numbers are from OpenJDK 21 benchmarks.String parsing is 18% faster on average.The most common use case just got noticeably quicker.Document doc = Jsoup.parse(htmlString);InputStream parsing is 11% faster.Good news if you’re parsing HTTP responses or file streams directly.Document doc = Jsoup.parse(inputStream, "UTF-8", baseUri);Source position tracking is 70% faster.If you use Parser.htmlParser().setTrackPosition(true), this is a big one. It was the slowest mode before. Not anymore.Parser parser = Parser.htmlParser().setTrackPosition(true);Document doc = Jsoup.parse(htmlString, baseUri, parser);Source-tracked DOMs use 58 to 65% less memory on medium to large documents.Get Rajen Trivedi’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe gains hold under concurrent parsing without introducing new contention. If you parse in parallel, you get the memory savings without thread safety trade-offs.Security fixThe Cleaner had an issue where malformed HTML could sneak markup through when cleaned with a custom Safelist that permitted certain raw-text elements.// Custom Safelists with raw-text elements were affectedSafelist safelist = Safelist.relaxed().addTags("script");String cleaned = Jsoup.clean(malformedHtml, safelist);// In previous versions, some markup could survive this incorrectlyBuilt-in Safelists like Safelist.basic() and Safelist.relaxed() are not affected. But if you built a custom Safelist with unusual raw-text tag permissions, update now.What else changedBetter HTML spec alignment.Parsing of noscript, CDATA, SVG, and MathML now aligns more closely with the HTML living standard. If your parser results on edge-case documents ever felt slightly off, this release tightens that up.Spec-correct HTTP redirects.Redirect handling is now safer and follows the HTTP spec more accurately. Fewer surprises when dealing with servers that do non-standard redirect chains.Fast immutable Element#classList().Returns an immutable view of the element’s class list. Faster to call, safer to use since you can’t accidentally mutate it.Element el = doc.selectFirst("div.card");Set<String> classes = el.classList();// immutable, no defensive copy neededSystem.out.println(classes); // [card, featured, active]Direct outer-HTML output to an Appendable.You can now write an element’s outer HTML directly to a StringBuilder, Writer, or any Appendable without going through a String allocation first.StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();element.outerHtml(sb);// no intermediate String createdBug fixes also landed across RCDATA parsing, XML conversion, tag-name handling, and Cleaner link detection.Should you update?Yes, especially if you:Use setTrackPosition(true): the 70% speed gain alone is worth itParse large documents concurrently: the memory savings are realBuilt a custom Safelist with raw-text elements: the security fix applies to youFor everyone else, it’s still an easy drop-in upgrade with no API changes.This post also appeared on Dev.to. If you found it there first, welcome.Reference: jsoup releases on GitHub

title: Pocketflow #Week1 - The Core Idea & Multiplatform Architecture
excerpt: Welcome to the first update of my build-in-public journey for Shipaton 2026 by Revenuecat ! Continue reading on Medium »
content: ShipatonRevenuecatKotlin MultiplatformKotlinJetbrainsPocketflow #Week1 - The Core Idea & Multiplatform ArchitectureAk DeepankarFollow3 min read·3 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWelcome to the first update of my build-in-public journey for Shipaton 2026 by Revenuecat !If you’ve ever played around with generative AI, you know that the real magic happens when you chain models together: generating an image from a prompt, converting that image into a video, synthesizing a voice script, and combining them into a final ad or video. While tools like ComfyUI make this easy on desktop, mobile creators are left out.My mission with Pocketflow is to change that: bringing a powerful, node-based generative AI workflow editor right to iOS and Android.To build this natively on both iOS and Android without having to maintain two separate codebases, I will be going with Compose Multiplatform. But before starting my project, I spent this week doing a sanity check: Can Compose Multiplatform actually handle this? Here is the plan and the features I figured out that will make this work:1. Navigating the Infinite Canvas — Honestly, I was terrified of having to build the drag-and-drop node graph UI twice. But I spent the week reading up on Compose Multiplatform’s Canvas API and gesture detectors like detectTransformGestures for handling panning and pinch-to-zoom. By connecting the dots between those APIs and drawing Bezier curves between node coordinates, I realized I can build the entire node-editor interface once in shared code and have it render natively on both iOS and Android.2. Tackling the Heavy File Problem — AI generation produces heavy files (MP4s, PNGs, MP3s). The default cache directories on mobile are temporary and get wiped on system restarts. I need a way to save these assets persistently. I figured out that I can abstract the local file system using Kotlin Multiplatform’s expect / actual declarations. The shared logic will just call a simple save function, but compile-time actuals will route it to the persistent NSDocumentDirectory on iOS and filesDir on Android:Get Ak Deepankar’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inIn commonMain (Common Code)expect object LocalStorage { fun saveMediaToTemp(bytes: ByteArray, extension: String): String }In iosMain (iOS side of the bridge)actual object LocalStorage { actual fun saveMediaToTemp(bytes: ByteArray, extension: String): String { // Grab iOS Document directory and write raw bytes... } }3. Bringing in Native SDKs (OneSignal & Share Sheets) - Since rendering videos via AI takes time, I want to trigger push notifications when the generation is done. However, push notifications require native setup.I figured out that I don’t need a pure Multiplatform library for this. I can set up OneSignal natively inside the iOS Swift app and Android Kotlin app, and expose a tiny interface bridge to the shared module. When the AI rendering finishes, the shared Compose code will simply trigger that interface, launching a native notification or the system’s sharing overlay.The Next StepThe research is done and the architecture design is locked in. Next week to start vibe coding the layout and infinite panning math of the canvas. I’ll act as the architect directing the vision. Let’s see how fast we can turn these ideas into a working prototype!

title: Why Modern Android Testing Is Different
excerpt: ReadMore https://leanpub.com/modern_android_testing Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidKotlinTestingSoftware TestingWhy Modern Android Testing Is DifferentMahmoud RamadanFollow13 min read·3 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeReadMore https://leanpub.com/modern_android_testingYou have probably lived some version of this story.A team inherits a healthy-looking Android codebase. The test suite is green. Coverage sits at a respectable seventy-something percent. Everyone feels safe. Then a routine refactor — renaming a repository method, extracting a use case, swapping one dependency-injection binding for another — turns two hundred tests red. Not one of those failures represents a real bug. They failed because they were welded to the shape of the old code, not to what the app actually does. An afternoon disappears into mechanically updating tests that never protected anyone in the first place.Meanwhile, the failures that would have mattered — a button that renders off-screen on a small display, a login form that shows a success state while quietly dropping the auth token, a list that flickers empty for one frame on a slow network — sail through untouched, because nothing in that carefully maintained suite ever looked at them.This chapter is about why that happens, and why the answer is not “write more tests” or “hit ninety percent coverage.” The answer is a different model of what tests are for, and a toolchain that finally makes the good model cheap enough to live by. Modern Android — Jetpack Compose, JVM-based rendering, unidirectional state, screenshot testing — has quietly dismantled the assumptions that most Android testing advice was built on. Before we write a single test in this book, it is worth understanding what changed and why it changes everything downstream.1.1 The Pyramid We InheritedAlmost every discussion of test strategy starts with the testing pyramid, popularized by Mike Cohn in Succeeding with Agile back in 2009. The idea is simple and, for its time, correct. Tests come in layers. At the base sit unit tests: many of them, fast, cheap, isolated. In the middle, fewer integration tests. At the top, a thin cap of end-to-end tests that drive the whole system through its real UI: slow, expensive, and prone to breaking for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.The pyramid encodes an economic argument. A unit test costs almost nothing to run and fails fast, so you can afford thousands. An end-to-end test spins up the entire system, so each one costs real time and real flakiness, and you should own as few as you can get away with. Invest heavily where tests are cheap; ration yourself where they are expensive.For its era, this was excellent advice. And one part of it is timeless: fast feedback is a feature, and a suite you have to babysit for forty minutes is a suite people stop running. The pyramid’s instinct — push work down to the cheapest layer that can still catch the bug — is one this book keeps.But notice the assumption doing the heavy lifting. The pyramid treats “UI test” and “expensive, slow, flaky” as synonyms. That assumption was baked in during an era of server-rendered pages and heavyweight browser automation, and it arrived in Android through Espresso running on an emulator: boot a device, install an APK, wait for the app, poke at views through an idling-resource dance, and pray the animation finished before the assertion ran. On that toolchain, the pyramid’s economics are exactly right.The trouble is that the toolchain changed and the mental model didn’t.1.2 Why the Pyramid’s Assumptions Don’t Hold on Modern AndroidFour shifts, all landing within the last few years, have broken the pyramid’s core assumption that testing the UI is inherently costly.Compose UI can render on the JVM. With Robolectric-backed tools, and with screenshot libraries like Paparazzi and Roborazzi, you can render real composables and assert on them without an emulator in the loop. A test that would once have needed a booted device now runs in the same millisecond-scale JVM process as your unit tests. When the cost of a “UI test” drops by two orders of magnitude, the line the pyramid drew between the cheap base and the expensive top stops describing reality.The semantics tree replaced brittle view matching. Compose tests don’t hunt for a widget by resource ID or class name. They query the semantics tree — the same accessibility-oriented description of the screen that a screen reader consumes. You find a node by the text a user reads or the content description they’d hear, and you act on it the way they would. This is a subtle but profound change: the natural way to write a Compose UI test is already a behavior query, not an implementation query. The tooling nudges you toward the resilient style instead of fighting you.Unidirectional data flow turned UI logic into pure state. In a state-driven Compose architecture, a screen is a function of its state. “What should the user see when login fails?” is no longer a question you can only answer by driving a live screen — it is a question about a state object, and state objects are trivially testable as plain values. A huge slice of what used to require UI testing collapses into ordinary unit testing of state transformations.Screenshot testing became a first-class category. The pyramid has no slot for “assert that this screen looks the way it’s supposed to.” Visual regressions — a truncated label, a broken dark-mode contrast, a layout that shatters at a 2x font scale — are invisible to text-based assertions. Screenshot testing catches an entire class of defect that the pyramid literally cannot represent, and modern JVM-based screenshot tools make it fast enough to run on every pull request.Put those together and the pyramid’s foundational trade-off — cheap-but-shallow at the bottom, expensive-but-realistic at the top — no longer maps onto the tools we actually have. On modern Android, you can get high realism and low cost in the same test. The question stops being “which cheap layer can I pus

title: Two things called “State”: how mutableStateOf and StateFlow really work underneath
excerpt: You have two imports open. Both types have a .value. Both are “observable.” Both hold a single piece of state that something else reacts… Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidJetpack ComposeKotlinTwo things called “State”: how mutableStateOf and StateFlow really work underneathAngelina AndronovaFollow24 min read·4 days ago31ListenShareYou have two imports open. Both types have a .value. Both are “observable.” Both hold a single piece of state that something else reacts to:import androidx.compose.runtime.mutableStateOf // Compose Stateimport kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow // coroutines Stateval a = mutableStateOf(0) // a.valueval b = MutableStateFlow(0) // b.valueThey look like siblings. They are not. They come from different libraries, solve overlapping problems with completely different machinery, and — this is the interesting part — Compose could not have just reused StateFlow.1. First, agree on what “observable state” has to doStrip away the branding. Any observable state primitive has three jobs:Hold a current value.Allow readers to register themselves.Notify readers when the value changes, so they re-run.Both types do all three. The entire difference is how they register readers and notify them — and that difference cascades into threading, consistency, equality and lifecycle.StateFlow: you register manually, by calling collect. From then on, values are pushed to you on a coroutine.Compose State: you don’t register manually — the framework does it for you, by watching reads. While composition runs, every state read is recorded, and a later write invalidates whoever read that value.The flow model is the simpler machine, so it comes first — and what it cannot do is what the rest of the article is about.2. kotlinx.coroutines: StateFlow underneath2.1 Holding the value: one cellHolding the value gets the cheapest possible solution. MutableStateFlow(0) is a StateFlowImpl, and its entire storage is a single atomic reference — call it the cell. Reading .value is an atomic load from any thread; writing .value overwrites it in place. There is no history and no queue, only the latest value.That is all the storage there is. Everything else in StateFlow exists to solve the second problem — getting collectors to re-run — and it is worth deriving rather than describing, because each piece is forced by the one before it.2.2 Delivering to a collector: why a plain loop is not enoughA collector is a coroutine you launchedviewModelScope.launch { flow.collect { … } }collect is a suspend function, so its loop runs on your coroutine, not on anything the flow owns.Start with the simplest thing that could work: watch the cell in a loop and deliver whenever it differs from what you delivered last.override suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>) { // naive version var oldState: Any? = null while (true) { val newState = _state.value // read the cell if (oldState == null || oldState != newState) { collector.emit(newState) // "deliver" = call YOUR collect { } body oldState = newState // remember what I last delivered } }}The issue is — nothing in that loop blocks, so a collector with no news spins as fast as the CPU allows — one busy core per idle collector. So the loop has to suspend when the cell has not changed.Suspending is what forces everything that follows. A suspended coroutine is not running, so it cannot notice that the cell changed — something else has to resume it. That means a writer needs somewhere to look up “how do I resume this particular collector,” and it needs one such place per collector.That place is the slot. The flow owns an array of them, one handed out to each active collect { } and freed when that collector is cancelled. Note what the slot is for: it is coordination for suspend-and-resume. It never holds a value, because the collector can always read the cell itself.2.3 The lost wake-up, and the states that prevent itYou would expect a slot to need two states: empty, or holding a resume handle. It needs more, because of a race.Deciding that there is nothing new and actually suspending are two separate steps, and a writer can land in the gap between them. The writer overwrites the cell, then looks in the slot for a resume handle and finds none, because the collector has not stored one yet. So it resumes nobody. The collector then suspends, on a value that is already stale, and nothing will ever resume it. The signal is lost.Press enter or click to view image in full sizePreventing that needs one more piece of information in the slot: something changed while you were still running, so do not suspend. That is the pending flag, and now the four states the runtime actually uses are all accounted for:free — an unused entry in the array; no collector here.running, nothing pending — the collector is caught up.running, pending — the cell changed while it was working; it must not suspend at the bottom of the loop.suspended — holding the handle a writer uses to resume it.Which gives the real loop. takePending() atomically consumes the flag and answers “was there news?” — if yes, go round the loop again; if no, suspend:override suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>) { val slot = allocateSlot() // this collector's own slot var oldState: Any? = null while (true) { val newState = _state.value // read the cell (top of every loop) if (oldState == null || oldState != newState) { collector.emit(newState) // "deliver" = call YOUR collect { } body oldState = newState // remember what I last delivered } if (!slot.takePending()) // nothing new? slot.awaitPending() // → suspend until resumed }}The producer side is the mirror of it. Writing .value overwrites the cell, then walks every slot: a suspended collector is resumed, and a running one only gets the pending flag set, since you cannot resume something that is already running. The value is never handed to a slot — there is nowhere to put it, and no need, because a resumed collector re-reads the cell at the top of its loop. That is also where conflation comes from: if the cell advances twice while a collector is busy, it sees only the newest value, because the intermediate one was never stored
