title: Stop Writing Compose Like It’s 2024–10 Recent Updates Every Android Developer Should Know
excerpt: Your Compose code compiles. It works. And half of it now has a better alternative. You open an old Compose project. Everything compiles. Everything runs. And yet, a surprising amount of the code you’re writing today has a better replacement shipped in the last twelve months. Navigation changed fundamentally. State handling got a new tier. Scroll performance quietly caught up with RecyclerView. Text fields got a completely different state model. Shadows finally work the way designers expect. If y
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizeYour Compose code compiles. It works. And half of it now has a better alternative.Jetpack ComposeAndroidMaterial 3AndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentStop Writing Compose Like It’s 2024–10 Recent Updates Every Android Developer Should KnowSubhankar BagFollow12 min read·2 days ago16ListenShareYou open an old Compose project.Everything compiles. Everything runs. And yet, a surprising amount of the code you’re writing today has a better replacement shipped in the last twelve months.Navigation changed fundamentally. State handling got a new tier. Scroll performance quietly caught up with RecyclerView. Text fields got a completely different state model. Shadows finally work the way designers expect.If you’re still writing Compose the way you did in 2024, you’re not wrong; you’re just doing extra work the framework no longer requires.Here are the ten changes that actually matter, with the old way and the new way side by side. Everything below is based on stable releases — August ’25 (Compose 1.9, BOM 2025.08.00), December ’25 (Compose 1.10 + Material 3 1.4, BOM 2025.12.00), and April ’26 (Compose 1.11, BOM 2026.04.01) — with the handful of experimental APIs explicitly called out where they appear. Treat BOM 2025.12.00 as the minimum baseline for these features; the current stable target as of this writing (mid-2026) is:implementation(platform("androidx.compose:compose-bom:2026.04.01"))TL;DR: what changed and what to do about it:Pausable composition (default on) — Bump the BOM, re-run your benchmarksretain {} API — Move players and bitmaps out of ViewModels they never belonged inNavigation 3 stable — Type-safe keys, you own the back stackdropShadow() / innerShadow() — Retire your shadow workaroundsLazyLayoutCacheWindow (experimental) — Tune prefetch on heavy listsTextFieldState + SecureTextField — Migrate off value/onValueChangeonVisibilityChanged — Migrate off the now-deprecated onFirstVisibleAutofill + auto-sizing text — Add semantics to login flowsMaterial 3 Expressive — Prototype one screen nowv2 testing APIs (StandardTestDispatcher default) — Migrate the test suite, fix flakes on your termsNow the details: with old-way vs new-way code for each.1. Scroll Performance Now Rivals Views — For a BOM BumpThis is the headline nobody should skip, so let’s scope it honestly. With the December ’25 release, Google reported that its internal hero scroll benchmarks show Compose matching View-based performance on scrolling jank. That’s a specific claim — jank parity in Google’s benchmark scenarios, not blanket performance parity across every workload — but it’s precisely the scenario that has fueled the “Compose is slower” argument since 2021. The announcement and methodology are in the December ’25 release post; your app’s numbers are the ones that matter, so measure before you quote.The mechanism behind it is pausable composition in lazy prefetch, now enabled by default.Previously, once a composition started, it had to run to completion. A complex item in a LazyColumn could blow past the frame deadline and you'd feel it as jank. Now the runtime can pause mid-composition when it's running out of frame budget and resume next frame — especially effective when prefetching content ahead of the viewport.What you have to do: upgrade the BOM. That’s it. No API change, no flag.If you spent 2023–2024 defending RecyclerView for heavy lists in performance reviews, it's time to re-run your benchmarks with Macrobenchmark. The argument has materially changed — and now you get to settle it with current data instead of 2023 folklore.2. retain {} — The Missing Tier of State ManagementYou know the drill:remember → survives recomposition, dies on configuration changerememberSaveable → survives config change and process death, but must be serializableThere was always an awkward gap: objects that should survive rotation but can’t be serialized. Players, flows, lambdas, bitmaps, connections. The classic workaround was hoisting them into a ViewModel even when they were purely UI-scoped — not because they were business logic, but because ViewModel was the only thing that survived rotation.Compose 1.10 fills the gap with retain:❌ Old way: ViewModel as a bucket for a player:class PlayerViewModel(app: Application) : AndroidViewModel(app) { val exoPlayer = ExoPlayer.Builder(app).build() override fun onCleared() { exoPlayer.release() }}✅ New way: retained in composition, released via the retention lifecycle:@Composablefun MediaPlayer(mediaUri: String) { val appContext = LocalContext.current.applicationContextval exoPlayer = retain(mediaUri) { ExoPlayer.Builder(appContext).build().apply { setMediaItem(MediaItem.fromUri(mediaUri)) prepare() } } // Cleanup belongs to the retention lifecycle, not the composition. // onRetire fires only when the value is permanently discarded - // not on rotation, not on transient recomposition. RetainedEffect(exoPlayer) { onRetire { exoPlayer.release() } } // Playback survives rotation. No ViewModel ceremony. No leak.}The root cause worth understanding here: DisposableEffect's onDispose fires on configuration change, which is exactly the moment you don't want to release a retained player — that would defeat the entire point of retaining it. RetainedEffect exists precisely for this: its onRetire block runs once, when the retained value permanently leaves. Player survives rotation, resource never leaks. If you adopt retain without RetainedEffect, you've traded a rotation bug for a resource leak.retain persists across configuration changes but not process death — deliberately. It's the right tool for non-serializable, UI-lifecycle-bound objects. The design was influenced by the community (notably Slack's Circuit team), which tells you how real this pain point was.Rule of thumb going forward: remember for composition, retain for config changes, rememberSaveable for process death, ViewModel for business logic. Four tiers, each with a job.3. Navigation 3: You Own t

title: Android Skills — What Google Just Released and Why Most Developers Are Already Using It Wrong
excerpt: Here’s the counterintuitive philosophy behind Google’s new agent system — with code. Image by mammela from Pixabay You’ve probably seen the announcement. Android Skills launched in April; the response surpassed Google’s expectations, and yesterday the Android Developer Relations team published a deep dive explaining the philosophy behind the project. Most developers read it as a release note. It’s actually a set of architectural decisions about AI-assisted Android development — and if you miss t
content: AndroidKotlinArtificial IntelligenceAndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentAndroid Skills — What Google Just Released and Why Most Developers Are Already Using It WrongHere’s the counterintuitive philosophy behind Google’s new agent system — with code.DilipchandarFollow6 min read·2 days ago571ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeImage by mammela from PixabayYou’ve probably seen the announcement. Android Skills launched in April; the response surpassed Google’s expectations, and yesterday the Android Developer Relations team published a deep dive explaining the philosophy behind the project.Most developers read it as a release note.It’s actually a set of architectural decisions about AI-assisted Android development — and if you miss them, you’ll end up with an agent setup that costs more, runs slower, and produces worse output than if you’d done nothing at all.What Android Skills Actually AreSkills are modular, markdown-based SKILL.md instruction sets that provide a technical specification for a task and are designed to trigger automatically when your prompt matches the skill’s metadata — no need to manually attach documentation to every prompt.The initial release covers Navigation 3 setup and migration, edge-to-edge support, AGP 9 and XML-to-Compose migrations, and R8 config analysis.But the most important thing to understand is what skills are not. They are not a general-purpose Android knowledge base. They are surgical interventions for the specific areas where today’s frontier models actively produce wrong output. The distinction matters enormously in practice.The Hidden Cost of Installing Too Many SkillsHere’s the counterintuitive decision most developers will get wrong.Every installed skill injects 100–200 tokens into the baseline context of every task. If that skill activates, that count jumps into the thousands. For a team running 150 tasks per day across 10 unnecessary skills, that’s easily $500–600 per year in wasted token spend on context the model already knows — plus degraded output quality from increased noise.Google’s guidance is explicit: before installing a skill for writing basic Kotlin or Compose, consider if your LLM actually needs it, or whether it already knows those topics well enough.The correct mental model:Android Knowledge Base first → Targeted Skills second → Custom Skills thirdThe Knowledge Base via android docs covers breadth. Skills cover confirmed failure modes. Install the Knowledge Base always. Install skills deliberately.The Real Difference a Skill Makes — Navigation 2.8+ Type SafetyHere is concrete before/after output for the prompt: Set up navigation with a home screen and detail screen that receives a user ID// ❌ WITHOUT Navigation 2.8+ skill — Legacy / String-Based (Pre-2.8)val navController = rememberNavController()NavHost(navController = navController, startDestination = "home") { composable("home") { HomeScreen( onNavigateToDetail = { userId -> navController.navigate("detail/$userId") } ) } composable( route = "detail/{userId}", arguments = listOf(navArgument("userId") { type = NavType.StringType }) ) { backStackEntry -> DetailScreen( userId = backStackEntry.arguments ?.getString("userId") ?: "" ) }}// ✅ WITH Navigation 2.8+ skill — Modern Type-Safe (2.8.0+)@Serializable object Home@Serializable data class Detail(val userId: String)val navController = rememberNavController()NavHost( navController = navController, startDestination = Home) { composable<Home> { HomeScreen( onNavigateToDetail = { userId -> navController.navigate(Detail(userId = userId)) } ) } composable<Detail> { backStackEntry -> val detail: Detail = backStackEntry.toRoute() DetailScreen(userId = detail.userId) }}Why it matters: Both approaches compile and run. However, the legacy approach relies on string parsing and manual bundle extractions that are prone to typos and runtime crashes. The 2.8+ type-safe approach catches routing errors at compile time and eliminates manual argument parsing entirely.How Google Decides Whether a Skill Should ExistGoogle only creates a skill when there’s a verifiable knowledge gap in state-of-the-art models. Each skill must pass a comprehensive eval before publication:timeout_s: 1200repository: working_dir: wear_compose_m3_empty_appprompt: |- Add a horizontal pager to MainActivity.kt with three pages showing "Page 1", "Page 2", "Page 3" centered on screen.commands: build: - ./gradlew assembleDebugacceptance_criteria: project_builds: true llm_diff_judge: - Must use `HorizontalPagerScaffold` - Each page must use `AnimatedPage` wrapping `ScreenScaffold`The eval doesn’t just check that it compiles — it verifies the agent used the correct Wear OS APIs. This is why there are around 20 official skills, not 200. Each one represents a confirmed, measurable failure mode. If a model reliably gets something right, there’s no skill for it — and there shouldn’t be.A Production-Ready AGENTS.mdThe difference between a mediocre agent setup and a great one often comes down to a well-written AGENTS.md. Here's a realistic template for an Android project:# AGENTS.md## DocumentationAlways consult the Android Knowledge Base (android docs) before suggesting any Jetpack API.## Architecture- MVVM + Hilt — do NOT suggest Koin or manual DI- ViewModels use StateFlow — never LiveData for new code- Repository pattern required for all data access## UI- All new screens use Jetpack Compose — no new XML layouts- Reference HomeScreen.kt as the Compose pattern for this project## Navigation- Navigation 3 with type-safe routes — not navigation-compose 2.x- All routes must be @Serializable — reference NavGraph.kt## Build- AGP 9 — use libs.versions.toml, no direct build.gradle.kts deps## Testing- JUnit 5 + MockK for unit tests — not Mockito or Espresso- Coroutine tests use runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test## Never- Thread.sleep() → use delay()- GlobalScope → use viewModelScope- Broad catch(Exception) → handle specific types- !! operator → handle nullability explicitlyThe ke

title: Why My Flutter Timer Needed a Native Android Service
excerpt: How I combined a smooth Flutter UI with a Kotlin foreground service, monotonic time, and state snapshots. Continue reading on Medium »
content: FlutterAndroid App DevelopmentKotlinMobile App DevelopmentProgrammingWhy My Flutter Timer Needed a Native Android ServiceTomFollow9 min read·2 days agoListenShareHow I combined a smooth Flutter UI with a Kotlin foreground service, monotonic time, and state snapshots.The problemI started building Loop because I wanted a timer that stayed out of the way. Set an active interval, add a rest period, choose the number of rounds, and start.The UI was the enjoyable part: animated progress, clear controls, and a timer that felt responsive. The difficult part only became obvious when I pressed the Home button.A countdown that works while the app is open is easy. A countdown that remains accurate while Flutter is paused, the screen is off, or Android is busy doing something else is a different problem.This article explains the approach I ended up using in Loop: Flutter owns the visible experience, while a native Android foreground service keeps track of the session in the background. When the app becomes active again, Flutter asks Android for a snapshot and restores its state from that.For Loop, I only needed to solve one narrow case: keeping a user-started interval timer accurate while Flutter was paused.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeLoop interval timer running alongside its Android foreground-service notification.Why a Dart timer was not enoughMy first instinct was the obvious one: update the countdown periodically in Dart and let the UI react to it.That is fine while the Flutter engine is active. It is not a good foundation for background timing. Once the app moves into the background, execution can be throttled or paused. Even in the foreground, repeatedly subtracting a fixed duration introduces another problem: the callback does not necessarily run at the exact requested time.If a callback scheduled every 50 milliseconds arrives late, subtracting another 50 milliseconds hides the delay instead of accounting for it. Small errors accumulate. An interval timer makes those errors especially visible because every active-to-rest transition depends on the previous one.The rule I ended up relying on was simple:A timer should be derived from elapsed time, not from the number of ticks received.Flutter could still animate the interface smoothly. I just did not want that animation to be the only source of truth once the app was no longer active.Splitting the responsibilitiesLoop effectively has two cooperating timer implementations:Flutter manages the screen, controls, animations, navigation, and Riverpod state.A Kotlin foreground service manages elapsed background time, phase transitions, sound, vibration, a partial wake lock, and the ongoing notification.Both start from the same configuration. User actions such as pause, resume, or adding ten seconds are sent to both sides. When Flutter resumes, it treats the native snapshot as authoritative and rebuilds the UI from it.That boundary kept the platform-specific part relatively small. I did not move the whole feature into Kotlin; Android only owns the work that needs to survive Flutter being paused.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeFlutter owns the experience; the Android service owns background timing.Keeping the Flutter boundary boringI wanted the Flutter side to know as little as possible about Android. The interface contains only the operations the timer screen actually needs:abstract interface class TimerBackgroundService { Future<void> start(TimerBackgroundConfiguration configuration); Future<void> pause(); Future<void> resume(); Future<void> adjust(Duration amount); Future<TimerBackgroundSnapshot?> getSnapshot(); Future<void> stop();}The Android implementation uses one MethodChannel:class AndroidTimerBackgroundService implements TimerBackgroundService { static const _channel = MethodChannel( 'com.tomvogel.loop/timer_background_service', ); @override Future<void> adjust(Duration amount) async { if (Platform.isAndroid) { await _channel.invokeMethod<void>('adjust', { 'durationMs': amount.inMilliseconds, }); } } @override Future<TimerBackgroundSnapshot?> getSnapshot() async { if (!Platform.isAndroid) return null; final snapshot = await _channel.invokeMethod<Map<Object?, Object?>>( 'getSnapshot', ); return snapshot == null ? null : TimerBackgroundSnapshot.fromMap(snapshot); }}I provide this implementation through Riverpod. That is useful for more than dependency injection aesthetics: widget tests can replace the native service with a small fake and verify that tapping pause, resume, or the adjustment controls sends the expected command.On the Android side, MainActivity translates those method calls into service intents:when (call.method) { "start" -> startTimerService( LoopTimerService.startIntent( context = this, activeDurationMs = call.argument<Number>("activeDurationMs")!!.toLong(), restDurationMs = call.argument<Number>("restDurationMs")!!.toLong(), totalSets = call.argument<Number>("totalSets")!!.toInt(), hapticsEnabled = call.argument<Boolean>("hapticsEnabled") == true, soundEnabled = call.argument<Boolean>("soundEnabled") == true, ), ) "pause" -> sendTimerAction(LoopTimerService.ACTION_PAUSE, result) "resume" -> sendTimerAction(LoopTimerService.ACTION_RESUME, result) "getSnapshot" -> result.success(LoopTimerService.currentSnapshot())}There is no continuous stream of timer ticks crossing the channel. That would add unnecessary traffic and create awkward ownership questions. Flutter renders its own progress while visible; the channel is used for commands and reconciliation.The part that prevents driftThe Android service runs a Handler callback every 50 milliseconds, but the callback interval is not used to calculate the remaining time. It only determines how often the service checks the clock.For the actual timing, I use Android’s monotonic SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() and store a deadline:val now = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()lastAccountingMs = nowdeadlineMs = now + remainingMsUsing a monotonic clock matters. Wall-cl

title: Common Mistakes Android Developers Make When Learning Jetpack Compose (and How to Avoid Them)
excerpt: Introduction Continue reading on Medium »
content: Jetpack ComposeKotlinProgrammingLearningAndroidCommon Mistakes Android Developers Make When Learning Jetpack Compose (and How to Avoid Them)StevenFollow28 min read·2 days agoListenShareIntroductionJetpack Compose is arguably the biggest shift in Android UI development since the platform launched. For over a decade, Android developers built interfaces with XML layouts, findViewById, and imperative view manipulation. Compose throws that model out and replaces it with a declarative, function-based approach borrowed from ideas popularized by React and Flutter.The promise is compelling: less boilerplate, a single source of truth for UI state, easier previews, and UI code that lives next to the logic that drives it. But the transition is rarely painless. Developers who have spent years mastering the XML/View system often carry that mental model directly into Compose — and that’s where the trouble starts.The difference between imperative and declarative UI is the crux of the problem.In the imperative world, you tell the system how to change: “find this TextView and set its text to X.” You are responsible for keeping the UI in sync with your data, step by step, mutation by mutation.In the declarative world, you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and the framework figures out how to get there. You don’t mutate views — you describe them as a function of state: UI = f(state). When the state changes, Compose re-executes (recomposes) the relevant functions and produces a new UI description.This sounds simple in theory, but in practice, most of the mistakes developers make when learning Compose come from one root cause: they keep an XML mindset while writing Compose code. They try to “update the UI” instead of “describing the UI based on state.” They treat Composable functions like ViewGroups. They store mutable data in the wrong place. They fight recomposition instead of embracing it.This article walks through 18 concrete mistakes Android developers commonly make while learning Compose, along with practical examples and ways to avoid them.XML Mindset vs Compose MindsetBefore diving into the mistakes, it’s worth explicitly naming the mental model shift, because almost everything else in this article traces back to it.View Manipulation vs State-Driven UIIn the XML/View system, a screen is a tree of long-lived, mutable objects. You hold a reference to a TextView, and whenever something changes, you reach out and mutate it directly:// XML / View systembinding.usernameText.text = "Hello, John"binding.loadingSpinner.visibility = View.GONEbinding.submitButton.isEnabled = trueThe view objects persist across changes. Your job as a developer is to remember every place the UI needs to be touched whenever the underlying data changes. Miss one spot, and your UI silently goes out of sync with your data — a classic and painful class of Android bugs.In Compose, there are no persistent view objects that you mutate. Instead, you write a function that takes state and emits a UI description:@Composablefun Greeting(username: String, isLoading: Boolean, canSubmit: Boolean) { if (isLoading) { CircularProgressIndicator() } else { Text("Hello, $username") Button(onClick = { /* ... */ }, enabled = canSubmit) { Text("Submit") } }}When username, isLoading, or canSubmit change, Compose re-invokes Greeting() (or just the parts that depend on the changed value) and produces updated UI. You never say "hide the spinner" or "enable the button" — you simply describe what the UI looks like given the current state, and Compose handles the transition.Updating UI Manually vs Describing UI Based on StateThis is the single biggest habit to unlearn. In XML-based development, “updating the UI” is an action you perform. In Compose, there is no such action — there is only state changing, which causes recomposition, which produces new UI.If you find yourself writing code that tries to imperatively “change what’s on screen” inside a Composable (e.g., manually toggling visibility flags stored outside of state, or calling methods on a component reference), that’s a strong signal you’re still thinking in XML terms.How the Developer’s Mental Model Must ChangeTo work effectively with Compose, you need to internalize a few principles:State is the single source of truth. The UI is a reflection of state, not the other way around.Composable functions can run again, and often. Don’t treat them as “run once and mutate later” — treat them as pure(ish) rendering functions that may re-execute many times.Side effects need explicit handling. Anything that isn’t “just describe the UI” (network calls, logging, starting animations) needs to be wrapped in an effect handler (LaunchedEffect, SideEffect, etc.) so it doesn't run uncontrolled on every recomposition.Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) replaces two-way manual syncing. State flows down, events flow up. You don’t reach into a child and mutate it; the child reports events and the parent decides how state should change.With that mental shift in mind, let’s go through the mistakes.Main Section: 15 Common Mistakes1. Treating Compose Like XML LayoutsWhy developers make this mistake: Years of muscle memory. Developers try to map LinearLayout → Column/Row and ConstraintLayout → ConstraintLayout (Compose has one too) without rethinking composition and reusability. They build one giant Composable per screen, mirroring the "one XML file per screen" pattern.Why it’s problematic: XML encourages a flat, layout-centric structure because that’s all it can do — it’s a static UI description with no functions. Compose is code, and code should be broken into small, composable, reusable, testable units. Treating Compose as “XML but in Kotlin” throws away its biggest advantage: composability.Bad example:@Composablefun ProfileScreen() { Column { Row { Image(painter = painterResource(R.drawable.avatar), contentDescription = null) Column { Text("John Doe") Text("Android Developer") } } Divider() Row { Text("Followe

title: Kotlin const val, val, and var: What’s the Difference?
excerpt: When learning Kotlin, you’ll quickly encounter three ways to declare values: Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinAndroidConst ValKotlin BeginnersVariablesKotlin const val, val, and var: What’s the Difference?haloFollow5 min read·2 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhen learning Kotlin, you’ll quickly encounter three ways to declare values:const valvalvarThey look similar, but they communicate different intentions. Understanding these differences will help you write code that is safer, clearer, and easier to maintain.Let’s break them down.The short answerconst val declares a compile-time constant.val declares a read-only reference.var declares a mutable reference that can be reassigned.Here’s a quick example:const val MAX_RETRIES = 3val username = "Alex"var score = 0score = 10Now let’s look at each one more closely.What is var?A variable declared with var can be reassigned after initialization.var age = 20age = 21This is useful when the value genuinely needs to change.var downloadProgress = 0downloadProgress = 25downloadProgress = 50downloadProgress = 100However, mutable state can make code more difficult to understand. When a variable can change in several places, you must keep track of its current value and every operation that could modify it.For that reason, Kotlin developers generally prefer val unless reassignment is necessary.What is val?A value declared with val cannot be reassigned after it has been initialized.val username = "Alex"// Compilation errorusername = "Sam"You can think of val as a read-only reference. Once the reference points to a value or object, it cannot point somewhere else.But there is an important distinction:val does not automatically make an object immutable.Consider this example:val names = mutableListOf("Alex")names.add("Sam") // AllowedAlthough names cannot be reassigned, the mutable list it references can still be modified.This is not allowed:val names = mutableListOf("Alex")names = mutableListOf("Sam") // Compilation errorThe reference cannot change, but the object may still change if the object itself is mutable.If you want a read-only list, use a read-only collection:val names = listOf("Alex", "Sam")This distinction between a read-only reference and an immutable object is one of the most important concepts to understand when working with Kotlin.What is const val?const val declares a value that is known at compile time.const val MAX_RETRIES = 3const val API_VERSION = "v1"Unlike a regular val, a compile-time constant must follow several rules:It must be declared at the top level or inside an object or companion object.Its value must be available at compile time.It can use primitive types or String.It cannot use a custom getter.It cannot be initialized using a function call.This is valid:const val DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5_000This is not:const val CURRENT_TIME = System.currentTimeMillis()The function call runs at runtime, so its result is not a compile-time constant. A regular val is appropriate instead:val currentTime = System.currentTimeMillis()Constants inside a companion objectIn Android and Kotlin projects, constants are often placed inside a companion object:class ProfileActivity { companion object { const val EXTRA_USER_ID = "extra_user_id" }}You can then access the constant using the class name:val key = ProfileActivity.EXTRA_USER_IDThis is commonly used for intent keys, preference keys, request codes, and other fixed identifiers.Does const val improve memory performance?Not necessarily — and usually not in a way worth optimizing for.Get halo’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inBecause a const val is known at compile time, the compiler may insert its value directly wherever it is used. This process is called inlining.For example:const val MAX_RETRIES = 3if (retryCount < MAX_RETRIES) { retry()}The compiled caller may effectively use the number 3 directly.However, the performance or memory difference between this and a regular val is generally negligible for typical applications. You should choose const val because the value is conceptually and technically a compile-time constant—not because you expect a major performance improvement.In fact, inlining has an important consequence: if a public constant is changed in a library, code using that library may need to be recompiled to receive the new value.Does val improve memory performance?val does not automatically reduce memory usage.Consider this example:val user = User("Alex")Memory is still allocated for the User object. The val keyword only prevents the user reference from being reassigned.user = User("Sam") // Compilation errorChoosing val is primarily about correctness and maintainability—not memory optimization.It makes the programmer’s intention clear: this reference should not change.That has several benefits:Fewer accidental state changesCode that is easier to reason aboutSafer refactoringSimpler debuggingBetter support for concurrencyThese benefits are usually much more valuable than tiny low-level optimizations.const val versus valA regular val can be initialized at runtime:val username = loadUsername()val timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis()val user = User("Alex")A const val cannot:const val APP_NAME = "My App"const val MAX_ITEMS = 100The key question is not whether the value changes. Both are read-only after initialization.The key question is:Does the value need to be known at compile time?If yes, and it meets Kotlin’s restrictions, use const val. Otherwise, use val.Choosing between const val, val, and varA useful default strategy is:Start with val.Change it to var only if reassignment is required.Use const val when the value is a genuine compile-time constant.For example:const val APP_NAME = "Task Manager"val user = loadCurrentUser()var selectedTab = 0Each declaration clearly describes its purpose:The application name is fixed at compile time.The current user is loaded at runtime but should not be reassigned.The selected tab changes while the application is running.Final thought

title: Android Engineering From Scratch
excerpt: #001 — Why Kotlin Prefers val Over var (and Why Android Developers Should Too) Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidMobile App DevelopmentKotlinAndroid DevelopmentTechnologyAndroid Engineering From ScratchDora BadrinathFollow5 min read·2 days ago11ListenShare#001 — Why Kotlin Prefers val Over var (and Why Android Developers Should Too)One of the easiest ways to write better Kotlin isn’t learning a complex feature — it’s choosing the right keyword when declaring a variable.IntroductionOne of the first things you’ll notice when learning Kotlin is that there are two ways to declare a variable: val and var.At first, the difference seems simple.val name = "Badrinath"var age = 25Most tutorials explain them in one sentence:val is immutable.var is mutable.Technically, that’s correct — but it doesn’t explain why Kotlin introduced two keywords or why Android developers overwhelmingly prefer one over the other.As I started writing more Kotlin, I realized this wasn’t just a language feature. It’s a design philosophy that encourages writing code that’s easier to understand, safer to maintain, and less likely to break as an application grows.Let’s explore why.The Question Kotlin Wants You to AskWhen coming from Java or similar languages, it’s common to declare almost everything as mutable.var userName = "Badrinath"It works.But Kotlin encourages a different way of thinking.Instead of asking:Can this value change?Ask:Does this value actually need to change?If the answer is no, Kotlin recommends using val.That small habit changes how you design your code.Understanding valA val creates a read-only reference.Once a value has been assigned, the variable cannot point to another value.val company = "OpenAI"println(company)Trying to reassign it results in a compiler error.company = "Google"Val cannot be reassignedThis isn’t Kotlin being restrictive.It’s Kotlin protecting you from accidental changes.Instead of discovering the mistake while testing your application, the compiler catches it before the app even runs.So… Why Is That Useful?Imagine you’re storing information that shouldn’t change while your program is running.val appName = "Dormiq"val apiVersion = "v1"val supportEmail = "support@dormiq.in"These values represent facts.Allowing them to change would only increase the chances of introducing bugs.Using val communicates intent.When another developer reads your code, they immediately know:“This value is expected to remain the same.”Sometimes, the biggest benefit of good code isn’t what the compiler understands — it’s what other developers understand.When var Makes More SenseNot every value stays the same.Some values naturally change throughout an application’s lifecycle.For example:var downloadProgress = 0downloadProgress = 25downloadProgress = 50downloadProgress = 100Or a login state.var isLoggedIn = falseisLoggedIn = trueIn these situations, mutability isn’t just acceptable — it’s necessary.The key takeaway isn’t:Always use val.It’s:Use var only when the value genuinely needs to change.val vs var in Android DevelopmentModern Android development revolves around predictable state.Whether you’re working with Jetpack Compose, MVVM, or ViewModels, you’ll often come across models like this:data class UserUiState( val isLoading: Boolean = false, val users: List<User> = emptyList(), val errorMessage: String? = null)Notice something?Everything is declared with val.Instead of changing the existing object, Android applications often create a new version of the state.val updatedState = currentState.copy( isLoading = true)This makes every state change explicit and much easier to track while debugging.It’s one of the reasons Kotlin fits so well with modern Android architecture.A Common Beginner MisunderstandingOne mistake I made early on was assuming that val made an object completely immutable.It doesn’t.Consider this example.val technologies = mutableListOf( "Kotlin", "Compose")technologies.add("Coroutines")println(technologies)Output:[Kotlin, Compose, Coroutines]Wait… why is this allowed?Get Dora Badrinath’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inBecause val protects the reference, not the object itself.The variable still points to the same list.The list simply happens to be mutable.However, this is not allowed:technologies = mutableListOf()Understanding this distinction early prevents a lot of confusion later, especially when working with collections.Which One Should You Choose?A simple rule has helped me avoid unnecessary var s.Before declaring a variable, ask yourself:Will this variable point to a different value later?If the answer is no, use val.If the answer is yes, use var.That’s it.You don’t need complicated rules.Just choose the option that best represents how the data behaves.Try It YourselfCreate a small Kotlin program and experiment.fun main() { val language = "Kotlin" var version = 1 version++ println(language) println(version)}Now try two things:Change language to another value.Replace var version with val version .The compiler’s feedback explains the difference better than memorizing definitions.Interview Corner1. What is the difference between val and var in Kotlin?Answer:val creates a read-only reference, meaning it cannot be reassigned.var creates a mutable reference, allowing reassignment.val name = "Badrinath"// name = "Android" ❌var city = "Hyderabad"city = "Bengaluru" // ✅2. Does val make an object immutable?Answer:No.val makes the reference immutable, not necessarily the object.val technologies = mutableListOf("Kotlin")technologies.add("Compose") // ✅However:technologies = mutableListOf()is not allowed because the reference cannot point to another object.3. When should you prefer val over var?Answer:Use val whenever the value doesn't need to be reassigned.Switch to var only when reassignment is genuinely required.This results in safer and more predictable code.4. Why does modern Android development encourage using val?Answer:Modern Android architectures like MVVM and Jetpack Compose rely heavily on immutable state bec

title: The Bugs That Don’t Fail
excerpt: What writing a MongoDB driver for Kotlin/Native taught me about testing Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinMongodbThe Bugs That Don’t FailPavel VotyakovFollow8 min read·2 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhat writing a MongoDB driver for Kotlin/Native taught me about testingKotlin/Native has no official MongoDB driver. mongodb-driver-kotlin-coroutine is JVM-only, and if you compile a Ktor service to a native binary — no JVM, one file, twelve times less resident memory — your data layer is where the plan stops.So I wrote one. mongkn is a cinterop binding over the official C driver, libmongoc, with an API whose shape is taken from the Kotlin coroutine driver: suspend fun insertOne(…), fun find(…): Flow<Document>. It covers 24 of the 30 collection operations, sessions and transactions, change streams, sharded clusters, TLS and x509. It has 294 tests and passes 71 of the 75 official MongoDB specification scenarios.None of that caught the four most expensive bugs in the project.They were found in an afternoon, by migrating one real service onto it. Every one of them was silent: MongoDB returned no error, the query executed, the response came back empty. This article is about that class of bug — why a test suite that hunts for crashes cannot see it, and what I changed after.The most expensive four lines of code I have writtenHere is the first one. The library had an infix DSL for filters:collection.find { Landing::shopId eq shopId }shopId is a String in the domain model, but on the wire it is an ObjectId, converted by a custom serializer:@Serializable(with = StringAsBsonObjectId::class)val shopId: StringThe filter builder encoded the value by its Kotlin runtime type. A String became a BsonString. The stored field was a BsonObjectId. For MongoDB those are different BSON types, not the same value in two shapes, so the condition never matched.Nothing failed. find returned an empty flow, deleteMany deleted nothing and reported that it had deleted nothing, and the cleanup job that trimmed old versions quietly stopped trimming.The fix is to encode the filter value with the field’s serializer rather than the value’s runtime type. That is harder than it sounds — a SerialDescriptor describes the shape of a class but does not carry the serializers that write it. The information exists one level down, in childSerializers() on the generated serializer, which is @InternalSerializationApi. I checked that it works on Kotlin/Native before designing around it:generated=true [0]_id->Custom [1]plain->kotlin.Int [2]opt->Custom?Custom serializers, nullable wrappers, all of it. So filter { } and update { } now resolve the field's serializer and encode through it. Both forms — the property reference and the string form, which is the only one available for a field renamed with @SerialName("_id").The same defect existed on the write path, in setTo, where it is worse: a wrong type there does not fail to match, it lands in the document and stays.Three more of the same familyid does not become _id by itself. The serializer sets the type of a value; the field name comes from descriptor.getElementName, which is the Kotlin property name. Without @SerialName("_id") the document goes out with an ordinary id field, and MongoDB generates its own _id — silently, with an unrelated value. Nothing you look up by your own id is ever found again.A sparse index does not save you from an explicit null. The encoder wrote an absent optional field as an explicit BsonNull. A sparse index treats only a missing key as missing — two documents with null are two identical values, so a unique sparse index collides on the second user without an email. The lever is on the model side: @EncodeDefault(NEVER) removes the field from the document entirely.A TTL index does not work on a string. Write an ISO timestamp instead of a BSON date and the index does not break with an error. It just stops deleting documents, and you find out from the size of the collection.Notice the shape of all four. None of them is a crash, an exception, or a wrong value you could assert on. Each is an absence: a query that matches nothing, an index that deletes nothing, a document that is never found. A test suite built to check that operations succeed has no way to see them, and 71 specification scenarios did not.What I actually changedThe interesting part is not the fixes. It is that the library already had exactly one defence of this kind, and it worked.Inside filter { }, a property reference is checked against the class descriptor. If you write Doc::id for a field renamed by @SerialName, the call fails immediately, with the list of names that do exist. That check caught the _id mismatch on the first run of the migration — loudly, with a message that named the problem.So the pattern was already there. It just guarded the field name and nothing guarded the value. The fix extended a defence that had proven itself rather than inventing a new one, which is usually the right way round.Get Pavel Votyakov’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inAnd a testing rule came out of it, written into the repository:Native storage layers are verified by integration tests against a real mongod, not by unit tests. Everything here that could break broke silently, and only a real server showed it.Measurement is a different kind of lyingThe second half of the project was performance, and it produced a lesson I did not expect.The read path had been profiled into a five-level ladder: a bare cursor, plus BSON conversion, plus flow { }, plus flowOn(dispatcher), plus the public API. Each level adds exactly one layer, and the difference between neighbours is the cost of that layer. It said the coroutine channel cost 0.22 µs per document, and building the intermediate Document cost 0.43 µs of about 0.93 µs total.Two optimisations followed. Batching documents across the channel — 64 at a time instead of one — was predicted to save 0.22 µs. It saved 0.47 µs on macOS and 0.30 on Linux, mo

title: The Snapshot-Test Matrix, Two Ways: Parameterized JUnit vs TestBalloon
excerpt: Snapshot testing has a shape, and the shape is a matrix. My app has 27 screen states to capture, each rendered in five configurations —… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Press enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Gaelle Marcel on UnsplashKotlinParameterized TestsSnapshot TestingTestballoonThe Snapshot-Test Matrix, Two Ways: Parameterized JUnit vs TestBalloon🇺🇦 Eugen MartynovFollow4 min read·2 days agoListenShareSnapshot testing has a shape, and the shape is a matrix. My app has 27 screen states to capture, each rendered in five configurations — baseline, longest locale, dark mode, tablet, font scale 2.0 — because dark mode is where hardcoded colours hide, and font scale is where layouts fall apart. That’s 135 golden images, and nobody wants to manually declare 135 tests. JUnit annotations can’t express this: Robolectric Config annotation takes compile-time constants, and you can’t loop over annotations. So the matrix has to be converted to code. Here are two ways to do that, on the same stack — Roborazzi on Robolectric, JVM, no emulator.The parameterized runnerThe established road is the one Sergio Sastre documented: feed the matrix throughParameterizedRobolectricTestRunner and apply configuration at runtime.@RunWith(ParameterizedRobolectricTestRunner::class)class CoffeeDrinkSnapshotTest(private val testItem: TestItem) { companion object { @JvmStatic @ParameterizedRobolectricTestRunner.Parameters(name = "{0}") fun testData() = /* states × devices × configs as TestItems */ } @Test fun snapshot() { RuntimeEnvironment.setQualifiers(testItem.deviceQualifier) RuntimeEnvironment.setFontScale(testItem.config.fontScale) captureRoboImage(testItem.screenshotId) { CoffeeDrinkListItem(drink = testItem.coffeeDrink.uiState) } }}Each matrix cell becomes its own test, and his AndroidUiTestingUtils library rounds the pattern off with a cross-product combinator and a @Rule that applies the config. It’s stock JUnit 4, adoptable in any Android codebase this afternoon, and it works.But notice what the pattern is working around. In JUnit, the unit of everything is the class and its annotations. A test is an annotated method — so without the parameterized runner, every new case means writing yet another @Test function by hand. Reuse across suites means inheritance, because a base class is the only composition tool the model offers. And anything the framework didn’t anticipate has to squeeze through the single @RunWith slot and annotation arguments frozen at compile time. The parameterized runner is the escape hatch the model itself provides — the best one available — but you’re always negotiating with the framework rather than writing plain code.The TestBalloon DSLTestBalloon is a Kotlin Multiplatform test framework where a suite is an expression — so a test per list element is just a loop, and I could shape the same matrix into a small DSL. A screen’s whole snapshot coverage is one file:val MainScreenSnapshotTests by testSuite { snapshotSuite<MainScreenSnapshotContent>("MainScreen") }class MainScreenSnapshotContent(variant: String) : SnapshotSuiteContent<MainState>( goldenPrefix = "main_screen", variantName = variant, render = { state -> MainScreen(state = state, onAction = {}) }, scenarios = { scenario("locations_list", MainState(locations = listOf(albertHeijn, jumbo))) scenario("loading", MainState(isLoading = true)) scenario("error", MainState(error = MainError.Network)) // ... seven more states }, )The five variants live in one enum for the whole app, each changing exactly one axis from baseline:enum class SnapshotVariant( val qualifiers: String, val fontScale: Float, val isDark: Boolean = false) { BASELINE(qualifiers = "+en-w411dp-h891dp", fontScale = 1.0f), DARK(qualifiers = "+en-w411dp-h891dp-night", fontScale = 1.0f, isDark = true), FONT_SCALE(qualifiers = "+nl-w411dp-h891dp", fontScale = 2.0f), // LOCALE, TABLET}A ten-line snapshotSuite function multiplies them: for each variant it registers a Robolectric suite whose sandbox is configured up front — SDK, qualifiers, font scale — through TestBalloon’s TestConfig.robolectric, no setQualifiers mutation inside a running test. Inside, a JUnit4RulesContext fixture still wraps createComposeRule(), so the Compose Rule survives untouched. The report comes out as a tree — MainScreen snapshots (dark) → error — rerunnable and filterable per node, instead of 135 flat concatenated names. And where the parameterized runner has to smuggle the whole matrix across Robolectric’s sandbox classloader (which is why Sergio’s parameters are carefully enums and strings), here exactly one String crosses: the variant’s name.Get 🇺🇦 Eugen Martynov’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe complete working machinery — the full variant enum, the suite builder with its Robolectric config, and a whole example screen — is in this ✨gist.I’ll admit the sentiment plainly: I like how elegant this reads. And because a suite is plain Kotlin all the way down, the DSL is mine to bend. If tomorrow I want a golden for every error type the screen can show, an ordinary loop inside the scenarios block does itMainError.entries.forEach { scenario("error_${it.name.lowercase()}", MainState(error = it)) }no framework bend, no inheritance, and pure composition.That’s my gut feeling after living with both models: with the DSL I customise, with JUnit I negotiate. Credit where due, though — it was Sergio’s parameterize-over-state framing that pushed my DSL to its current form.The final pitOne sharp edge in particular: the current public release of TestBalloon cannot run this Compose-on-Android setup at all — Android test targets hit a missing-entry-point bug (issue #84). An experimental branch fixes it, and my project runs a snapshot build pinned from that branch until the fix lands in a release.My app is a small Compose Multiplatform project.TestBalloon: github.com/infix-de/testBalloonRoborazzi: github.com/takahirom/roborazzi

title: I Shipped a Photo-Streak App in Three Weeks with One Kotlin Codebase. Here Is What I Learned.
excerpt: How a solo Android engineer used Kotlin Multiplatform to build StreakShow for Shipaton 2026, and the three mistakes that almost sank it. Continue reading on Medium »
content: ShipathonRevenuecatKotlinJetbrainsKmpI Shipped a Photo-Streak App in Three Weeks with One Kotlin Codebase. Here Is What I Learned.Rudra DaveFollow4 min read·2 days agoListenShareHow a solo Android engineer used Kotlin Multiplatform to build StreakShow for Shipaton 2026, and the three mistakes that almost sank it.Most habit apps fail for the same reason. They ask you to remember to open them. StreakShow flips that. You take one photo a day for a challenge, and that single image becomes proof you showed up. Miss a day and the streak resets. It is simple, a little brutal, and weirdly addictive.I am a solo Android engineer with six years in the trenches. I built StreakShow for Shipaton 2026, the global buildathon with a prize pool in the hundreds of thousands. The deadline is October 1. The app had to run on Android and iOS from one codebase. Here is the story, the stack, and the lessons that cost me real time.The idea: a photo is harder to fake than a checkboxPlenty of apps track habits with a tap. The problem is that a tap costs nothing. You tap “done” while doing nothing, the streak grows, and the app stops meaning anything.A photo changes the game. When the challenge is “one skincare photo a day” or “one workout photo a day,” you have to actually be there with the camera. The image is the receipt. Over a week the calendar fills with small squares of your real life, and that visual proof is what keeps you coming back.StreakShow has public challenges across fitness, skincare, reading, mindfulness, and creative categories. You join one, take your daily photo, watch the streak build on a living calendar heatmap, and share a Strava-style card when you hit a milestone.The stack: one codebase, two platformsI used Kotlin Multiplatform with Compose Multiplatform. The shared module holds the data layer, ViewModels, and most UI. The Android app is native, and the iOS app reuses the same Compose code through the KMP toolchain.Why this mattered: I am one person. Maintaining two separate codebases would have killed the project before launch. With KMP I write the streak logic once and it runs on both stores. The camera, photo review, and gallery screens are shared. The result is less code, fewer bugs, and a real iOS build without hiring a Swift developer.For persistence I used Room on Android and shared storage on the KMP side, with Firebase Auth and Firestore for accounts and the leaderboard. Leaderboard writes are fire-and-forget so an outage never blocks a photo save.Mistake one: I hid half the product behind the navigationThe app supports multiple streaks at once. You might run a fitness challenge and a skincare challenge in the same week. Early on, the bottom navigation had a “My Streak” tab that only showed one challenge. The second streak existed, counted correctly, but you could not reach it from the main tab.A user with two habits effectively lost one of them. For a product whose whole point is tracking several routines, that was a silent failure. The fix was a challenge switcher, pill chips at the top of the streak screen, so one tap moves between your streaks. Never invent a fallback challenge. Show a clean empty state instead.Get Rudra Dave’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inIf your app can do more than one thing, the navigation has to make all of it reachable. Hidden features are unshipped features.Mistake two: a paywall with no priceMonetization was a late thought, and it showed. The paywall listed three plans, monthly, yearly, lifetime, with no dollar amounts anywhere. Just buttons.A paywall with no price does two bad things. It scares users who assume the worst, and it risks a store rejection for unclear billing. The fix is obvious once you see it: pull the localized price string from the purchase SDK and print it on the button. “$9.99/mo” beats a mystery button every time.I also had copy implying a free trial that the product did not actually offer. That is a policy strike waiting to happen. Either wire a real trial SKU or delete the words. Do not promise what you do not sell.Mistake three: I treated account deletion as optionalPlay Store requires an in-app way to delete your account and all its data. I nearly shipped without it. When I built it properly, the flow had to purge Firestore leaderboard rows, delete local photos, wipe the database, clear preferences, and remove the Firebase user, then drop the user back at onboarding.It is not a nice-to-have. It is a launch blocker. If your app has accounts, build deletion first, test it on a real device, and confirm the photos are actually gone. I verified zero files remained after delete. That check is the difference between compliant and rejected.Why Shipaton, why nowBuildathons like Shipaton are a forcing function. The deadline removes the luxury of endless polishing. You ship something real to the store, and real users poke holes you never would.The prize pool is large, but the bigger win is the discipline. Three weeks of focused building beats three months of weekend tinkering. The community streams walk through how judges score, which is gold if you pay attention.What is nextStreakShow is in review on Play Console and connecting to billing. The iOS build compiles from the same code. I am polishing the capture experience, adding a front camera, and making the upsell fair instead of a one-time popup.If you build habits, or you build apps, the lesson is the same. Make the core action impossible to fake, make every feature reachable, show the real price, and respect the user’s right to leave. Do those four things and the rest is just execution.StreakShow ships October 1. You can follow the build and try the beta from my blogs.

title: How Kotlin 2.4.20 simplifies equality and uniqueness checks
excerpt: allEqual, allEqualBy, allDistinct, and allDistinctBy look like convenience methods. The interesting part is what they let us stop doing —… Continue reading on Level Up Coding »
content: KotlinSoftware DevelopmentSoftware EngineeringMobile App DevelopmentMobileHow Kotlin 2.4.20 simplifies equality and uniqueness checksDmitry Glazunov11 min read·2 days ago----ListenShareallEqual, allEqualBy, allDistinct, and allDistinctBy look like convenience methods. The interesting part is what they let us stop doing — and the edge cases they force us to think about.Press enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Omar Flores on UnsplashKotlin’s standard library already gives us dozens of ways to transform, filter, group, and aggregate collections. Yet until now, two very ordinary questions had no direct vocabulary:Are all these values equal?Is every value unique?Of course, we could answer both questions before. We usually did it with toSet(), distinct(), map(), first(), or a custom loop. The problem was not capability. It was that the code described a mechanism instead of the rule we were trying to enforce.Kotlin 2.4.20-Beta2, released on July 22, 2026, adds four experimental standard-library functions for exactly these checks. They are available for collections, sequences, and arrays, use structural equality, and require an ExperimentalStdlibApi opt-in.@file:OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)The names are almost self-explanatory:allEqual() checks the elements themselves.allEqualBy(selector) checks whether every selected key is equal.allDistinct() checks the elements themselves for uniqueness.allDistinctBy(selector) checks whether every selected key is unique.But “almost self-explanatory” is where bugs like to hide.The old code was readable — until it wasn’tA uniqueness check commonly looked like this:val hasUniqueRecords = records.toSet().size == records.sizeOr, when uniqueness depended on a property:val hasUniqueIds = records .map { it.id } .distinct() .size == records.sizeEquality checks were often even less consistent:val hasSingleOwner = records .map { it.ownerId } .distinct() .size == 1These expressions work in many cases, but each carries baggage.The uniqueness versions build a complete set or distinct result even when the second element is already a duplicate. The property-based versions add a transformation pipeline that exists only to answer a Boolean question. And the equality expression quietly returns false for an empty collection because 0 == 1, while Kotlin’s new allEqualBy() returns true.That last difference is not an optimization. It is a semantic decision.There is another issue: the old expressions are easy to modify incorrectly. A reviewer has to reconstruct what the pipeline means, check how it behaves for zero and one element, and notice whether the selector is evaluated more than necessary. A named Boolean operation compresses that reasoning into a contract.This is similar to the difference between none { ... } and filter { ... }.isEmpty(). Both can express the same condition, but only one tells the reader immediately that no result collection is needed. Standard-library vocabulary matters because it aligns implementation, performance expectations, and code-review language across a codebase.The new functions also avoid a false choice between concise Kotlin and an imperative loop. Before this API, the most efficient version was often the least declarative one:fun <T, K> Iterable<T>.hasUniqueKeys( selector: (T) -> K): Boolean { val seen = HashSet<K>() for (element in this) { if (!seen.add(selector(element))) { return false } } return true}That helper is perfectly valid. But every team had to name it, test it, document empty-input behavior, and decide whether the selector could be evaluated more than once.Putting the concept in the standard library removes that local design work.A real example: validating a multipart uploadImagine a backend or mobile sync layer assembling parts of one upload. Every part must belong to the same upload, and every part index must be unique.data class UploadPart( val uploadId: String, val index: Int, val checksum: String)@OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)fun validateUpload(parts: List<UploadPart>) { require(parts.isNotEmpty()) { "Upload must contain at least one part" } require(parts.allEqualBy { it.uploadId }) { "Mixed upload IDs" } require(parts.allDistinctBy { it.index }) { "Duplicate part index" }}This reads like the domain rule:There must be at least one part.All parts belong to the same upload.All indexes are distinct.There is no temporary list of IDs, no set-size comparison, and no need to explain why distinct().size == 1 means “same upload.”This is where a small standard-library API earns its place. It does not make previously impossible code possible. It gives a common invariant a common name.The four functions do not have the same costThe Kotlin 2.4.20-Beta2 implementation is deliberately split into two strategies.allEqual() stores the first element and compares it with every subsequent element. allEqualBy() does the same with the first selected key. Both stop at the first mismatch. In the worst case, they are linear in the number of elements and require constant extra space.The generic allDistinct() and allDistinctBy() implementations maintain a HashSet of values already seen. Some primitive-array overloads use specialized implementations, but the general strategy is the same: retain enough observed values to detect the first duplicate. They stop as soon as an insertion fails because the value is already present. For the hash-based overloads, expected running time is linear with well-behaved hashes, while extra memory grows with the number of unique values visited before termination.That creates an important practical distinction:val sameHash = replicaHashes.allEqual()val uniqueTokens = sessionTokens.allDistinct()The first check can traverse a million equal hashes while retaining only the first one. The second may need to retain almost a million tokens before it can prove that all of them are unique.So these functions are more expressive than the old workarounds, but they do not repeal the cost of proving uniqueness

title: One SDK for Android, iOS, Flutter, React Native and KMP: A Deep Dive Into Measure, the Open Source…
excerpt: Crashlytics tells you what broke. It rarely tells you why. And if your team ships on more than one stack, it tells you that in five… Continue reading on Medium »
content: MeasureAndroidIOSFlutterMobileOne SDK for Android, iOS, Flutter, React Native and KMP: A Deep Dive Into Measure, the Open Source Crashlytics AlternativeAnand GaurFollow15 min read·2 days ago501ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeCrashlytics tells you what broke. It rarely tells you why. And if your team ships on more than one stack, it tells you that in five different places.Every mobile developer knows this feeling.It is 11 PM. A release went out three hours ago. Crashlytics shows a spike, and there it is: IndexOutOfBoundsException in a list adapter, 340 users affected, crash-free rate down from 99.6 to 98.1 percent.You open the issue. You get a stack trace. You get a device model, an OS version, a memory reading, and maybe four breadcrumbs that someone on your team added eight months ago and never updated.And then you sit there and ask the only question that actually matters: what was the user doing?Crashlytics does not answer that. Not because it is a bad tool, it is a genuinely great crash reporter and it is free, but because answering that question was never its job. The rest of the job got scattered across Google Analytics, Performance Monitoring, BigQuery exports, Cloud Functions and whatever third party bug reporting tool your team bolted on.Now multiply that by your stack count. Android team here. iOS team there. A Flutter app for one product line. A React Native app that came in through an acquisition. Same problem, five times over, with five different debugging cultures.This blog is a deep look at Measure, an open source, mobile first monitoring platform that covers Android, iOS, iPadOS, Flutter, React Native and Kotlin Multiplatform1. The hidden tax of “free”Let us be honest about what Crashlytics actually gives you out of the box.You get crash reporting. You get ANR reporting. You get a dashboard. That is genuinely valuable and it costs nothing.Now list what a real production debugging workflow needs beyond that:What you need What it costs in the Firebase world Performance traces Firebase Performance Monitoring add-on, sampled What the user was doing Enable Google Analytics, then manually instrument breadcrumbs Screen view tracking Requires Google Analytics In-app bug reports A third party SDK Raw data analysis BigQuery export, billed separately Custom alerting logic Cloud Functions, billed separately Network request monitoring Partially available, sampledSo the SDK count in every one of your apps keeps growing. The number of browser tabs you open during an incident keeps growing. Method count, bundle size and build time grow along with them.The free tier is real. The completeness is not.Measure’s argument is simple: instead of five SDKs and five dashboards per platform, use one SDK per platform against one backend, and make session context the default rather than something you instrument by hand.2. Session Replay changes the debugging loopThis is the single biggest difference, so it deserves the most space.In Crashlytics, context comes from breadcrumbs you write yourself:FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().log("User tapped checkout")FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().setCustomKey("cart_size", cartSize)This works. It also has three problems that every team eventually runs into:You only get context you predicted. You add breadcrumbs where you expect trouble. Crashes happen where you did not expect trouble.It rots. Someone refactors the checkout flow, the log line stays pointing at a screen that no longer exists, and nobody notices for two releases.It is manual labour forever. Every new screen, every new flow, every new feature needs the same instrumentation work again, on every platform you ship.Measure takes the opposite approach. It auto-captures the session:Gestures (taps, scrolls, swipes)Navigation and screen transitionsLifecycle eventsHTTP requests and responsesLogsCPU and memory signalsOnly that last one asks anything of you, and it is a one-line addition where you build your client, not per-screen instrumentation that rots over time.And it attaches a full replay of that sequence to every crash, ANR and error. Not a sample. Every one. The feature is called Session Replay and it works the same way on every supported platform.So instead of reading a stack trace and reverse-engineering a user’s path, you watch the timeline: user opened the product screen, scrolled, tapped filter, the API returned a 200 with an empty list, the adapter got an empty list, the crash happened. That is a five second diagnosis instead of a two hour one.The mental shift is real. You stop asking “can I reproduce this?” and start asking “what actually happened?”3. Stack traces that cover every thread, on every stackMost crash reporters give you the stack trace of the thread that blew up. That is enough for a clean null pointer dereference. It is close to useless for concurrency bugs, deadlocks and ANRs, where the interesting information is in what the other threads were doing.Measure captures the stack trace across every thread. And crucially, it de-minifies correctly per platform:Android. R8 and ProGuard mapping files are uploaded automatically by the Gradle plugin, so you read your original class and method names with line numbers intact.iOS and iPadOS. Traces are symbolicated automatically, turning raw memory addresses back into your Swift and Objective-C function names, files and lines. You upload dSYMs through an Xcode build phase or straight from your .xcarchive.React Native. JavaScript errors are symbolicated from your sourcemaps, and crashes from the native Android and iOS layers underneath are captured and mapped too. Sourcemaps and native mapping files upload automatically.Kotlin Multiplatform. Frames from your shared Kotlin code are included, deobfuscated on Android and symbolicated on iOS, so a crash in shared business logic reads like shared business logic instead of two unrelated mysteries.Flutter. Dart errors and the native crashes underneath both land in the same s

One of its most interesting features is that you can choose how you deal with enemies. To the MoonIf you’re looking for a game with an emotional story, To the Moon deserves your attention.The game follows two doctors who travel through the memories of a dying man to fulfill his final wish. Instead of focusing on combat, the game puts almost all of its attention on storytelling.Its simple visuals mean that even older computers should have no trouble running it.Best for: Players who enjoy emotional stories and character-driven adventures.3. Its 2D art style is also much less demanding than modern 3D games.Why you should try it:Atmospheric storyInteresting dialogue systemMystery and supernatural elementsLightweight visual style6. Papers, PleaseWhat if you could experience a story through a job instead of traditional combat?Papers, Please puts you in the role of an immigration inspector working at a fictional border checkpoint. You must examine documents and decide who can enter the country.As you progress, your decisions become increasingly difficult, and the game presents moral choices that can have serious consequences.It’s simple, unusual, and surprisingly addictive.7.
