title: How We Moved 1,500 Android Screenshot Tests to Roborazzi
excerpt: The porting process and the challenges we faced along the way Continue reading on Thumbtack Engineering »
content: AndroidSoftware TestingRoborazziMobileTechnologyHow we moved 1,500 Android screenshot tests to Roborazzi.Zachary WanderFollow8 min read·2 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeIntroductionIf you’re a mobile developer you’re probably no stranger to screenshot tests. Making sure that layouts remain consistent as time goes on and code changes is important for ensuring functionality and accessibility. Since Thumbtack uses Kotlin and Jetpack Compose for its Android apps, we had historically been using Firebase Test Lab to capture and compare layouts. However, using Firebase can be slow, tedious, and error-prone, so we decided it was time for a change. Instead of Firebase, we decided to migrate to using Roborazzi, a screenshot testing framework that runs fully locally inside the local JVM instead of relying on remote emulators and devices.For more details on why we migrated and the alternatives we evaluated, check out the previous blog post from Brian. This post is going to go into the details of how we migrated, and the challenges we faced along the way.Porting LoopBecause the purpose of screenshot tests is ensuring consistency over time, we wanted to bring over our existing test suites into Roborazzi. Deleting the old ones and just creating new tests as we built new layouts was a potential option, but it would wipe out a lot of our automated verification. Instead, we ported our existing Firebase Test Lab screenshot test suites over to Roborazzi.In general, the porting process was pretty simple:Delete the old screenshots.Move the test suites over from androidTest to test.Adjust the code for any API differences.Record new screenshots.Compare the old and new screenshots in the git diff to make sure nothing is broken.Fix broken screenshots.Since Roborazzi uses Robolectric, and Robolectric implements the Android API, most of the test suites needed very few changes to work, with updating the main test rule and test annotations being enough to get them running. A few, like those that relied on permission granting rules or interacted directly with the test Activity, needed some more work. In order to make the process of comparing the old and new screenshots more manageable, and fixing broken ones where needed, porting was done in batches of 20 suites.FixesEven though getting the tests to compile and run was generally fairly simple, there were some challenges with making rendering work as expected. A lot of ported tests would just capture blank images, wouldn’t properly inject test data, or would throw errors because of differences in when objects are injected between Firebase and Roborazzi. Most of the fixes for these issues involved changing where and when objects were injected, like moving the operation to its own step after the initial instantiation, but a couple were more challenging.Test IsolationRunning tests in Roborazzi also removes a feature we had been implicitly relying on with on-device captures: full test isolation. In an emulator, the app process is relaunched for each capture, resetting any in-memory changes to app-wide variables or temporary configurations. Roborazzi runs all tests in a single process and runs multiple tests in parallel. This led to a few issues, but the most notable involved a single capture showing vastly different font sizes locally and in CI.Get Zachary Wander’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inThe problem turned out to be caused by differing resource configurations in a view test suite and a screenshot test suite that both used the same font cache. Locally, the suites would run in one order, causing the font size to be loaded and cached using one suite’s resource configuration. In CI, though, they consistently ran in an order where the other suite would run first, caching a different font size. This was a tough one to debug, since even a local Debian VM didn’t reproduce the CI behavior and execution order. We were only able to solve it by arranging for SSH access to one of the CI runner nodes and using JetBrains Gateway to remotely debug the project.ShadowsAnother problem we ran into was shadow rendering. When capturing and comparing screenshots on an Android emulator, as long as the original and comparison emulators have the same display specs and Android version, the screenshots will be exactly the same, no matter what operating system the emulator is running on. Since Robolectric runs in the JVM, the same consistency isn’t guaranteed. Even though Java itself is built to run on many platforms, there are still behavior differences across host operating systems and even different runtime implementations, especially when graphics are involved. For the most part, the differences didn’t actually matter, except for shadows.Our Android team currently all works locally on macOS, but that isn’t a requirement, and our CI runs our screenshot comparisons on Debian. While the screenshots generated by macOS and CI looked visually identical, there was apparently enough difference in how shadows are rendered between the operating systems to cause the screenshot comparisons to fail. Luckily, the current mobile design trend doesn’t emphasize shadows very much, so most tests were unaffected, but for those that were, we had to look into a few options.Maybe the simplest and most obvious solution would be to run our screenshot comparison tasks on macOS, but this would’ve required some pretty big changes to our stack and would have added a lot of extra cost. Another option was to increase our tolerance threshold — something we already had implemented for differences in font anti-aliasing — for differences in screenshots, but the shadows we had needed surprisingly high thresholds and we didn’t want to risk real layout changes slipping through. The solution we went with was to disable shadows entirely in screenshot tests, but even this wasn’t that simple. Robolectric do

title: Android System Design: Pagination
excerpt: Imagine an e-commerce application with 100,000 products. Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidAndroid App DevelopmentAndroid DevelopmentSystem Design InterviewMobile System DesignAndroid System Design: PaginationNematFollow11 min read·2 days ago3ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by Cooper Hofmann on UnsplashImagine an e-commerce application with 100,000 products.The user opens the product listing screen.Should the Android app download all 100,000 products?Obviously not.Apart from the huge response size, this would result in:Slow initial loadingHigh memory usageIncreased battery consumptionExcessive network usageLonger JSON parsing timePoor scrolling performanceInstead, the application loads a small subset of data and retrieves more as the user needs it.This is pagination.Pagination is one of the most important concepts in mobile system design because it sits at the intersection of API design, Android architecture, database design, caching, and user experience.In this article, we’ll explore how pagination works, different pagination strategies, how to implement it in Android using Paging 3, and how pagination fits into a production-ready architecture.What Is Pagination?Pagination is the process of dividing a large dataset into smaller chunks and loading those chunks incrementally.Instead of:Request → 100,000 recordswe do:Request → 20 recordsRequest → next 20Request → next 20...For example:GET /products?page=1&pageSize=20The server returns the first 20 products.When the user reaches the bottom:GET /products?page=2&pageSize=20The next 20 products are loaded.Why Pagination Matters in Mobile ApplicationsPagination isn’t just about reducing response size.It solves several problems simultaneously.1. Network EfficiencyThe application downloads only the data it needs.2. Memory EfficiencyThe app doesn’t need to hold a massive dataset in memory.3. Faster Initial LoadingThe first page can be displayed quickly.4. Better User ExperienceUsers can start interacting with the screen while additional data loads.5. Backend ScalabilityThe server doesn’t need to retrieve and serialize enormous datasets for every request.Pagination ArchitectureA typical Android pagination flow looks like this:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeThe important part is that pagination shouldn’t become a responsibility of the UI.The UI should simply consume a stream of paginated data.Common Pagination StrategiesThere are three approaches you should understand for system design interviews:Offset-based paginationCursor-based paginationKeyset paginationLet’s look at each one.1. Offset-Based PaginationOffset pagination uses a page number or offset.For example:GET /products?page=1&pageSize=20Or:GET /products?offset=20&limit=20The server essentially says:Skip the first 20 records and return the next 20.ExampleSuppose the database contains:12345...100Request:GET /products?offset=0&limit=20returns:1 - 20Next request:GET /products?offset=20&limit=20returns:21 - 40And so on.Advantages of Offset PaginationOffset pagination is:SimpleEasy to understandEasy to implementConvenient for numbered pagesIt’s often perfectly adequate for smaller or relatively static datasets.Problems with Offset PaginationThe biggest problem appears when data changes while the user is paging.Imagine the user loads:Page 1Products 1 - 20Now another user adds a new product at the beginning.The dataset becomes:New Product123...When the Android app requests:offset=20the results may shift.The user could see:Duplicate itemsMissing itemsInconsistent orderingPerformance ProblemsLarge offsets can also become expensive.For example:GET /products?offset=900000&limit=20Depending on the database and query, the backend may have to scan or skip a large number of records before returning the requested rows.This makes offset pagination less attractive for very large, frequently changing datasets.2. Cursor-Based PaginationCursor pagination solves many of these problems.Instead of saying:Give me page 5.the client says:Give me the records after this position.Example:GET /products?limit=20&cursor=abc123The server returns:{ "items": [ { "id": 101, "name": "Laptop" }, { "id": 102, "name": "Phone" } ], "nextCursor": "xyz789"}The client then uses:GET /products?limit=20&cursor=xyz789Cursor FlowRequest Page 1 │ ▼Items + nextCursor │ ▼Request with nextCursor │ ▼Items + nextCursor │ ▼Request with nextCursorThe client doesn’t need to know where the next page starts.The server controls the cursor.Why Cursor Pagination Is Better for FeedsConsider a social media feed.New posts can appear at any time.Offset pagination can cause items to move between pages.Cursor pagination can provide a more stable traversal through the dataset.This makes cursor-based pagination particularly useful for:Social feedsChat messagesNotificationsActivity feedsLarge e-commerce catalogsFrequently changing datasetsCursor Doesn’t Mean Random StringA cursor is often an encoded representation of a position in the dataset.For example, the backend could internally use:createdAt + idand encode it into a cursor.The client doesn’t need to understand the cursor.It should treat it as an opaque value.For example:eyJjcmVhdGVkQXQiOiIyMDI2...The client simply sends it back.3. Keyset PaginationKeyset pagination uses a value from the previous result set to find the next set of records.For example:GET /products?limit=20&afterId=100The database can execute something conceptually similar to:SELECT *FROM productsWHERE id > 100ORDER BY idLIMIT 20;This can be much more efficient than skipping a large number of rows.Cursor vs Keyset PaginationThese concepts are closely related but aren’t exactly the same.Keyset pagination describes the database/query technique.Cursor pagination describes the API mechanism exposed to the client.A cursor can encapsulate the keyset information.For example:Client │ │ cursor=abc123 ▼API │ │ decode cursor ▼Database │ │ WHERE createdAt < ... ▼ResultsThe client doesn’t need to know how the backend implements the cursor.Offset vs CursorPress enter or click to view image i

title: Building Redoubt Analytics: A Counter-UAS Risk Intelligence Platform
excerpt: Airports, ports, data centers, and energy grids all share a growing vulnerability: low-cost, high-capability drones. A few years ago, a… Continue reading on Medium »
content: DroneWarRisk ManagementAndroidAppsBuilding Redoubt Analytics: A Counter-UAS Risk Intelligence PlatformAlfino HattaFollow9 min read·2 days agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizePhoto by RUT MIIT on UnsplashAirports, ports, data centers, and energy grids all share a growing vulnerability: low-cost, high-capability drones. A few years ago, a serious counter-UAS conversation was mostly a military one. Today it belongs on the desk of any Chief Security Officer responsible for a large physical site, because the barrier to entry for building or buying a capable drone has collapsed while the value of the assets sitting under our skies has only gone up.Unlike traditional physical security threats, Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) are cheap, fast-moving, and hard to model with conventional risk frameworks. A fence, a badge reader, and a guard rotation are all static countermeasures against a mostly static threat. A drone swarm is neither static nor predictable, and it doesn’t respect a perimeter fence in the way a person on foot does.When I started looking into how security teams actually approach this problem, I found a gap. Most security stacks that deal with counter-UAS are fragmented: a radar system from one vendor, a jammer from another, a kinetic interceptor bolted on as an afterthought, and no unified way to answer the question every Chief Security Officer eventually asks: “If we spend the next dollar on defense, where does it do the most good?”That question, more than any single piece of technology, became the seed for Redoubt Analytics, a project I built to bring quantitative, simulation-based reasoning to counter-UAS risk management. I didn’t want to build another sensor dashboard. I wanted to build something closer to an actuarial model for airspace risk, one that treats security spending the way a portfolio manager treats capital allocation.Framing the Business Problem Before Writing Any CodeBefore touching a line of Kotlin, I spent time thinking through who would actually use this system and what decisions they needed to make with it. That framing shaped almost every architectural decision that followed, so it’s worth laying out.The core objectives I set for the platform were:Quantify risk. Provide a standardized “Exposure Score” for a given site, derived from a site-specific digital twin rather than a generic industry average.Optimize spend. Use simulation output to identify which countermeasures (radar, jammers, kinetic interceptors) provide the highest risk reduction per dollar spent, rather than relying on vendor claims or gut feel.Regulatory readiness. Generate reports suitable for insurance underwriters and government compliance bodies (TSA, EASA, and similar), because a growing share of infrastructure risk now shows up on an insurance ledger before it ever shows up in an incident report.And the target users fell into three distinct roles, each with different needs and different relationships to the data:Chief Security Officers, who care about long-term strategic planning and need to justify multi-year capital investment in defense infrastructure.Risk Officers, who use the platform’s output to negotiate insurance premiums and assess liability exposure, meaning the numbers need to hold up to outside scrutiny.Security Operations Center (SOC) Managers, who live in the platform day-to-day for real-time monitoring, sensor health, and equipment maintenance, and who need something that works reliably on a phone at 2 a.m., not just in a quarterly board deck.Designing for all three of these personas at once is harder than it sounds. A CSO wants a clean executive summary and an ROI number. A Risk Officer wants an audit trail and defensible methodology. A SOC manager wants a live heatmap and push notifications when something changes. Redoubt had to be one coherent system that could present three very different faces depending on who was looking at it.ArchitectureI split the system into three cooperating pieces: a mobile client, a backend API, and a simulation engine. Keeping these cleanly separated turned out to be one of the more important decisions in the project, because each piece has a very different performance profile and a very different failure mode.User (Security Officer) | vAndroid App (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose) | REST + WebSocket vSpring Boot API ---- Auth Service (JWT) | +-- Simulation Engine -- Threat Scenario Library | +-- MySQL Database ^IoT Sensor Logs ---The Android app is the primary touchpoint for the people using this system day to day: dashboards, simulation triggers, and reporting, built for people who need situational awareness without being tied to a desk. It has to work well on a phone screen in a control room and be legible on a tablet in a boardroom.The Spring Boot API owns the business logic: user state, authentication, and, critically, gating access to sensitive simulation data. A lot of what this platform produces (site vulnerability scores, identified defense gaps, breach probability estimates) is exactly the kind of data an organization does not want leaking to a competitor or, worse, to someone planning an actual incursion. The API layer is where I put the most thought into access control.The simulation engine is the computational core of the whole platform. It runs Monte Carlo simulations against each site’s digital twin to calculate breach probabilities across thousands of iterations per scenario. This is the piece that actually answers the question “how exposed are we, really,” and it’s deliberately kept separate from the request-serving path of the API.MySQL persists site configurations, equipment inventories, and historical run results, so risk trends can be tracked over time rather than treated as one-off snapshots. A single simulation result is interesting; a year of simulation results run against the same site as its defenses evolve is what actually lets a Risk Officer show an insurer that exposure is trending down.Why I Chose an

content: AndroidMarializ Sánchez PegueroFollow4 min read·2 days agoShare---Earnne: una forma sencilla de ganar dinero realizando actividades desde el celularHoy en día, muchas personas buscan alternativas para aprovechar el tiempo libre utilizando su teléfono celular. Entre las plataformas que ofrecen diferentes actividades para obtener recompensas se encuentra Earnne, una aplicación que reúne encuestas, juegos, tareas, videos, cursos y otras actividades que permiten acumular ganancias.Una de las cosas que me parece interesante de Earnne es que no se limita a una sola manera de ganar. Dependiendo de las opciones disponibles para cada usuario, se pueden encontrar diferentes actividades y escoger las que resulten más convenientes. La plataforma explica que sus usuarios pueden realizar encuestas, probar aplicaciones, jugar, completar tareas, ver contenido educativo, realizar cursos y otras actividades disponibles dentro de la aplicación.¿Cómo registrarse en Earnne?El proceso para comenzar es bastante sencillo. Primero, el usuario debe descargar la aplicación oficial de Earnne o entrar a su página web. Después debe crear una cuenta siguiendo las instrucciones que aparecen en la plataforma.[Página oficial de Earnne](https://earnne.com/?lang=es&utm_source=chatgpt.com)Al crear la cuenta, es importante utilizar información verdadera y completar correctamente el perfil. Esto puede ayudar a que la plataforma muestre actividades que correspondan con el perfil del usuario. Según la información publicada por Earnne, el registro es gratuito y no requiere introducir una tarjeta de crédito para comenzar.Una vez creada la cuenta, el siguiente paso es entrar al área de actividades disponibles. Allí se pueden revisar las diferentes opciones para encontrar aquellas que sean de interés y que estén disponibles para la cuenta.¿Cómo se puede ganar dinero con Earnne?Earnne funciona mediante diferentes actividades. Una de ellas son las encuestas, en las que los usuarios responden preguntas sobre diferentes temas y productos. También existen actividades relacionadas con juegos y aplicaciones, donde se deben seguir las condiciones indicadas para recibir la recompensa.Otra alternativa son las tareas en línea. La plataforma también presenta cursos, videos y contenido de lectura que pueden generar recompensas al completar las actividades correspondientes.Es importante leer las instrucciones de cada actividad antes de comenzar. Algunas tareas pueden tener requisitos específicos, como alcanzar determinado progreso, completar una actividad en un tiempo determinado o realizar ciertos pasos. Por eso, no se debe comenzar una oferta sin revisar primero qué es lo que solicita.Después de completar correctamente una actividad, la recompensa correspondiente puede aparecer en el balance de la cuenta una vez que haya sido validada. Earnne indica que ofrece diferentes opciones para retirar las ganancias, que pueden incluir PayPal, cuenta bancaria o billeteras digitales, dependiendo de las opciones disponibles para cada usuario y región.Get Marializ Sánchez Peguero’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign in¿Qué es lo que más me gusta de Earnne?Personalmente, lo que más me gusta de la propuesta de Earnne es la variedad de actividades. Me parece interesante que una persona no tenga que depender únicamente de las encuestas, sino que pueda encontrar otras alternativas como juegos, videos, cursos, lectura y tareas.También me gusta que la plataforma esté pensada para utilizarse desde el celular y que las actividades puedan realizarse en diferentes momentos del día. Esto permite aprovechar algunos ratos libres sin tener que dedicar todo el tiempo a una sola actividad.Otra característica que considero positiva es que antes de realizar una tarea se pueden revisar sus condiciones. Esto es importante porque permite saber qué se necesita hacer para completar correctamente una oferta y evitar perder tiempo realizando una actividad sin conocer sus requisitos.Mi enlace de referencia de EarnneSi quieres conocer Earnne y registrarte utilizando mi referencia, puedes hacerlo mediante el siguiente enlace:[AQUÍ DEBES PEGAR TU ENLACE PERSONAL DE REFERENCIA DE EARNNE]Este enlace debe ser mi enlace personal de referencia, ya que es el que permite identificar que una persona llegó a la plataforma mediante mi recomendación.ConclusiónEarnne es una plataforma que reúne diferentes formas de obtener recompensas mediante actividades realizadas desde el celular. Entre sus opciones se encuentran encuestas, juegos, aplicaciones, tareas, cursos, videos y lectura. La posibilidad de escoger entre diferentes actividades es una de las características que más me llama la atención.Para comenzar, lo principal es crear una cuenta, completar correctamente el perfil, revisar las actividades disponibles y leer cuidadosamente los requisitos de cada una. Después de completar las actividades y recibir las recompensas correspondientes, el usuario puede revisar las opciones de retiro disponibles para su cuenta.Como con cualquier plataforma para obtener recompensas por Internet, es importante tener expectativas realistas: no se debe considerar como un salario fijo, porque la cantidad de actividades y las ganancias pueden variar. Lo mejor es utilizarla de manera responsable y comprobar siempre las condiciones de cada oferta antes de realizarla.En definitiva, Earnne puede ser una alternativa interesante para quienes quieren utilizar parte de su tiempo libre realizando pequeñas actividades desde el teléfono y acumulando recompensas.Referencia oficial: [Earnne](https://earnne.com/?lang=es&utm_source=chatgpt.com)---

title: On-Device AI Series (Part 4): LiteRT
excerpt: Full tensor-level control for custom machine learning models on Android. Every team building on-device AI eventually reaches a point where pre-packaged task pipelines no longer suffice. You might need to deploy a custom-trained model, implement a specialized quantization strategy, or pipe raw tensor outputs directly from one neural network into another. That’s where LiteRT operates. It is the core runtime engine that powers MediaPipe Tasks and handles low-level model execution on Android. Introd
content: AndroidAndroid App DevelopmentAndroidDevArtificial IntelligenceLLMOn-Device AI Series (Part 4): LiteRTOğuzhan AslanFollow8 min read·1 day ago1ListenShareFull tensor-level control for custom machine learning models on Android.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeEvery team building on-device AI eventually reaches a point where pre-packaged task pipelines no longer suffice. You might need to deploy a custom-trained model, implement a specialized quantization strategy, or pipe raw tensor outputs directly from one neural network into another.That’s where LiteRT operates. It is the core runtime engine that powers MediaPipe Tasks and handles low-level model execution on Android.Introducing LiteRT: What It Is & What Models It Can RunLiteRT (formerly TensorFlow Lite) is Google’s runtime framework for running machine learning and generative AI models on edge devices across Android, iOS, Web, and desktop platforms. It provides two main runtime interfaces: the modern CompiledModel API, which optimizes hardware acceleration for new applications, and the legacy Interpreter API, maintained for backward compatibility.LiteRT executes both classical ML (.tflite) and modern generative AI models. For Generative AI, LiteRT supports open-weight large language models like Gemma, Llama, Phi, Qwen, and SmoLM (often packaged in .litertlm formats, which we will cover in detail in a future article). For classical ML, it natively runs architectures for vision (EfficientNet, MobileNet, ResNet), natural language (BERT, MobileBERT), and audio (YAMNet). Custom models built in PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX can be converted into .tflite flatbuffers for deployment.Although LiteRT can run most models, deployment is strictly limited by the target device’s physical capabilities:Memory Constraints: Running a quantized 3B or 7B parameter LLM requires several gigabytes of available RAM, making it unusable on budget smartphones with less than 4GB-6GB of system memory.Compute & Hardware Acceleration: Modern generative AI models require Dedicated NPU (Neural Processing Unit) or high-end GPU acceleration to achieve acceptable tokens-per-second speeds; running them on a standard mobile CPU results in severe latency.Storage & Battery: High-capacity model files (even compressed via INT4/INT8 quantization) demand significant disk space and cause rapid battery drain due to continuous high-power compute cycles during inference.Hands-on Implementation SamplesEvery LiteRT workflow follows a predictable three-step pattern:Press enter or click to view image in full sizeImage Classification: EfficientNet-Lite0 QuantizedThe LiteRTImageClassifier classifies a bitmap into ImageNet categories using an 8-bit quantized model. Here, quantization parameters are extracted directly from embedded metadata:class LiteRTImageClassifier(val context: Context) { private var compiledModel: CompiledModel? = null private var labels: List<String> = emptyList() private var outputScale: Float = 1f / 255f private var outputZeroPoint: Int = 0 suspend fun classify(bitmap: Bitmap): ImageClassificationOutput? { loadModel() // --- Step 1: Prepare Tensor Buffers --- val inputBuffers = compiledModel?.createInputBuffers() ?: return null val outputBuffers = compiledModel?.createOutputBuffers() ?: return null inputBuffers[0].writeInt8(extractPixelBytes(bitmap)) // --- Step 2: Execute Inference --- val startTime = SystemClock.uptimeMillis() compiledModel?.run(inputBuffers, outputBuffers) val inferenceTime = SystemClock.uptimeMillis() - startTime // --- Step 3: Parse Output Tensors --- val rawOutput = outputBuffers[0].readInt8() val categories = postprocess(rawOutput) return ImageClassificationOutput(categories, inferenceTime) } private fun loadModel() { if (compiledModel != null) return compiledModel = CompiledModel.create( context.assets, "efficientnet_lite0.tflite", CompiledModel.Options(Accelerator.CPU), null ) // Extract quantization params from embedded metadata val metadataExtractor = MetadataExtractor(getModelBuffer(context)) val quantParams = metadataExtractor.getOutputTensorQuantizationParams(0) outputScale = quantParams.scale outputZeroPoint = quantParams.zeroPoint } private fun postprocess(rawOutput: ByteArray): List<ImageCategory> { return rawOutput.mapIndexed { index, byte -> val score = outputScale * ((byte.toInt() and 0xFF) - outputZeroPoint) ImageCategory(labels.getOrElse(index) { "#$index" }, score) } .filter { it.score >= PROBABILITY_THRESHOLD } .sortedByDescending { it.score } .take(MAX_RESULTS) }}Unpacking: The writeInt8() and readInt8() methods interact directly with raw byte buffers. Extracting scaling factors dynamically via MetadataExtractor keeps the quantization pipeline robust against hardcoded configuration drift.Text Classification: BERT Intent ClassifierText models require manual tokenization before tensor ingestion. The expanded BertClassifier example below demonstrates complete buffer lifecycle management, input tensor shaping, and logit probability normalization:class BertClassifier(val context: Context) { private var compiledModel: CompiledModel? = null private val sequenceLength = 128 private val labels = listOf("greeting", "support", "billing", "feedback", "unknown") suspend fun classify(text: String): ClassificationResult? { loadModel() // --- Step 1: Prepare Tensor Buffers --- val inputBuffers = compiledModel?.createInputBuffers() ?: return null val outputBuffers = compiledModel?.createOutputBuffers() ?: return null // Tokenize text into fixed-length integer array [1, sequenceLength] val tokenIds = tokenizeAndPad(text, sequenceLength) // Write int32 token IDs directly into the input tensor buffer inputBuffers[0].writeInt32(tokenIds) // --- Step 2: Execute Inference --- val startTime = SystemClock.uptimeMillis() compiledModel?.run(inputBuffers, outputBuffers) val inferenceLatency = SystemClock.uptimeMillis() - startTime // --- Step 3: Parse Output Tensors --- // Read raw classification logits from output tensor val rawLogits = outpu

title: Your Compose App Isn’t Slow — Your State Is
excerpt: You’ve done everything right. You bumped the BOM. Pausable composition is on. Your shadows are real dropShadow() calls now, not three stacked gradients. (If none of that sounds familiar, start with [ Stop Writing Compose Like It's 2024 ] — this article picks up where that one left off.) And your screen still stutters when you drag it. Here’s the uncomfortable truth I’ve learned debugging Compose performance in production: the framework is rarely the bottleneck anymore. In almost every janky scre
content: AndroidJetpack ComposeAndroidDevAndroid App DevelopmentUXYour Compose App Isn’t Slow — Your State IsSubhankar BagFollow10 min read·1 day ago1ListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeYou’ve done everything right.You bumped the BOM. Pausable composition is on. Your shadows are real dropShadow() calls now, not three stacked gradients. (If none of that sounds familiar, start with [Stop Writing Compose Like It's 2024] — this article picks up where that one left off.)And your screen still stutters when you drag it.Here’s the uncomfortable truth I’ve learned debugging Compose performance in production: the framework is rarely the bottleneck anymore. In almost every janky screen I’ve profiled, the root cause wasn’t Compose being slow — it was state being read in the wrong place, at the wrong granularity, or at the wrong time. The framework did exactly what we told it to. We just told it to do far too much.This article is about the seven state mistakes I keep finding, why each one triggers work you never asked for, and the before/after fix for each. No new APIs to learn — everything here works on any recent stable BOM.TL;DR: the seven mistakes and their fixes:Reading state too high in the tree — Push reads down into the smallest scope that needs themReading animated values in composition — Defer reads to the layout/draw phase with lambda modifiersRecomposing on every scroll pixel — Convert rapid state into meaningful state with derivedStateOfUnstable parameters defeating skipping — Know what strong skipping fixed, and what it didn’tOne giant UiState for the whole screen — Split state along recomposition boundariesBackwards writes — Never write to state that the current composition just readGuessing instead of measuring — Recomposition counts and composition tracing, in that orderNow the details — but first, the mental model that explains all seven.The One Rule That Explains Everything BelowCompose doesn’t recompose functions. It recomposes scopes — and it decides which scopes by tracking where state is read, not where it’s declared.When you read a State<T> value, the nearest restartable scope around that read subscribes to it. When the value changes, that scope — all of it — is invalidated and re-executed. Declare state wherever you like; it's the location of the read that determines the blast radius.Every mistake in this article is the same mistake wearing different clothes: a state read placed so that its blast radius is bigger than the pixels that actually changed. Keep that sentence in mind and the rest of this article becomes almost obvious.1. Reading State Too High in the TreeThe most common one, and the easiest to ship without noticing.❌ Old way: the whole screen subscribes to the search query:@Composablefun ProfileScreen(viewModel: ProfileViewModel) { val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()Column { SearchBar( query = uiState.query, // read here... onQueryChange = viewModel::onQueryChange ) ProfileHeader(uiState.user) // ...recomposes on every keystroke PostGrid(uiState.posts) // ...this too FollowerStats(uiState.stats) // ...and this }}Every keystroke in the search bar invalidates ProfileScreen's scope, because that's where uiState.query is read. The header, the grid, and the stats didn't change — but they're inside the blast radius, so Compose has to re-execute them and diff the results. On a modest phone with a heavy grid, that's your typing lag.✅ New way: push the read down into the component that needs it:@Composablefun ProfileScreen(viewModel: ProfileViewModel) { Column { SearchBar( query = { viewModel.query }, // read deferred into SearchBar onQueryChange = viewModel::onQueryChange ) ProfileHeader { viewModel.user } PostGrid { viewModel.posts } FollowerStats { viewModel.stats } }}@Composablefun SearchBar(query: () -> String, onQueryChange: (String) -> Unit) { TextField(value = query(), onValueChange = onQueryChange) // The read happens HERE. Only this scope invalidates per keystroke.}Passing a lambda instead of a value moves the read — and therefore the subscription — into the child. The parent never reads the state, so the parent never recomposes for it. This is the single highest-leverage refactor in Compose performance work, and it costs you a pair of braces.(You don’t need to lambda-ify everything. Do it where state changes frequently: text input, scroll positions, animation values, progress. Stable, slow-changing data can stay as plain parameters.)2. Reading Animated Values in CompositionThis one produces the most dramatic before/after numbers, because the state in question changes every frame.❌ Old way: recompose 60–120 times per second:val offset by animateDpAsState(targetValue = targetOffset)Box( Modifier .offset(x = offset) // read in composition - recomposes every frame .size(80.dp))✅ New way: skip composition entirely, read at layout time:val offset by animateDpAsState(targetValue = targetOffset)Box( Modifier .offset { IntOffset(x = offset.roundToPx(), y = 0) } // lambda overload .size(80.dp))The root cause: Compose has three phases — composition, layout, draw. The value-based offset(x: Dp) reads state during composition, so every frame of the animation re-runs your composable, re-runs layout, re-runs draw. The lambda-based offset { } defers the read to the layout phase — composition is skipped entirely, every frame.Same pattern, same fix, different modifiers:Modifier.offset(x, y) → Modifier.offset { IntOffset(...) }Modifier.background(color) on an animated color → Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(animatedColor) }Modifier.alpha(a) / scale(s) / rotate(r) on animated values → one Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = a; scaleX = s; rotationZ = r }If a value changes every frame and you’re reading it without a lambda, you’re paying for a full pipeline when you needed one-third of it.3. Recomposing on Every Scroll PixelThe classic: show a “scroll to top” button after the user scrolls past the first item.❌ Old way: subscribe to a value that chan

title: String Interpolation in Kotlin: Write Cleaner and More Readable Strings
excerpt: When building Kotlin applications, we often need to combine text with values stored in variables. Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinKotlin BeginnersStringInterpolationBest PracticesString Interpolation in Kotlin: Write Cleaner and More Readable StringshaloFollow4 min read·1 day agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeWhen building Kotlin applications, we often need to combine text with values stored in variables.Suppose we have a student’s name and score:val name = "Alex"val score = 85One way to create a message is string concatenation:println("Student " + name + " scored " + score)This works, but Kotlin provides a cleaner feature called string interpolation:println("Student $name scored $score")Both examples produce:Student Alex scored 85What Is String Interpolation?String interpolation means inserting the value of a variable or expression directly inside a string.In Kotlin, string interpolation is also commonly called a string template.Kotlin provides two forms:$variableand:${expression}Using a Simple VariableWhen inserting a simple variable, place $ before its name:val name = "John"println("Hello, $name!")Output:Hello, John!Braces are optional for a simple variable, so this also works:println("Hello, ${name}!")However, $name is shorter and usually preferred.Using ExpressionsUse ${...} when inserting an expression:val firstName = "John"val lastName = "Smith"println("Full name: ${firstName + " " + lastName}")Output:Full name: John SmithYou can perform calculations inside the braces:val price = 20val quantity = 3println("Total: $${price * quantity}")Output:Total: $60In this example:The first $ is ordinary text representing the currency symbol.${price * quantity} evaluates the Kotlin expression.Accessing Object PropertiesConsider this data class:data class Student( val name: String, val scores: List<Int>)Create a student:val student = Student( name = "Alex", scores = listOf(75, 90, 82))To access a property inside a string, use braces:println("Student name: ${student.name}")Output:Student name: AlexThe braces are necessary because student.name is a property-access expression.This does not work as intended:println("Student name: $student.name")Kotlin interprets only $student as the string template. It treats .name as ordinary text.Calling Functions Inside a StringYou can call functions inside ${...}:val name = "alex"println("Student name: ${name.uppercase()}")Output:Student name: ALEXAnother example:val scores = listOf(75, 90, 82)println("Number of scores: ${scores.size}")println("Highest score: ${scores.maxOrNull()}")println("Average score: ${scores.average()}")Output:Number of scores: 3Highest score: 90Average score: 82.33333333333333You can format the average:println("Average score: ${"%.2f".format(scores.average())}")Output:Average score: 82.33Working with CollectionsCollections such as lists usually have a readable string representation:val scores = listOf(75, 90, 82)println("Scores: $scores")Output:Scores: [75, 90, 82]Use joinToString() when you want a custom format:println("Scores: ${scores.joinToString(", ")}")Output:Scores: 75, 90, 82You can customize it further:println( "Scores: ${scores.joinToString( separator = " | ", prefix = "[", postfix = "]" )}")Output:Scores: [75 | 90 | 82]Filtering Values During InterpolationExpressions inside ${...} can include collection operations.Get halo’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inTo print only scores greater than 80:println( "Scores greater than 80: ${ student.scores.filter { score -> score > 80 } }")Output:Scores greater than 80: [90, 82]Using Kotlin’s implicit it parameter, we can make it shorter:println( "Scores greater than 80: ${ student.scores.filter { it > 80 } }")For output without brackets:println( "Scores greater than 80: ${ student.scores .filter { it > 80 } .joinToString(", ") }")Output:Scores greater than 80: 90, 82Property Access and Function Calls Inside String TemplatesConsider the following statement:println( "New Student is ${newStudent.name.uppercase()} and has scores $newStudent.scores")This statement contains two different forms of interpolation:${newStudent.name.uppercase()}and:$newStudentThey do not behave the same way.The expression with braces${newStudent.name.uppercase()}Kotlin evaluates everything between { and } as one expression:It accesses newStudent.It reads its name property.It calls uppercase() on the name.It inserts the result into the string.Given:val newStudent = Student( name = "Alex", scores = listOf(15, 25, 30))this expression produces:ALEXBraces are required because this is more than a simple variable — it includes property access and a function call.What happens with $newStudent.scores?In this part:$newStudent.scoresKotlin interpolates only the simple variable immediately following $:$newStudentThe .scores portion is treated as ordinary text.Because Student is a data class, $newStudent calls its automatically generated toString() function. The complete output might therefore be:New Student is ALEX and has scores Student(name=Alex, scores=[15, 25, 30]).scoresKotlin does not interpret $newStudent.scores as “read the student’s scores.”The correct versionPlace the complete property expression inside braces:println( "New Student is ${newStudent.name.uppercase()} and has scores ${newStudent.scores}")Output:New Student is ALEX and has scores [15, 25, 30]For custom score formatting:println( "New Student is ${newStudent.name.uppercase()} and has scores ${ newStudent.scores.joinToString(", ") }")Output:New Student is ALEX and has scores 15, 25, 30Without an expressionWhen you have a simple variable, braces are unnecessary:val name = "Alex"println("New Student is $name")Kotlin can clearly identify name as the variable to insert.The braced version is also valid:println("New Student is ${name}")However, the shorter $name form is normally preferred for simple variables.Use this rule:"$name" // Simple variable"${newStudent.name}" // Property access"${newStudent.name.uppercase()}" // Function call"${newStudent.scores.filter { it > 20

title: Building Type-Safe Navigation for Android & iOS in Kotlin Multiplatform (Part 6)
excerpt: Designing clean, type-safe navigation with shared ViewModel intents while keeping Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI navigation fully native. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin MultiplatformKotlinAndroid DevelopmentIOS DevelopmentMobile App DevelopmentBuilding Type-Safe Navigation for Android & iOS in Kotlin Multiplatform (Part 6)Kaushik KumarFollow15 min read·1 day agoListenShareDesigning clean, type-safe navigation with shared ViewModel intents while keeping Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI navigation fully native.Press enter or click to view image in full sizePrerequisitesThis article assumes basic familiarity with:Kotlin MultiplatformJetpack Compose and SwiftUIMVVM / Clean ArchitectureKotlin Flow and StateFlowIf you’re following the series, Parts 1–5 already establish the architecture used here.Navigation in Kotlin Multiplatform raises an important architectural question:Should navigation itself be shared between Android and iOS?Our application shares business logic, repositories, use cases, and ViewModels — but Android uses Jetpack Compose, while iOS uses SwiftUI.Trying to force both platforms through the same navigation implementation can create unnecessary coupling.Instead, we’ll use a simple principle:Share navigation intent. Keep navigation execution native. Shared ViewModel ↓ Navigation Intent ↙ ↘ ↓ ↓ Android Compose SwiftUI ↓ ↓ NavController NavigationStackThe shared layer decides what should happen.Each platform decides how navigation happens.What We’ll CoverShared Intent, Native NavigationType-Safe DestinationsNavigation EffectsSafe Argument PassingAndroid Navigation ComposeiOS NavigationStackBack NavigationDeep LinksNavigation TestingCommon Navigation MistakesComplete KMP Navigation ArchitectureWhat We’ll BuildBy the end of this article, we’ll have:Type-safe navigation destinationsShared navigation intentsShow List → Show Details navigationSafe argument passingAndroid Navigation Compose integrationSwiftUI NavigationStack integrationBack navigationDeep-link-ready architectureNavigation testingCommon navigation mistakesThe goal is not to share every line of navigation code.The goal is to create a clean navigation boundary between shared business logic and native UI.🏗️ Architecture DecisionNavigation intent belongs in shared presentation logic, while the actual navigation stack remains platform-specific.This lets Android and iOS follow their native navigation patterns without duplicating business decisions.✅ Quick RecapBusiness navigation decisions can be shared.Android owns NavController.iOS owns NavigationStack.Shared code should not know about either framework.Next, we’ll define our type-safe navigation destinations and see how a ShowDetail(showId) destination can travel from shared Kotlin to either native UI.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeDefining Type-Safe Navigation DestinationsThe first step is to stop representing screens as raw strings.Avoid:navController.navigate("show/123")Prefer a strongly typed destination:sealed interface NavigationDestination { data object ShowList : NavigationDestination data class ShowDetail(val showId: Long) : NavigationDestination}Now the shared layer can express navigation without knowing anything about NavController or NavigationStack.ShowDetail( showId = show.id)This gives us one semantic destination that both platforms understand.Android MappingNavigation Compose supports type-safe serializable routes.@Serializabledata object ShowListRoute@Serializabledata class ShowDetailRoute( showId: Long)Navigation becomes:navController.navigate( ShowDetailRoute( showId = showId ))No manually constructed route strings.iOS MappingSwiftUI can model destinations using Hashable values inside NavigationStack.enum AppRoute: Hashable { case showList case showDetail( showId: Int64 )}Then:path.append( AppRoute.showDetail( showId: showId ))🏗️ Architecture DecisionThe shared layer owns the meaning:ShowDetail(showId)Each platform maps that intent to its native route type.Shared Destination ↓ShowDetail(showId) ↙ ↘Android Route iOS RouteThis gives us type safety without forcing Android and iOS to share the same navigation framework.✅ Quick RecapAvoid raw route strings.Share semantic navigation intent.Android uses serializable typed routes.iOS uses Hashable route values.Keep platform navigation APIs outside shared code.Next, we’ll emit these destinations from the shared ViewModel using a one-time navigation effect.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeEmitting Navigation from the Shared ViewModelNavigation is usually a one-time action, so it should not live inside persistent StateFlow state.Use a transient effect instead.sealed interface ShowListEffect { data class OpenShowDetail(val showId: Long) : ShowListEffect}The ViewModel emits the effect when the user selects a show:private val _effects = MutableSharedFlow<ShowListEffect>() val effects = _effects.asSharedFlow() fun onShowSelected(showId: Long) { viewModelScope.launch { _effects.emit( ShowListEffect.OpenShowDetail( showId = showId ) ) }}The shared layer does not call NavController or modify a SwiftUI NavigationPath.It only emits intent.AndroidCompose collects the effect and maps it to a native route:LaunchedEffect(viewModel) { viewModel.effects.collect { effect -> when (effect) { is ShowListEffect.OpenShowDetail -> { navController.navigate( ShowDetailRoute( showId = effect.showId ) ) } } }}iOSSwiftUI observes the same effect and updates its native navigation path:for await effect in viewModel.effects {if let detail = effect as? ShowListEffectOpenShowDetail { path.append( AppRoute.showDetail( showId: detail.showId ) ) }}🏗️ Architecture DecisionUse StateFlow for screen state and SharedFlow for navigation effects.StateFlow→ What should the screen show?SharedFlow→ What should happen once?This avoids duplicate navigation when the screen is recreated.✅ Quick RecapNavigation is a transient effect.The ViewModel emits intent.Android maps intent to NavController.iOS maps intent to NavigationPath.Shared code stays framework-independent.Next, we’ll handle safe argument passing for showId.Press enter or click to view image in full sizePassing Navigation Arguments Sa

title: Android Keystore in Practice: Key Generation, StrongBox, and Biometric Binding
excerpt: Everything you need to know to stop treating the Keystore as a black box — with a working, biometric-gated encryption example Continue reading on Medium »
content: AndroidMobile SecurityKotlinAndroid KeystoreBiometric AuthenticationAndroid Keystore in Practice: Key Generation, StrongBox, and Biometric BindingAlim ReshitovFollow7 min read·1 day agoListenSharePress enter or click to view image in full sizeEverything you need to know to stop treating the Keystore as a black box — with a working, biometric-gated encryption exampleI spent eight years building and hardening the Android client of a banking app. In that time I’ve seen the Android Keystore misused in almost every way possible: keys generated without hardware backing on devices that support it, biometric gates that silently stopped working after a fingerprint re-enrollment and crashed the app in production, and — more than once — encryption “protected” by a key that any other app on a rooted device could have exported.This is the first article in a series on Android security, drawn from that experience. We’re starting at the foundation: the Android Keystore system. If you get this wrong, everything you build on top of it — encrypted storage, biometric confirmation, secure token handling — inherits the weakness.By the end of this article you’ll have a production-ready pattern for generating a hardware-backed, biometric-bound AES key, and you’ll understand the failure modes that don’t show up until your app has been in users’ hands for a few months.What the Keystore Actually Is (and Isn’t)The most common misconception: the Android Keystore is not an encrypted storage system. It doesn’t store your data. It stores cryptographic key material in a way that makes the raw key bytes unextractable from the app process — ideally backed by dedicated hardware.When you generate a key “in” the Keystore, here’s what actually happens:On devices with a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) or a dedicated secure element, the private/secret key material never enters your app’s process memory in raw form. Your app gets a reference (a KeyStore.Entry), and every cryptographic operation — encrypt, decrypt, sign — happens inside that isolated environment.On devices without hardware support, Android falls back to a software-backed implementation, where the key is encrypted at rest but operations happen in a regular process. Still better than storing a raw key in SharedPreferences, but a materially different security guarantee.On top of the TEE tier, Google introduced StrongBox (API 28+): a separate, dedicated secure element chip — physically isolated from the main SoC, with its own CPU, memory, and true random number generator. This is the tier banking apps should target when available.Knowing which tier you’re actually on matters, because “I used the Keystore” is not a security property by itself — you need to know which Keystore you got.Generating Your First KeyLet’s generate a 256-bit AES key for authenticated encryption (GCM mode). This is the workhorse pattern you’ll reuse for encrypting transaction metadata, cached tokens, or anything else that needs to live on disk.import android.security.keystore.KeyGenParameterSpecimport android.security.keystore.KeyPropertiesimport java.security.KeyStoreimport javax.crypto.KeyGeneratorimport javax.crypto.SecretKeyobject TransactionKeyProvider { private const val KEYSTORE_PROVIDER = "AndroidKeyStore" private const val KEY_ALIAS = "transaction_pin_key" fun getOrCreateKey(): SecretKey { val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance(KEYSTORE_PROVIDER).apply { load(null) } (keyStore.getKey(KEY_ALIAS, null) as? SecretKey)?.let { return it } val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance( KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, KEYSTORE_PROVIDER ) val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder( KEY_ALIAS, KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT ) .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM) .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE) .setKeySize(256) .build() keyGenerator.init(spec) return keyGenerator.generateKey() }}A few details that are easy to get wrong here:BLOCK_MODE_GCM only, never ECB. ECB leaks structural patterns in the plaintext — it's not authenticated encryption, and it has no place in a banking app.The key never leaves this function as raw bytes. generateKey() returns a SecretKey handle backed by the Keystore, not the actual key material — that's the entire point.The alias is per-key, not per-app. If you need multiple independent secrets (session token, transaction PIN, biometric-gated key), give each its own alias and its own KeyGenParameterSpec — don't reuse one "master key" for everything with different security requirements.Encrypting and Decryptingimport android.util.Base64import javax.crypto.Cipherimport javax.crypto.spec.GCMParameterSpecdata class EncryptedPayload(val ciphertext: String, val iv: String)object TransactionCipher { private const val TRANSFORMATION = "AES/GCM/NoPadding" private const val GCM_TAG_LENGTH_BITS = 128 fun encrypt(plainText: String, key: SecretKey): EncryptedPayload { val cipher = Cipher.getInstance(TRANSFORMATION) cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key) // Keystore generates a fresh, random IV val ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plainText.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)) return EncryptedPayload( ciphertext = Base64.encodeToString(ciphertext, Base64.NO_WRAP), iv = Base64.encodeToString(cipher.iv, Base64.NO_WRAP) ) } fun decrypt(payload: EncryptedPayload, key: SecretKey): String { val cipher = Cipher.getInstance(TRANSFORMATION) val spec = GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH_BITS, Base64.decode(payload.iv, Base64.NO_WRAP)) cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, key, spec) val plainBytes = cipher.doFinal(Base64.decode(payload.ciphertext, Base64.NO_WRAP)) return String(plainBytes, Charsets.UTF_8) }}Note that we never generate the IV ourselves — in ENCRYPT_MODE, the Keystore-backed Cipher generates a cryptographically random IV for you, and you must persist it alongside the ciphertext to decrypt later. Never hardcode or reuse an IV with GCM — reuse breaks the confidentiality guarantee entirely.Get Alim Reshitov’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for

title: MVI Architecture in Android with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose: A Practical Guide with Clean…
excerpt: Building a predictable, testable login screen with StateFlow, ViewModel, and a three-layer Clean Architecture — no third-party MVI library… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android DevelopmentKotlinJetpack ComposeAndroid ArchitectureClean ArchitectureMVI Architecture in Android with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose: A Practical Guide with Clean ArchitectureAkhil BodhadeFollow14 min read·1 day ago3ListenShareBuilding a predictable, testable login screen with StateFlow, ViewModel, and a three-layer Clean Architecture — no third-party MVI library required.1. IntroductionMost Android screens start simple. A text field, a button, maybe a spinner. Then a screen gains a loading state. Then an error state. Then validation. Then a retry button. Six months later, the same screen has four booleans, two nullable strings, and a bug where the error message and the success message somehow show up at the same time.None of that is a Compose problem, and it isn’t really a ViewModel problem either. It’s a state modeling problem. This article works through one way to solve it — MVI, built on Unidirectional Data Flow — using the smallest example that still has enough moving parts to be worth talking about: a login screen with email, password, loading, success, and error states.By the end, you’ll have a complete, runnable Android project (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, StateFlow, Clean Architecture, unit tests) and a clear sense of when this pattern earns its keep and when it doesn’t.2. Why UI State Becomes DifficultA login screen has more states than it looks like at first glance:Nothing entered yetUser is typingLoading (request in flight)SuccessError (invalid credentials)Error (network problem)Loading while a previous error is still visibleIf each of those is tracked as an independent var inside a Composable or ViewModel — isLoading, errorMessage, isSuccess, and so on — nothing stops them from contradicting each other. You can absolutely end up with isLoading = true and errorMessage = "Invalid password" set at the same time, because nothing in the code says they're related.The fix isn’t a new library. It’s discipline about two things:One state object, not several independent variables.One direction of flow — state always flows from the ViewModel down to the UI, and the UI never mutates state directly, only requests changes to it.That second point has an official name.3. What Is MVI?MVI stands for Model — View — Intent, but reducing it to those three words undersells what it actually gives you day to day. In practice, MVI is a way of organizing a screen around:A single, immutable UI State that fully describes what’s on screen.Explicit Intents (or Events) that represent everything the user can do.A state transformation step that takes the current state plus an intent and produces the next state.A ViewModel that owns this loop and exposes the state as an observable stream.The View never edits state. It only reads state and emits intents. That constraint is the whole point — it’s what makes a screen’s behavior traceable: every UI change can be explained by “which intent caused this.”4. MVI and Unidirectional Data FlowIt’s worth being precise here, because these two terms get conflated constantly.Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) is the architectural principle: state flows in one direction (down), events flow in the other (up). It’s a principle described directly in Android’s own architecture guidance — not something invented by any specific pattern.MVI is one common way to apply UDF to a screen: it names the pieces (State, Intent) and gives you a consistent shape to put them in.State flows down: ViewModel → UIEvents flow up: UI → ViewModelYou could implement UDF without ever calling it “MVI” — plenty of modern MVVM code does exactly that with a single UiState StateFlow and a set of event/intent classes. MVI is a naming convention and a discipline on top of UDF, not a separate flow direction.5. MVI vs. Clean ArchitectureThese two solve different problems and it’s worth keeping them mentally separate:MVI is about how a single screen manages its state and events over time.Clean Architecture is about how responsibilities and dependencies are separated across the whole app — UI, business rules, and data access.You can use MVI without Clean Architecture (a ViewModel that calls Retrofit directly). You can use Clean Architecture without MVI (a traditional MVVM ViewModel with several LiveData fields). This article combines them because they complement each other well, not because one requires the other.6. What We Are BuildingA single login screen:Email fieldPassword fieldLogin buttonLoading indicatorSuccess messageError messageAuthentication is fake — this is a demonstration project and does not implement production authentication. The “backend” is a repository that waits one second (delay(1000)) and checks the input against a single hardcoded credential pair:Email: test@example.comPassword: password123Anything else returns a failure. No passwords are stored anywhere.7. Project ArchitectureThree layers, each depending only on the one below it:Presentation ↓Domain ↓DataPresentation — Compose UI, LoginViewModel, LoginUiState, LoginIntent.Domain — LoginUseCase, LoginRepository interface. Plain Kotlin, no Android imports.Data — FakeLoginRepository, the concrete implementation of LoginRepository.The Domain layer doesn’t know Compose exists, doesn’t know StateFlow exists, and doesn't know whether the data comes from a fake, Retrofit, or Room. That's deliberate — it's what lets you unit test business rules without an Android runtime, and swap the data source later without touching anything above it.8. Login UI StateTwo reasonable shapes were considered.A flat data class:data class LoginUiState( val email: String = "", val password: String = "", val isLoading: Boolean = false, val isLoggedIn: Boolean = false, val errorMessage: String? = null)A sealed hierarchy:sealed interface LoginUiState { data object Idle : LoginUiState data object Loading : LoginUiState data object Success : LoginUiState data class Error(val message: String) : LoginUiState}The sealed version looks more “MVI” on the surface, but it has a real

title: Use Compose Multiplatform Components in a UIKit Scroll View (Without Losing Your Mind)
excerpt: Embed self-sizing Compose Multiplatform components in native UIKit and Objective-C scroll views on iOS, with a height-measuring pattern. Continue reading on Medium »
content: Compose MultiplatformIOSKotlinSwiftObjective CUse Compose Multiplatform Components in a UIKit Scroll View (Without Losing Your Mind)Embed self-sizing Compose Multiplatform components in native UIKit and Objective-C scroll views on iOS, with a height-measuring pattern.Vincenzo PascarellaFollow11 min read·1 day ago1ListenShareIf I had to describe a nightmare for an iOS developer who is passionate about SwiftUI, I would talk about integrating Compose Multiplatform components into scrollable views in UIKit + Objective-C. That sentence is only half a joke…Press enter or click to view image in full sizeKotlin + Compose Multiplatform + Swift Image by Vincenzo PascarellaCompose Multiplatform (CMP) is a genuinely great way to share UI between iOS and Android: you author a component once in Kotlin, and it renders natively on both platforms. On iOS, that component reaches you as a plain UIViewController, produced by Compose’s ComposeUIViewController { } factory.The trouble starts the moment you try to place that component inside a scroll view, in an app that is still mostly UIKit and Objective-C. Because a Compose view does not tell UIKit how big it wants to be. And in a scroll view, “how big do you want to be” is the only question that matters.This article is a practical guide to how I solved that problem. It is written for iOS engineers who know UIKit Auto Layout and have at least brushed against Compose. You do not need to know Kotlin and Compose deeply. Every snippet is generic, so you can lift it straight into your own iOS app.One app, two UI toolkitsPicture the app most of us actually work on: a mature codebase, years of UIKit, a good amount of Objective-C, screens built from UIViewController subclasses that push and present each other. Now the design system team ships a shared component in Compose Multiplatform, and product wants it live on iOS this sprint.On iOS, a CMP component is handed to you as a UIViewController. That is the entire public surface. You get a view controller, you add its view to your hierarchy, and Compose takes care of drawing and touch handling. From UIKit’s point of view, it is just another child.So far this sounds trivial. Add the child, pin its edges, done. It is not done, and the reason is a single missing method.The core problem: Compose has no `intrinsicContentSize`UIKit Auto Layout sizes a lot of views by asking them one question: what is your intrinsicContentSize? A UILabel knows how tall it wants to be for its text. A UIImageView knows its image dimensions. Auto Layout reads that intrinsic size and builds the layout around it.A Compose-hosted view does not answer that question. It has no intrinsic content size. It simply fills whatever space its parent gives it. That is fine when the parent has a fixed size, and it is a disaster when the parent derives its size from its children.Here is the chicken-and-egg problem in its purest form:The container asks the Compose view: how tall are you?The Compose view answers: as tall as you make me.Put that Compose view inside a UIStackView with .fill distribution, then put the UIStackView inside a UIScrollView whose content size is driven by Auto Layout, and “as tall as you make me” collapses to zero. The component renders into a zero-height slot, and disappears. No warning, no crash, just an invisible view.One clarification before we go on: if your CMP content is the whole screen, filling a dedicated scroll view on its own, that is a simpler and different problem. This article is about the harder and far more common case: a CMP component sitting as one child among native components.So the integration cannot be “drop it in and pin the edges”. The Compose side has to measure itself and report its height back, and the UIKit side has to turn that report into a constraint. That reporting contract is the whole game.The contract: Compose measures, Swift resizesThe fix has two parts. Kotlin measures its content and calls back with a height. Swift receives that height and writes it into a constraint. Let us wire both parts for a small example component: an expandable FAQ row that shows a title, and reveals a longer answer when tapped.On the Kotlin side, the component exposes an onHeightChanged: (Float) -> Unit callback and uses Modifier.onGloballyPositioned to report its measured height in dp:@Composablefun DisclosureRow( title: String, detail: String, onHeightChanged: (Float) -> Unit) { var expanded by remember { mutableStateOf(false) } val density = LocalDensity.current Column( modifier = Modifier .fillMaxWidth() // fill WIDTH only, wrap content vertically .onGloballyPositioned { coordinates -> val heightDp = with(density) { coordinates.size.height.toDp().value } onHeightChanged(heightDp) // report the placed height back to Swift } .clickable { expanded = !expanded } .padding(16.dp) ) { Text(text = title, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium) if (expanded) { Spacer(Modifier.height(8.dp)) Text(text = detail, style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium) } }}Two facts about this callback matter enormously, and they will explain every bug you could hit later:Get Vincenzo Pascarella’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign in1. The root fills width only and wraps its content vertically. The component’s desired height is its natural content height. When it expands, that natural height grows.2. coordinates.size.height is the “placed” height, not the “desired” height. Compose coerces a node into whatever constraints it is handed. If the host UIView gives the Compose canvas less vertical room than the content wants, the node is placed at that smaller, coerced value, and that smaller value is what gets reported.Hold on to point 2. “The callback reports the room it was given, not the room it wanted” is the key idea behind the entire design.The ComposeUIViewController wrapper forwards the callback so the component can cross into iOS as a view controller:

title: Lazy initialization in Kotlin
excerpt: In Kotlin, lazy initialization is a design pattern that delays the creation of an object or computation of a value until the exact moment… Continue reading on Medium »
content: KotlinLazy InitializationInitializationInitialization ObjectLazy initialization in KotlinMuhammad Ali DevFollow3 min read·1 day agoListenShareIn Kotlin, lazy initialization is a design pattern that delays the creation of an object or computation of a value until the exact moment it is first accessed. If the property is never accessed during the application lifecycle, the initialization code never executes, saving memory and CPU cycles.It is implemented using the by lazy property delegate.1. Syntax and Basic Mechanismby lazy takes a lambda block containing the initializer code.Kotlinval heavyResource: HeavyClass by lazy { // Initialization block println("Initializing HeavyClass...") HeavyClass()}Key Rules:Read-Only (val): lazy can only be used with val properties, not var.Thread-Safe by Default: The initialization block is thread-safe out of the box.Cached Result: The lambda block executes only once. The result is cached and returned on all subsequent calls.2. Step-by-Step Execution FlowTo understand how lazy initialization operates at runtime, trace this sequence:Kotlinclass DatabaseManager { // Step 1: Property declaration (Not initialized yet) val connection: String by lazy { println("Connecting to Database...") "DB_CONNECTION_SUCCESS" }}fun main() { val manager = DatabaseManager() println("DatabaseManager instance created.") // Step 2: First access to 'connection' println(manager.connection) // Step 3: Second access to 'connection' println(manager.connection) }Execution Steps:Property Declaration: When DatabaseManager() is instantiated, memory is allocated for the delegate object, but the internal code block inside lazy { ... } is not executed.First Property Read (manager.connection):The delegate checks if the underlying variable has been assigned a value.Finding no cached value, it executes the lambda block ("Connecting to Database..." prints).The return value ("DB_CONNECTION_SUCCESS") is assigned to an internal hidden backing field.The value is returned to the caller.Subsequent Property Reads:The delegate sees that the backing field already holds a cached value.It bypasses the lambda block entirely and directly returns the cached string.3. Thread Safety Modes (LazyThreadSafetyMode)Kotlin provides three thread-safety modes for lazy, which can be specified via parameter: by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.MODE) { ... }.A. SYNCHRONIZED (Default)Locks the initialization so that only one thread can execute the lambda block at a time. Safe for multi-threaded access.Get Muhammad Ali Dev’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inKotlinval data: String by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED) { fetchRemoteConfig()}B. PUBLICATIONAllows multiple threads to execute the initialization lambda simultaneously, but only the first returned value will be cached and used by all threads.Kotlinval data: String by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { fetchRemoteConfig()}Use case: When initialization is safe to run multiple times in parallel, and you want to avoid lock overhead.C. NONEDisables thread-safety entirely. No locks or synchronization mechanisms are used.Kotlinval data: String by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) { computeLocalSetting()}Use case: Single-threaded environments (e.g., UI thread-only objects). Provides slightly higher performance by avoiding synchronization overhead. Warning: Undefined behavior if accessed concurrently from multiple threads.4. How It Works Under the HoodWhen compiled to Java bytecode, Kotlin generates an instance of Lazy<T>. For the default SYNCHRONIZED mode, it creates a SynchronizedLazyImpl object:kotlin// Simplified representation of compiled Kotlin bytecodeclass DatabaseManager { val connection: String by lazy { // Your initialization code here }}Inside SynchronizedLazyImpl, double-checked locking is performed:kotlinval value: Any? get() { val _v1 = this._value if (_v1 != UNINITIALIZED_VALUE) { return _v1 } synchronized(this.lock) { var _v2 = this._value if (_v2 == UNINITIALIZED_VALUE) { _v2 = this.initializer!!() this._value = _v2 this.initializer = null // Clears memory reference to the lambda } return _v2 } }Note: Once initialized, Kotlin clears the initializer lambda reference to free captured objects from memory.5. lazy vs lateinitFeatureby lazylateinitVariable TypeMust be val (read-only)Must be var (mutable)Data TypesAny type (primitives, objects, custom classes)Objects only (No primitive types like Int, Boolean)Initialization MethodDelays computation via a lambda blockAssigned imperatively later via explicit code (x = value)Thread SafetyThread-safe by default (SYNCHRONIZED)Not thread-safeNullabilityCan hold nullable types (String?)Cannot be nullable (String)6. Common Memory Leak PitfallBecause by lazy captures references inside its lambda, keeping a long-lived lazy delegate inside an object with a shorter lifecycle can lead to memory leaks.Kotlinclass Fragment : Component() { // DANGER: If 'this' (Fragment) is destroyed, the lazy block might still // reference the Activity context if captured improperly. val adapter by lazy { MyAdapter(requireContext()) }}Best Practice: Ensure any context or object captured inside the lazy closure does not outlive the class declaring the lazy property.

title: We Tested the 3uTools Android App — Here’s What Every Android User Should Know
excerpt: For most users, when you mention 3uTools, the first response is managing iPhones on a Windows device. For years, we felt the same way… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Android3utoolsTechnologyMobile AppsAndroid TipsWe Tested the 3uTools Android App — Here’s What Every Android User Should KnowThe 3uTools DeskFollow3 min read·1 day agoListenShareFor most users, when you mention 3uTools, the first response is managing iPhones on a Windows device. For years, we felt the same way. Moreover, we were obviously checking out the newly found features, and this made us realize that 3uTools has an Android application as well, so we instantly downloaded it on our Android Phone and tried to figure out what actually works.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeWe did not want to just read feature lists; we wanted to experience the app. We took it for a spin, and aside from our surprise when using the main tools, there was so much more. If you have an Android phone and you wish to track down your device easily and clean storage, do check out the 3uTools Android app.First ImpressionsEasy installation, with a simple interface appearing as soon as we opened the app. The home screen is organized simply, making the tools available easy to find rather than getting tangled up in cumbersome menus.Unlike many other Android utility apps that usually include a single-function gimmick, this one packs a good number of useful features in one place. That makes for easier, everyday device management.Exploring the Main FeaturesWe took some time testing each major function to see how it performs out in the wild.Data MigrationData Migration is something that interested us right away.For those who are upgrading an older Android phone to a newer one, the app offers a straightforward method of transferring all supported data between compatible Android devices. It is intuitive, as it clearly identifies the sending and receiving phone.This feature is useful and could potentially save time for those people who are upgrading to a new Android device, rather than sifting through the files one at a time.Device InformationThe Device Information page was one of our favorite features of the application.Before, you had to click through several different Android settings pages, but now we could easily see information like:· Battery information· Storage usage· RAM status· CPU activity· Android version· Device modelGet The 3uTools Desk’s stories in your inboxJoin Medium for free to get updates from this writer.SubscribeSubscribeRemember me for faster sign inHaving everything in one place is great, and checking out the phone’s overall health is a breeze.Phone SlimmingIf we use phones, storage is slowly filled with downloaded files and media in the form of photos, videos, and temporary data.Phone Slimming scans the device and arranges useless files in specific folders. This is a lot easier than trawling through folders to find out what you can safely delete.Mobile AcceleratorMobile Accelerator was another that we tried out; it helps curtail memory usage by controlling background applications.Although modern Android devices already come with memory management built right into the OS, having a dedicated optimization tool bundled in the app ensures that refreshing your device is just a tap away when it starts to feel sluggish.Our Overall ExperienceWhen testing out the application, we discovered it was lightweight, fast, and rather surprisingly useful.It doesn’t attempt to baffle users with higher-end technical choices. Rather, it zeroes in on the tools that almost all Android users use in day-to-day life: monitoring device info, wiping storage, boosting speed, and transferring supported types of data.That straightforward method makes the program accessible to both new and expert Android users.Who Should Try It?We think the 3uTools Android app is a good choice for:· Android users who will be on a new phone.· People who want to free storage space.· Individuals who want to track battery and hardware information.· Anyone looking for a lightweight Android management application.· Users already using the 3uTools Windows version.Final ThoughtsOur experience of testing the 3uTools Android app helped us understand how useful it could be in everyday use for your Android devices. Not intended to completely replace the mighty Windows build of 3uTools but acts as a companion app for those times when you only need some handy maintenance tools accessible straight from your phone.If you’re interested in seeing every feature with real screenshots, detailed explanations, and step-by-step guidance, we also created a complete 3uTools Android guide on our website.We’d love to hear about your experience as well. If you’ve already tried the app, which feature do you find most useful?
